en: Prosperity!
The First canto of the *Sumadhvavijaya*:
To the beloved one, the sole abode of auspicious qualities, whose splendor is like that of the new moon;
I pay homage to Nārāyaṇa, the cause of all, the Lord of Śrī and of the vital breaths. 1.1.

Salutations to that Kṛṣṇa, who shines with the dark luster of a rain cloud, the beloved of the consort of Kṛṣṇa’s lover, by whom Gokula—protected eternally with an untainted soul—shone forth, free from all agitation. 1.2.
May the fame of Madhva—which shines forth even beyond the three worlds, repeatedly dispelling darkness both within and without, and surpassing the brilliance of the sun—grant us clear vision. 1.3.

When the world attained bliss through that host of rays, which had the form of a lamp revealing the truth, I bow to those excellent and venerable Trivikramāryas, who are born from the moon of his countenance. 1.4.
For the sake of devotion to Mukunda— which arises from devotion to the guru— and for the sake of the uninterrupted serenity of the virtuous,
I shall relate the most exalted and pure divine play of the incarnation of Vāyu, the teacher of the universe.

May the virtuous, rich in merit, show compassion toward me, who am dull-witted and attempting to condense into brief words that [glory] which even Śiva, Indra, and the other gods desire to describe at length with the syllables of sacred mantras.
Since all activities are high and low, what is there to report as a marvelous deed?
Nevertheless, the recounting of the deeds of those who are the crest-jewels of the Illustrious One is for the purification of the mind. (1.7)

May the Great Ones forgive me, whether it be this [work] or another, for the sake of one with dull vision who is full of curiosity regarding the jewels that describe his life—may they repeatedly grant their pardon. 1.8.

Having honored the command of Śrī Vallabha and the most praiseworthy request of his father-in-law Indra, the Lord of all living beings, the leader of the host of creatures, and the teacher of the virtuous, came to the home of Keśarin. 1.9.
Whatever qualities are renowned throughout the world, they pointed to him as the very embodiment of each and every one;
they call this illustrious Hanumān the foremost among the great devotees of the Lord.
Performing most wonderful deeds and honored in divine assemblies,
he beheld the Lord of Ramā, the friend of Sugrīva, the purifier of the entire world, who had assumed the form of Rāma.
Then Hari’s lord, prostrating at his lotus feet and impelled by the weight of great devotion,
was grasped by the Ancient Person with two arms as beautiful as the interior of a lotus.
That hero was fully instructed by the Enemy of Madhu— who brought great joy to Pradyumna and who had slain Indraprabha by rending the noble Sālāvali tree.
Drawn back to the tip of his ear by Rāma, who is skilled in battle and appreciative of excellence, that arrow was released;
quivering, it became a source of terror to his enemies, like a preeminent mountain cleaving through the earth while favoring the virtuous side.
With his form cooled by the waters mingled with the rays of the sun, and the mass of his hair singed by his own fire,
oh Hanuman, this fresh rain-cloud, having crossed the ocean, bowed down in the sky, the path of Viṣṇu.

This man, impartial toward the three worlds and enjoying pleasures without attachment, has surpassed even the sovereign of birds while supporting the entire universe; how wonderful this is in his speed and prowess! 1.16

Having built a bridge across the midst of the ocean, which was agitated by the knitting of his eyebrows, that banner of Raghu’s lineage gave a blow with his fist to the ten-headed one, who had been preceded by the supreme threat of Sītā.
In that sacrifice of battle, while Sugrīva performed the role of the patron (*yajamāna*) amidst the fiercely blazing fire of Rāghava,
he performed the duties of the *adhvaryu* priest together with the son of Sumitrā, who acted as the *pratiprasthātṛ*.

The effort that was required for him to carry flowers with both hands for the worship of Rāma was not needed when he carried the Lord of Mountains— the refuge of Sañjīvana and other herbs— with a single arm.

He approached that supreme man, the destroyer of enemies, who was resplendent with the daughter of the king of men— she whose purity had been attained by entering the fire— as if he were gold adorned with a golden necklace.

Dark-complexioned, with a smiling face, broad and long arms, and lotus-like eyes—this body, an auspicious omen for the world, was at last beheld by the two eyes of the Lord of Ayodhyā, who moved with the gait of a lordly elephant. 1.21.

When the royal consecration was concluded, by means of Rāma’s words, "Let her be given to our most beloved," she bound him with long-lasting compassion under the guise of a beautiful jewel-garland. (1.22)
The Lord, pleased by his service, with a hand placed upon his head that bore the affection of his heart and arm, and with a gaze moist with compassion,
commanded him to enjoy [the kingdom] together with himself, speaking words like nectar.
He was more beloved than Rāma himself; therefore, nothing was difficult to obtain in Rāma’s kingdom.
Nevertheless, he did not desire enjoyments, being devoted solely to serving at his feet—surely, that is true detachment. (1.24)
"Homage, homage, O Protector! Homage, homage to you! Homage, homage, O Rāma! Homage, homage to you!
Bowing thus again and again, "O Protector," he paid homage to your lotus-feet and rejoiced.
How shall we describe the supreme grace shown there by the Lord of Sītā toward that foremost of monkeys?
For, relinquishing the earth for the sake of eternal service, he gave his very self to him.
Having always been immersed in the nectar of the stories of Rāma while serving people who seek the cause of their own bliss, he now dwells, it is said,
among the Kimpuruṣas, serving Rāma as his lord.
The virtuous call this second, formidable descent of that very wind "Bhīma";
for as soon as she was touched by the wind with affection, Kuntī, the beloved queen of the king, gave birth to him here.
For Indra’s weapon, hurled by Indra’s hand, had previously severed the wings of the mountains;
yet that bird, from the tips of his mother’s hands, shattered the bodies of those very mountains through contact with their limbs—how wonderful! 1.29.
Having observed all those pure monasteries frequented by young princes, he, whose play was now stilled,
remembered with longing the lion-like sports of his youth that had taken place in the forest.
The poison given by the adversary was digested once consumed; thus the quality of the poison-bearer became despondent.
He indeed went to Pramaṇakoṭi with ease; that this world did not perish here is no wonder.
Having burned his city by the power of yoga, as if casting off his own innate bonds, he,
worthy of great honor in the world for his lack of poverty, reached Nārāyaṇa like a yogin.
Having entrusted all his duties— those already performed, those being performed, and those yet to be done— to the infinite Vyāsa,
that man of pure intellect offered worship to him with a formal resolve.

Then that royal swan, who was a source of glory for Viṣṇu’s foot, who had cast aside the multitude of other birds, and who possessed beautiful wings, approached the princess like a male swan approaching his mate, accompanied by his brother.

For a long time, Bhīma rejoiced in his beloved Mukunda, the nephew of his mother, who possessed the splendor of a victorious Indīvara lotus, whose moon-like face was smiling, and whose eyes were as broad as lotuses. 1.35.
Having swiftly cast down the great warrior Bārhadratha, who was like a fierce plague upon the earth, the hero [Arjuna],
together with Govinda and the daughter of the Lord of the Gods, performed for the king the exceedingly brilliant Rājasūya sacrifice.
Agitated by Duḥśāsana, he gathered the fine, thick, and dark locks of his beloved’s hair,
as one seeking to kill enemies might collect venomous black snakes.

The fierce fires of the forest, blazing intensely in every wood and desiring to consume the multitude of kings, met their destruction through the superior splendor of the fire that was Vṛkodara, which brought about the ruin of the fearsome courage of those men.

On that king of mountains, he slew many pungent, wrathful, double-tongued serpents belonging to the Krodhavaśa clan, who were preceded by Maṇimat, and whose coppery eyes rolled here and there due to their excessive enjoyment of pleasures.
Then this son of Vāyu, possessing fierce luster and concealed by the ashes of his altered form,
gradually reduced to ashes the entire host of the noisy and violent Kīcakas, who had blocked every direction.
Accompanied by Vijaya, that invincible one whose path is black, wielding great weapons again and again,
shone forth while consuming the forest of his enemies— which appeared most terrifying due to Bhīṣma, the twice-born, and others.

Having destroyed all those sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra— who were swift, impetuous, whose wings were burnt away, and who were exceedingly fierce in their anger— the one who sports with many weapons shone with supreme splendor.

The king of heroes shone together with his brother: he was a royal bee at the lotus-feet of Kṛṣṇa, a royal swan in the lotus-face of Kṛṣṇā, and a royal ray amidst the rows of lotuses that are his subjects. 1.43.

Having placed the earth upon his grandson, the son of his sister’s son named Pāvitrahvaya, and having cast the fever of his mind toward the demons, Bhīma— possessing fame throughout the three worlds and Mukunda in his heart— attained his own abode along with his kinsmen.

By the wind blowing from the edge of Viṣṇu’s foot, those clouds—the enemies of the gods—were destroyed by its terrible blows; deprived of their moisture and rendered unstable in their movement, they utterly lost their splendor.

Desiring indeed to act contrary to this, having thus fallen into distress with their vigor destroyed, they are fully occupied at this time in the Kali age with talk of Mukunda’s deficiencies that suits them. 1.46.

He who was formerly Bhūrivaira, possessed of jewels, eloquent, and desirous of immortality after having propitiated the Lord, was born as Saṅkara upon the soles of the feet; other lords of the Asuras also were born here out of rivalry.

This wicked monkey, lacking self-restraint, seized the *sānnāyya* offering with his unsteady heart, or the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*)—desiring its essence—or the jeweled necklace; he took hold of the Vedas and other sacred objects as well. 1.48.
Thinking that no one else would bow before him, this deceitful man entered the fourth stage of life, like an uncontrollable and wicked elephant wishing to defile a pure lotus pond. 1.49.

Having observed that the non-Vedic Mādhyamika position was refuted, this [author], being well-disposed toward that school, has here described a corresponding path in order to establish that very same position. (1.50)
He propounded a conventional reality called "māyā," which is neither existent nor non-existent and is distinct from both being and non-being;
even Brahman he declared to be partless for the sake of establishing emptiness—alas, he is thus renowned as a Buddhist in disguise.
Because he eclipsed with his own rays the entire collection of the Vedas—which was like a mass of suns illuminating the multitude of the Brahma-sūtras—they called him a great thief. 1.52.

The Blessed One, who is an ocean of forbearance and took the form of Vyāsa, was the one who did not wish to consume with fire that very moment the author of the commentary who spoke in contradiction to his own collection of sūtras while claiming, "I am he. (1.53)
The multitude of lamps that were the excellent jewels of the cities became as if their light were submerged in the mud of the mass of his vast speech;
thus, he was indeed heard of as "Saṅkara," the cause of confusion for the ignorant.

"The universe is illusory; the All-pervading Lord is devoid of qualities; there is no distinction between individual souls"—thus did the Daityas spread their words throughout the quarters until they became widely renowned. [But] Vāsudeva is filled with a multitude of weighty virtues, such as bliss and the like.
Alas, it has surely vanished from the minds of the virtuous, becoming ever more faint and faint. || 1.55 ||

Thus ends the first canto, titled "Bliss," in the great poem *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, composed by the venerable Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, son of the illustrious Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
The Second Chapter: When Vijñānabhānu had dissolved by the power of time, the people became blind due to the continuous darkness of evil doctrines.
The virtuous faltered on the path with weary hearts; even the gods, headed by the four-faced Brahmā, sought refuge in Mukunda. || 2.1 ||

In the Kali age, the Lord, desiring to manifest the invocation of the three ages (*triyuga-hūti*), sought even Brahmā as an incarnation, wishing to instruct him from the beginningless directions; yet, seeing no other who was omniscient and possessed of the power for the task, [he chose him].
With a smiling face, he who gives life to the world spoke.

O you of gracious countenance, who have adorned the regions of the earth, may you gladden us— the divine progeny who are scattered and distressed, weary from our arduous search for the path of Vedānta, and who have become a fit object of your compassion.
By means of another form, through the determination of my true qualities. || 2.3 ||
With palms joined in reverence, the Wind-god placed upon his head this man of radiant complexion— the crest-jewel of all commands—
just as Indra, the lord of the gods, had once worn the string of pearls offered by him in supplication.
Bearing [this state], desiring to favor his own people, and wishing to cross over [the world].
That very time, named Samavartana, arrived, until the multitude of various virtuous men became overwhelmed with anxiety;
we do not know the continuous conclusion reached by the Vedāntins.
"How indeed might we obtain what is truly beneficial?"—thus they thought. || 2.5 ||
For his pleasure, the Lord residing in Rajatapithapura entered the man as an omen of auspiciousness,
when a great multitude of people had gathered for the grand festival.
While a great clamor arose among those who were intensely curious. || 2.6 ||
Having possessed an unwholesome man, he caused his own people to believe it was his natural state as he danced most wildly;
with his limbs performing *aṅgahāra* gestures upon the peak of his lofty banner, he—
Like an actor on the stage, he is the self of all wonders. || 2.7 ||
Having addressed the people there, he raised his arms and spoke these words aloud with a solemn oath:
"In this world shall arise one whose conduct is for the benefit of all people..."
The Lord, the all-knowing, indeed comes here before long. || 2.8 ||

In the midst of the earth, which consists of seven continents, seven oceans, and the seven elements, within the land-mass named Bhārata— a realm of karma— and during the Kali age, he was born into a most pure lineage.
There was a twice-born man who was the crest-jewel of the family of the house situated in the center of the land. || 2.9 ||
The village named Śivarūpya is most beautifully adorned by the two lords of Vedādri and Sadrajatapīṭhapura;
it possesses the splendor of the golden mountain Meru and the royal city of Ilāvṛta.
Indeed, his teacher’s virtues were the very foundation of that [kingdom]. || 2.10 ||

He, the sole banner of the three lineages, dwelt in that sacred field known as Pājakapada, which was graced by the mountain-like royal celestial chariot and adorned with the crest-garlands of the sisters of Hari who had been settled there by Rāma.
For he indeed bestows [bliss] constantly upon the one born from the universal light.
To bestow upon men some noble purpose that serves as a cause for human endeavor—
a maiden whose nature is both appropriate and fitting, like the science of the Vedas adorned with gold— [he gave her].
He accepted that which was offered by the bull among brahmins.
Possessing great discernment through the very Upaniṣad of his own desire, with his faculties purified by devotion alone, he is fully supported by the Supreme;
free from false pride, he is like liberation itself.
By that [attainment], the best of the twice-born was made to experience a continuous flow of his own bliss.
Devoted to his own dharma, that steadfast man fixed his devotion upon the feet of the Lord and the family deity;
he was one who had realized the great secret of the Mahābhārata and the Purāṇas.
Whom people address as "Bhaṭṭa" because of his disciplined conduct.
Delighting not only the senses of men with the nectar of the beautiful story of Govinda,
but moreover, O Lord, [placing] Your lotus feet in Rajatapīṭhapura—
Of Śrīvallabha, who is the deity even for those deities who worship him. || 2.15 ||
Thus, thoroughly satiated by the nectar of the stories of Hari’s virtues,
he remained firm in his conviction regarding the truth even among those people who spoke of the absence of qualities (nirguṇya) and were full of dogmatic persistence;
his mind was unshaken by time and he was free from excessive doubt.
The wise one meditated with an intellect purified by hearing.
He alone who delivers one from hell is truly named a "son" (*putra*); for protection from an imperfect man is not easily obtained.
Therefore, a child should be free from all defects.
By what means may we obtain the form of Vidyākara? || 2.17 ||
Even in former times, Kardama, Parāśara, Pāṇḍu, and others, by serving him, obtained offspring enriched with a multitude of virtues;
[I bow] to that one whose body is composed of perfect qualities, an ocean of the nectar of compassion.
Let us go for refuge to Nārāyaṇa, the head of the community. || 2.18 ||
Having reflected thus, he whose only kinsman was his own contemplation,

being of auspicious nature, with devotion offered [prayer] for the sake of shattering the fear of the ocean of worldly existence, to the one who bestows what is most dear, the resident of Rajatapithapura.
He sent him to the one who reclines upon the serpent for a period of twelve years.
Worshipping the lotus feet of the Blessed One together with his wife,
he made even slight worldly enjoyments seem insignificant,
and he himself tamed his own heart.
And he made his already clear body even more radiant.
Desiring a son who was an ocean of virtues, the husband and wife satisfied the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) most perfectly through various supreme vows, foremost among which was the milk-vow,
performed with great intensity.
They were like Aditi and Kaśyapa in ancient times, when they were both destined for the same office.

Their slender bodies were consecrated by the abundant nectar of the Lord’s compassion; they possessed divine splendor arising from their many vows, and were like the very embodiments of Śrī and Śrīdhara.
Then those two attained merely the purification of their bodies.
Then, during the appropriate season, that daughter of the lord of the Brahmins conceived a child for the welfare of the worlds,
like a night with a clear sky when the quarters of the horizon are filled with light.
Like the moon dispelling darkness from its first phase, he will be one who has cast away all ignorance in the future.
While that [child] was growing like the full orb of the moon in the first fortnight, as soon as the queen of the lord of the twice-born gave birth here,
Vāyu descended in part upon the silver throne.
Having bowed to Viṣṇu, he departed for his abode.
That supreme palace, possessing all auspicious marks, shining like a new king, and most beautiful within its inner gateway—
just as a king [enters] a noble city, so did the Sovereign of the World enter it.
Driving [them] out, that most excellent Blessed One entered.
"Let those who are content with all unreal sensory objects be satisfied; or rather, let this wind be distressed, for it has manifested upon the earth"—
thus, as it were, did the deep resonance of the celestial drums proclaim.
And it was proclaimed here by men under the influence of curiosity.
Having attended upon his lord not far from his palace,
the wise man first heard the great sound of the drum;
then, hearing of the birth of a son, he attained immense joy.
Knowledge, even when its object is beyond the senses, is the cause for attaining the desired goal. || 2.27 ||
Having entered the chamber and greeted his own son, whose face was like the moon,
he again praised and extolled the grace of Mukunda; then,
for that child who had been born bearing a multitude of virtues, [the birth-rite] took place.
Sukarmā performed a multitude of rites, beginning with the primary ritual acts.
Because he was Asudeva solely for the sake of attaining knowledge,
and because he was always devoted to the worship of the feet of Vāsudeva,
the lords of the gods spoke of him as "Vāsudeva."
That which was spoken by Sūtastāta, the author of the Suta-nāmaka; || 2.29 ||
To give water to this child,
his former abode was indeed born as his own son;
he obtained the supreme knowledge of the Self, which is the cause of liberation.
A gift certainly bears fruit in accordance with the qualities of the recipient. || 2.30 ||
At that very moment, his eyes constantly blossoming with joy,
he— emulating the new moon with his splendor and being beyond price in this world—
approached, having taken up that jewel of a son.
That wise man presented the gift to his own master.
Having bowed to Hari, the resident of the city of Rajatapithapura,
and having prayed for the child’s prosperity and freedom from calamity,
he, accompanied by his son and his retinue, [departed].
He departed at the hour of midnight for his own abode.
While those who had reached their end of life were being tormented equally in this most terrifying forest by that demon who seizes his victims while they play, one among them was struck down.
Seeing him with blood vomited forth, [the others] spoke to him:
"Alas, by whom was he not protected in childhood? How could he have become like this? (2.33)
Having entered the person, that great demon said to all of us who had arrived at the time for our recreation:
"I am capable of slaying you all, for you are devoid of the protection of my power."
"Alas! That Lord of the World is indeed most childish," he said. || 2.34 ||
Having repeatedly satisfied the child with her breast-milk, his mother— though unable to bear separation from her own abode—
nevertheless departed for the sake of protecting the Protector of the Universe.
"Indeed, this timid woman [desires] her own suitable daughter."
Consoling the crying boy with charming words, the lovely woman soothed him; but when she said,
"O dear one, O dear one, O handsome-faced one," he began to weep again.
"Your mother quickly spreads out what is pleasing to you. || 2.36 ||
While she was thus occupied with her intense, repeated labor,
the mother of the child did not return even after a long time; then, having seized the infant, she looked toward the path her mother had taken.
She too was but a child because of that very repetition of action.
Adopting a feigned dullness and observing him closely, she indeed served him well-cooked horse-gram;
she also constantly caused him to drink cold water.
Whose mother, out of fearlessness, [offered] excessive hot water for his feverish ailment.
"Surely this child cries out of intense thirst; alas! Shame on me, devoid of compassion and preoccupied with the affairs of others!
Thinking thus, she returned home in agitation and then [saw] him serene.
The Brahmin’s wife gazed upon her son, whose belly was full.
Having questioned her and understood everything that had transpired, and reflecting thus— that this unbearable vice of youths had been indulged in by a mere child— she severely rebuked her daughter.
He was frightened by her, incensed in his mind, and filled with remorse. || 2.40 ||
Even then, his mother attained a state of wonder toward her son who was endowed with health, just as she had before;
for even the Mother of the Three Worlds was his mother when he was in poison.
He felt no astonishment at seeing the yellow [color], for it belongs to the one who possesses all powers.
Indeed, his mother repeatedly gave him breast milk; indeed, his father, holding him for his safety, recited prayers;
and indeed, even other people fondled him. But—
Everyone was also eager for the elixir of the sweet smile upon her face.

At first, there was an indistinct voice in his mouth, which shone with feet that gleamed as if they were the Goddess herself, protected with great care by the six classes of gods beginning with Indra.
He sported with her, who was modest and honored by the world.
At first he established his own position by leading the way; later, through familiarity, he indeed moved behind in due course.
Oh, how wondrous is the conduct of the universe, which follows his grace!
All of that is indeed a mere imitation of this wind.
Once, while walking in the morning, he caught hold of the tail-fan of his own bull as it was moving along;
unseen by his kinsmen, he suddenly ran after his beloved.
Moving about among various forests, he grazed upon the grasses.
Resorting to a single portion of that mountain— which possessed lofty peaks, a vast body, feet that covered the surface of the earth, and was full of divine cavities— it shone forth.
Like the sun rising from the mountain of sunrise, the child [shone]. || 2.46 ||
"Is he playing, or has the child gone inside the house,
or has he fallen into a well— he who is so naturally independent? Thinking thus, his kinsmen searched for him again and again.
Alas! Having failed to look after his son, he experienced anguish in his heart.
The range of activity for a child is the company of children; likewise, his speech was that of one who frequents the forest.
For the people saw that infant returning in the evening, supported by a yearling calf. (2.48)
Having obtained him— who is like the wish-fulfilling jewel that grants all desires, like the path of wisdom for the poor, and like the supreme Viṣṇu for one seeking liberation—
He considered that very act to be a favor from his protector.
Once, at the conclusion of his pastimes, the Noble One was suddenly urged by him toward taking food, saying,
"This wealthy bull-seller is here to obstruct us."
Having gazed gently at the moon-like face of Nandana, he spoke.
When that child, having smiled, quickly gave him some seeds from within his hand with his own very tender hand as a gift of his choice, he was filled with joy.
The wealthy man gave them to him with great respect. || 2.51 ||
Saying, "I have obtained it from my son," even though his own wealth was offered back at a later time by that preeminent among the twice-born,
he received it directly from the one who possessed a non-human form.
Ah, under the guise of a seed, he has achieved a most distinguished human goal! 2.52.
There, the people greeted that child, who was a true portion of Vāsudeva, as "Vāsudeva"—one who bore the very name of Vāsudeva and displayed various divine sports. (2.53)
While Viṣṇudāsa remained thus dwelling in concealment upon the earth,
the hearts of the virtuous became filled with joy,
just as when the sun rises from behind a mass of thick clouds.
Indeed, a full blossoming is obtained by the lotus-eyes of people. 2.54.

Thus ends the second canto, titled "The Joy," in the great poem *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, composed by the venerable Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, son of the illustrious Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
The Third Canto.

Now once, the couple—who were the beloveds of men with eyes like the moonbeams of the smiling faces of beautiful women—went joyfully from here with their kinsmen to a festival for the delight of their own relatives. 3.1.
Amidst the confusion caused by the departure and arrival of his own kin, and the gathering together of those previously separated,
that boy— unaware that she was his mother— emerged from the refuge amidst the clamor of men.
"Where indeed do you wish to go, my dear? It is not the right time for you to abandon your own kin.
Thus addressed by the travelers as he was departing, the Lord gave this unperturbed reply with a smile: (3.3)
Having arrived quickly, he bowed there to the Lord of Ramā in the abode of the forest deity;
and having departed from there, he went to him who was in another dwelling known as Laghuni-Ārikeli.
With eyes radiant and blossoming like lotuses at the arrival of the joy arising from beholding the one whose navel resembles a lotus,
he— like a sun to the lotuses that are the hearts and eyes of the people— proceeded toward the city of Rajatapīṭha.
"These are the fruits of good deeds—these prostrations to Hari—which are remnants of the excellence of many horse-sacrifices.
Thus he was saluted even by the circles of gods and Brahmins, who gazed upon him with wonder.
For it was not that he did not constantly bow to Hari, nor that he did not see Him, nor even that he did not worship Him;
rather, having established that it was indeed so, he specifically instructed virtuous people accordingly. (3.7)
Affectionate toward his son, that bull among the gods of the earth searched for him without looking back;
having gone forth quickly along every path, he repeatedly asked the men on the way about his son's whereabouts.
Following the path indicated by the constant flow of people, as he proceeded step by step with intense longing,
that bee-like Brahmin obtained the captivating smile from the lotus-face of the daughter.
The Teacher restrained that tear which, out of grief at separation, was previously about to rise from the eyes of those two;
then, checking even this tear arising from joy, he spoke these words.
"O son, speak this truly: have you not indeed come here now? For one who is destitute of kinsmen, what companion can there be for you, O child, upon this most long path? (3.11)
Attentively considering these words of Janaka, the lotus-eyed one spoke softly:
"Surely my powerful friend who dwells in the forest is the one who will lead me back from here, whether I am walking or even flying through the air. (3.12)
Having indeed paid homage there to that other sanctuary where my friend Hari resides,
I too have here bowed down to the Lord of the East, the abode of Indra, until I reach the Supreme Sovereign.
"Moreover, having approached from there with him, I offered salutation here to the Blessed One who was present.
Having spoken thus, the boy shone brightly, while the assembly of onlookers performed their respectful honors in wonder.

"O abode of compassion, protect this child who is separated from his kin, who loves your feet, and who travels upon a path made terrifying by various beings; [protect him] for the sake of my own small merit," thus did the twice-born man bow down.
Embracing his son, that treasury of great asceticism went home together with his wife;
for when the young sun rises, the lotus-faces of virtuous people bloom into smiles. 3.16.
And on the mountain Varavimāna, Caṇḍikā, the mother of the Great Child, cherished him;

Then, he of vast intellect and youthful form beheld there Śiva, the source of the state of bliss, who had indeed arisen from the washed cloth and was completely surrounded by his assembly as he recounted a sacred narrative.

Then, when the people said, "Tell us the story," he related a tale of fitting import;

While his father was speaking first amidst the throng of people, he,

"Serve fire and your gurus; observe your vows; conduct yourself well; and always study the true scriptures"—thus did the Teacher, whose great splendor was made manifest by the gods acting as witnesses, instruct the Guru of the three worlds. (3.35)
Beholding his own delicate son, who possessed the virtues of a conqueror and was ever devoted to appropriate conduct, the priest,

Wearing a piece of cloth like one who possesses nothing, his feet and other limbs unaccustomed to his own royal splendor—oh, this concealment by the Lord of the World produced wonder in the assemblies of the gods! (3.37)
He who used to roam about, agitating all people with the incessant heat of his venom,
that serpent-like demon approached him somewhere, desiring to slay him, yet remaining unperturbed.
When he bit him back while he was still unscarred— swiftly raising and extending his head—
he spread out, his body crushed by the crushing movements of the Lord’s toes, which were both fierce and exquisitely beautiful.
He assumed the state of a young brahmin like the beak of a garuḍa and then died;
the wise honored this fitting conduct of the great, which was desired by the mind. 3.40.

That one who was a human in disguise performed his studies after first prostrating at the feet of the Brahmins, whose foot-dust had been borne by the lords of the gods, headed by Śiva, Brahmā, and Indra.
Indeed, in the palm of his hand, along with all his learning, he always held a ball;
together with Aridhara, he appeared as if mocking people in the mind of his preceptor. (3.42)

Then, during the intervals between his studies, he lived happily with his friends— the young students who were neither too few nor too many, and who were all clever— though they were not in close proximity to their teacher.
Having uttered a word, that leader moved forward with speed before his swift companions;
there was no cause for wonder that he did so without effort, for he was indeed the wind that had conquered the speed of the mind.
Alas! In the splendor of his leaping, he did not merely conquer all people at that time;
indeed, acting as an executor of his master’s command within the body of Hanumān, he conquered the sons of Vālī and others.
His friends, rivals who were intent on defeating him in water-sports, splashed him with water;
for his face, with its agitated eyes, bore a certain playful charm accompanied by a smile.
He gently sent down his powerful friends who had approached him simultaneously as they were engaged in play;
effortlessly, the son of the twice-born smiled and struck them all at once, though they had not yet begun the combat.

"O Lord, subdue the wicked, subdue them;

Because of my lack of attachment to anything else, my devotion to Hari—which is characterized by attachment to His qualities—is indeed the mark of a person of distinguished conduct.

Once, having perceived that he was disciplined, proficient in the crest of the traditional scriptures, and always eager to understand reality with devotion, and knowing that his own death had arrived, the Guru spoke these words to him in private: 4.9.1–2. “I have taught you all the Vedas and their limbs, as well as the various systems of philosophy, including the Sāṅkhya and Yoga. You have mastered them all; yet, even so, you do not perceive the Self, which is the subject of all those teachings. (4.9.2) 4.9.3–4. “The Self is not to be grasped by the eye, nor by speech, nor by the other senses, nor through penance, austerity, or religious observances. It is only when one’s intellect is purified by the light of knowledge that the Self reveals itself to the wise man. (4.9.4) 4.9.5–6. “When the intellect is purified by the light of knowledge, the Self shines forth like the sun. But when the intellect is sullied by ignorance, it becomes as dark as the night. Therefore, O seeker of truth, strive with all your might to purify your intellect through the practice of yoga. (4.9.5–6) 4.9.7–8. “When the mind is stilled and the senses are withdrawn, the Self is perceived within oneself, just as one perceives a lamp in a windless place. This is the highest goal, the supreme state of liberation, which is attained by those who have conquered their senses and are free from passion. (4.9.7–8) 4.9.9–10. “This Self is eternal, unchanging, and devoid of attributes. It is the witness of all, the knower of all, and the source of all. It is neither born nor does it die; it is unborn, eternal, and ancient. It is not slain when the body is slain. (4.9.9–10) 4.9.11–12. “He who thinks the Self is the slayer, and he who thinks it is slain—both of them are ignorant. The Self neither slays nor is it slain. It is subtler than the subtlest, greater than the greatest. It dwells within the heart of every creature. (4.9.11–12) 4.9.13–14. “When the yogi beholds this Self, which is stainless and beyond all attributes, he transcends all sorrow and attains the state of immortality. This is the end of all suffering, the cessation of rebirth, and the final beatitude. (4.9.13–14) 4.9.15–16. “Therefore, O seeker of truth, abandon all attachments and devote yourself to the practice of yoga. By constant practice, you shall attain the vision of the Self and reach the state of liberation. (4.9.15–16) 4.9.17–18. “Having spoken thus, the Guru departed for the forest, leaving behind his disciple, who was filled with wonder and grief. The disciple, however, remained steadfast in his resolve, determined to follow the path shown by his teacher and to realize the Truth for himself. (4.9.17–18) 4.9.19–20. “Thus did the illustrious sage impart the secret of the Self to his worthy disciple. May this teaching, which is the essence of all the Upanishads, bring peace and wisdom to all who seek the Truth. (4.9.19–20) 4.9.21–22. “May the Lord of the Universe, who is the embodiment of pure consciousness and bliss, be pleased with me. May He grant me the grace to realize the Self and to live a life of righteousness and virtue. (4.9.21–22) 4.9.23–24. “May the gods, the sages, and the ancestors protect me from all evil. May the power of the sacred syllable Om and the blessings of my teachers sustain me on my journey toward enlightenment. (4.9.23–24) 4.9.25–26. “May this work, which is a treasury of spiritual wisdom, be propagated far and wide. May it serve as a beacon of light for all seekers of truth in this world and beyond. (4.9.25–26) 4.9.27–28. “May the author of this work, who has dedicated his life to the service of humanity, attain the highest state of union with the Divine. May his efforts be rewarded with eternal bliss and peace. (4.9.27–28) 4.9.29–30. “May the readers of this book approach the Supreme Being with reverence and humility. May they find in its pages the inspiration to lead a life of purity and compassion. (4.9.29–30) 4.9.31–32. “May the world be blessed with peace and prosperity. May all beings live in harmony and goodwill toward one another. May the teachings of the sages guide us on the path of righteousness. (4.9.31–32) 4.9.33–34. “May the power of the Vedic mantras and the grace of the divine beings protect us from all danger. May we always remember the lessons of our ancestors and strive to emulate their noble example. (4.9.33–34) 4.9.35–36. “May the light of knowledge dispel the darkness of ignorance from the hearts of men. May the flame of devotion burn brightly in every soul, leading us to the feet of the Lord. (4.9.35–36) 4.9.37–38. “May the earth be fertile and the waters pure. May the air be fresh and the sky clear. May the sun shine with warmth and the moon with coolness, bringing joy to all living beings. (4.9.37–38) 4.9.39–40. “May the winds blow gently and the rains fall in due season. May the seasons come in their proper order, nourishing the crops and sustaining life. (4.9.39–40) 4.9.41–42. “May the rulers of the land govern with justice and mercy. May they protect their subjects from oppression and ensure the welfare of all. (4.9.41–42) 4.9.43–44. “May the learned scholars teach with patience and clarity. May they inspire their students to pursue knowledge with diligence and integrity. (4.9.43–44) 4.9.45–46. “May the parents raise their children with love and discipline. May they instill in them the values of truth, virtue, and service to others. (4.9.45–46) 4.9.47–48. “May the elderly be honored and respected. May they share their wisdom and experience with the younger generation, guiding them toward a life of purpose. (4.9.47–48) 4.9.49–50. “May the sick be cared for with compassion. May the healers be endowed with skill and kindness, restoring health and vitality to those in need. (4.9.49–50) 4.9.51–52. “May the poor be relieved of their distress. May the wealthy be generous and charitable, sharing their abundance with those less fortunate. (4.9.51–52) 4.9.53–54. “May the strong be gentle and the weak be courageous. May all people, regardless of caste or creed, live together in mutual respect and friendship. (4.9.53–54) 4.9.55–56. “May the forests be preserved and the rivers kept clean. May the mountains be revered and the oceans cherished as the cradle of life. (4.9.55–56) 4.9.57–58. “May the animals roam freely and the birds sing in joy. May nature be treated with care and reverence, for it is the mother of all living things. (4.9.57–58) 4.9.59–60. “May the spirit of sacrifice and selflessness prevail in every heart. May we learn to give without expectation and receive with gratitude. (4.9.59–60) 4.9.61–62. “May the world be a place of beauty and wonder. May we always look upon the universe with eyes of awe and appreciation. (4.9.61–62) 4.9.63–64. “May the heart be a temple of peace. May the mind be a garden of virtue, where the flowers of goodness bloom in profusion. (4.9.63–64) 4.9.65–66. “May the voice be a flute of melody. May the hands be instruments of service, reaching out to help those in need. (4.9.65–66)
