Then, having approached his preceptor and propitiated him, this teacher of the world— having been graced by the favor of the best of gods,
the Lord of the Suras— though he always partakes in all stages of life, specifically honored the stage of the householder.

Having performed the entire collection of rites according to the method of the rules for the proper time, he repeatedly offered the placement of all [mantras] solely for the sake of pleasing Lord Hari, who is ever-pleased. (4.31)

The wise declare that which consists of the accumulation of the *praṇava* preceded by three measures and ending with an infinite measure; at that time, he assumed the form of the future four-faced Brahmā, and the ascetic qualified for its recitation was indicated. 32.

"Wise in knowledge, elevated in accordance with his virtues"—this was the name by which he, who was honored by throngs of brahmins and possessed of vast fame, was called; for he was not merely one whose complexion was like that of a mantra, but he was truly one whose very appearance was that of a mantra.

Beholding him wearing the *dhṛtāṣāḍha* bark garment—devoid of bodily ointment, free from facial cosmetics, yet serving as an ornament that adorned the world itself—living beings perceived that his natural beauty was beyond compare. (4.34)

He bowed to those ascetics who were preceded by their gurus—ascetics who were like serpents, lords of beings, and birds on foot, waiting for the opportune moment; oh, how great is the mockery of the great! 4.35.
Desiring to instruct him in the specific practices of the excellent stages of life (āśrama), and observing his conduct,
the Lord of Ascetics, whose intellect was steadfast, attained a special instruction himself and experienced wonder within his vast heart.
When the Great-minded One joyfully bowed to the Lord who dwells in the silver throne,
he was immediately grasped by the arm of that serpent-reclining one who had entered the human body.
"Since you have long served me with the desire to awaken to the true reality, I shall grant you the fruit thereof";
having said this, he then led him away and bestowed it upon that one whose self is Acyuta.

Having respectfully accepted that favor with joy and remembering the sense of fulfillment he had attained, he—though naturally unattached—became closely associated with him; for indeed, association with the virtuous is the ornament of non-attachment.
When the sage of vast mind, bowing again and again and entreating for permission, desired to go to his own riverbank, the Guru,
his heart distressed by the fear of the fire of future separation, thought only of his Master.
"On the third day from now, the river of heaven will come to our lake for your sake;
therefore, you must not depart. Thus did Hari, the compassionate one, speak to him at that time, having entered [the lake] in some form.
At his command, the people bathed there in the waters of the Ganges along with Pūrṇabuddhi;
thereafter, for twelve years, she who was marked by his grace would always return.

When ten days had passed in brief, having reached the excellent hermitage adorned with leafy branches, he conquered the victorious scholars led by the one named Vāsudeva, who were harsh in their many arguments. (4.43)
Then, as his teacher desired to make his own disciple clever, he began to listen to the instruction;
for even by this great-souled one, who was indifferent, the ocean of quibbles and fallacies was mastered for the sake of attaining his desired goal.

When the Guru declared that the circle of faults present in the first verse of that work—consisting of two sets of sixteen—had been cast out from above, the student said to him, "Please explain it further. (4.45)

While the Lord of Vows was thus speaking with indignation, "I have no capacity for such preaching as yours," even among those men who were present at that assembly of Māyā, the sprout of doubt regarding his censure arose. (4.46)

A wise man, desiring liberation for himself, should certainly listen to this teaching; one who is not yet wise, and especially an ascetic, should do so because of the exhortation of the world. Thus the one of perfect intellect proclaimed this doctrine of Māyā.

People rich in learning, clever, and desirous of knowledge, eagerly sought to hear his teaching—which was presented without flaw, free from doubt, possessed of a traditional lineage, and characterized by firm arguments—and to meet with him. 4.48.
Once, while five or six twice-born men devoted to hearing were writing and reciting the Bhāgavata in many ways in the presence of their guru,
the Lord firmly declared one particular method.
When it was asked, "Since other possibilities are also possible, how is your determination in this matter reached?
Mukundabodha spoke from his great heart, clearly explaining one possibility brought about by the Blessed One. (4.50)
"Let the prose be recited right here, if you know the state of the works of the Teacher of the World.
When the best of ascetics spoke thus, he whose heart was full [of devotion] spoke in accordance with what had been said.
Then, by his command, all the disciples examined every single book for the sake of testing him;
yet, alas, as he set aside one particular volume, he did not mention that entire collection of chapters.
When he was told, "How is it that this which you have not studied in this life appears so victorious?",
Amitabuddhi replied, "For in previous births, I indeed knew all of this."
Thus, as his mind was occupied with many kinds of wondrous thoughts, his fame— though new— spread throughout the world;
like the radiance of the sun, it thoroughly dispelled the pervasive darkness.
Like moonlight that brings joy to the multitude of white water-lilies that are virtuous people.

Thus ends the fourth canto, titled "Bliss," in the great poem *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, composed by the venerable Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, son of the illustrious Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
The fifth canto:
While the venerable Guru was resolving to install him in the governance of his own kingdom of Vedānta knowledge,
that one of vast intellect was first consecrated with waters drawn from lotus-filled pools.

He who composed the excellent scriptures that bestow bliss upon the wise who regard him as a vessel for the Supreme Being whose nature is bliss, became truly worthy of the title "Ānandatīrtha" (The Ocean of Bliss) bestowed upon him by his guru. 5.2
Once, a mendicant friend of Govindabuddhi, surrounded by many disciples, arrived there;
at that time, his disciples, who had been trained in inference, became arrogant and sought to defeat their teacher’s intellect. (5.3)
"The distinction [between the two] is easily established"— this inference, which was employed by them as a swift terror for their opponent,
was clearly shattered by him of unimpaired intellect, who was skilled in defining the subject, just as the cosmic Virāṭ devours a serpent.

Furthermore, they asserted that "the object of dispute is false because it is an object of cognition, like something free from dispute"; by this, the inference was stated that "the object of dispute is real because it is an object of cognition, like a jar and so forth. (5.5)

When they, full of curiosity, quickly declared that there was no over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the reason and were thus free from astonishment, he defeated them by saying such things as: "The silver in a mother-of-pearl shell and the like are not considered [real] silver; that which is perceived otherwise is [merely] so perceived. (5.6)

Whether the truth was real or unreal, when he spoke an inference regarding it while being himself unable to establish its foundation, he defeated all the learned scholars in the assemblies; thus, by his very name, he attained the status of an "inference-tirtha. (5.7)

He who was the first to arrive here, a lion among disputants, traveling upon this earth with the desire for debate and capable of crushing the elephants of all the lords of speakers—him, the ocean of wisdom, [I salute]. 5.8.

Desiring to conquer that man who was arrogant due to the fortitude of his thighs, Mukundadhi quickly took up a sharp arrow from the quiver within the monastery by means of the hand of his disciple—an arrow skilled in finding its mark and seeking the path of the auspicious *tīrtha*. (5.9)
Observing the race of men hastening forward, agitated by curiosity regarding their claims to victory,
he of most profound intellect approached and paid homage to his Guru, who was seated upon an excellent throne of silver.

In the midst of the circle of scholars, that confident man repeatedly shattered the profound speech of the lion of debaters with sharp, concise, and swift words, like a mallet struck by an arrow. (5.11)
Feeling resentment, he pondered intensely on some matter in eighteen ways;
meanwhile, people began to doubt the victory of the conqueror of the world, though his mind was already full [of success]. (5.12)
Then, swiftly shattering millions of conceptual constructions, the one of vast intellect shone forth with a smiling face,
like the sun, having resorted to the pure rays of light and the eternal abode of Viṣṇu, dispelling the masses of darkness.

The one born from the jar of the Great Lake (Agastya) indeed made even the ocean of intellect—profound within himself yet exceedingly haughty, and who had cast aside the entire multitude of Sarasvatīs—seem light. 5.14.
"Let the debate take place tomorrow," said one; "If it seems fit, let the reply be uttered," said the other.
When Mādhava spoke thus, the two were defeated by the people, who concluded from their fleeing at night that they were not wise.

"Ah! This man, without any effort, has in a mere moment attained the glory of victory long earned by that preeminent disputant who roamed the earth with an ocean of intellect"—thus were the people utterly amazed. (5.16)
Once, surrounded by people expert in logic, he explained a commentary composed of jewels;
Sammodatīrtha, with a smile of amusement, spoke words that bestowed joy upon the gods.
When the existence of the six systems has been investigated and the underlying intentions of their respective commentaries have been discerned by those of purified intellect,
alas, no venerable common lineage between these two is seen, for they have suppressed their fierce and hidden dogmatism toward one another.

While he was speaking thus and repeatedly pointing out powerful defects in this commentary, these [opponents], though their minds were filled with wonder, could not steadfastly remove those [objections] despite their efforts. (5.19)
"Let the higher meaning of this Sūtra be stated, which you dismiss as mere commentary.
"That which cannot be refuted in any way by poets such as yourself," said these eloquent men. (5.20)

Then he took up that loud recitation, which followed a sequence of unblemished words and expressed the possible meaning of the sūtras; it was a momentary director for the *tāṇḍava* dance of the future narrative, wherein the Smṛtis were joined with the authoritative Vedic tradition.

Whether people had come desiring to learn and free from envy, or whether they had come with a desire for victory and full of envy, he repeatedly brought about their defeat through this method of argumentation—those who were experts in sacred learning as well as great logicians. (5.22)

On one occasion, that noble and excellent man, gentle-minded, became gracious toward him even though he had been made dejected by some cause; for alas, a virtuous person, greedy for the ocean of good qualities, becomes pleased. (5.23)
With his eyes as cupped palms, he constantly drank the imperishable nectar of splendor residing within the vessel of Nanda’s body;
and that wise man, with the hollows of his ears, drank the nectar of knowledge filled in the great jar of his speech.

During a playful debate with his teacher on the occasion of the Teacher of the World, when such a circumstance had arisen, the teacher addressed him with a challenge: "O knower of the meaning of the Sūtras, compose a Bhāṣya correctly! (5.25)
Then that supreme king of swans took up only the pure water, leaving aside the turbidity;
for the virtuous are satisfied with even a fraction of a quality, just as they disregard water that is devoid of its fruit.

Once, with great devotion, Jyeṣṭha— a renunciant born of the Likuca lineage, endowed with the qualities that adorn the state of a paramahaṃsa, such as dispassion, frankness, and eloquence— spoke to him.
If this commentary and other works are in contradiction with the excellence of the established conclusions of the Vedānta, what loss is there?
Tell us, however, the meaning intended by the Sūtras and the Upaniṣads, which is appropriate for the wise. (5.28)

When this [work], called the *Vyākhyā*, which illuminates the station of Viṣṇu, shone forth with its speech full of auspiciousness like the autumn season, then the moonlight of the moon-like face of Pramodātīrtha was revealed. (5.29)

Once, it is said, as he set out toward the quarter protected by Yama intending to conquer it, accompanied by Acyutabuddhi, he paid homage to Viṣṇu—the auspiciousness of the world—adorned with perfect wisdom and the blessing of Viṣṇu. (5.30)

When the giver of alms had repeatedly offered and eaten a heap of plantain fruits for the sake of testing him, the Guru spoke in private to that best of noble men, who was filled with irresistible wonder at his effortless [attainment]: (5.31)

"O Bhikṣu, although your slender belly was filled with more than two hundred fruits that were gathered and consumed at the end of your alms-round, how is it that there is no heaviness in it? O one of noble mind, tell me the truth. (5.32)
"Know that my Jātavedas, the size of a thumb, is established within the stomach, blazing brightly;
it is eternally beneficial and consumes all things. Thus he spoke then, "He whose mind is the Lord of All. (5.33)

Having passed through various regions and doctrines— abounding in many confused streams of eloquence, yet supported by logic and endowed with diverse meanings— that one of beautiful intellect proceeded by his desired path.

Seeing on the road a milch cow, worshipped by brahmins, which had effortlessly cast down a multitude of kings, which bestowed purity of intellect, and which served as the ornament of Kerala, he remembered the future Caṇḍikā.
Then, proceeding by degrees, he arrived at and paid homage to the Lord of Śrī,
who has the beautiful luster of a blue lotus, whose navel is like a lotus, who reclines upon the serpent, in the city of the eternal Ananta.

This one, the foremost among those who know the final truth, expounded the Vedānta-sūtras for his circle of disciples in the assembly, repeatedly establishing that the Brahman known as Acyuta is an ocean of qualities and distinct from the multitude of individual souls. (5.37)

"An excessive mixture arising from the addition of new, unmeasured ingredients, which leads once again to hostility—this is a great transgression," Asūyu said here, "for there is no scriptural authority for those who have not composed a commentary on the meaning of the aphorisms. (5.38)

"If we were to compose a commentary here, it would appear as a mere rebuttal; for the creative work of the Teachers of the World is not to be obstructed by force. At these smiling words of his teacher, all the people rejoiced. (5.39)
When the Lord was described by the wise as one whose body was endowed with all the marks of a Great Man,
even those who were excessively corpulent there offered praise only for his buttocks.

He presented the buttock-girdles in full number according to the rules of the manual; however, he made them hear the breaking of that staff, for such is the nature of the wicked when they are unable [to endure it]. (5.41)
Having bathed here in the sacred fords— specifically at Kanyakātīrtha, Sutīrtha, and Sukhatīrtha—
and having immersed himself at the ocean-setu, he offered salutations to Viṣṇu as Śrī Rāmanātha.
Seeing that Asura approaching in the guise of an ascetic, he [the King] laughed and spoke aloud:
"O fierce one, if your staff were not broken by you, you would be a eunuch, a fool, and one whose speech is barren. (5.43)

Then, bowing with shame and seeking his own welfare, that wicked man was ignored by the leaders of the twice-born who were arguing, "Who here would hate that wise man who gladdens the world with the moon of his face? (5.44)
Whatever subjects were proposed by various men, clever in their learning, in assemblies during their gatherings,
in each and every one of those sciences that radiant Lord of Knowledge appeared and conquered them.
Unshaken by the fickle and weak-willed of the wicked here below,
that high-minded teacher dwelt for four months like a lion who has entered his cave, unmoved by dogs.

Having arrived, the one of profound intellect paid homage to the God who is an ocean of erotic sentiment, who reclines upon the serpent Śeṣa, whose dwelling is Śrīraṅga, who bestows blessings upon the virtuous, and who is served by the daughter of Kavi (the Ganges), the Himavat (the Gaṅgā), and the wind (the Yamunā). 5.47.
Then, having turned back and bowed to the Supreme Person, he wandered through various shrines;
illuminating the northern quarter with his superhuman splendor, he proceeded there by degrees. (5.48)
Then, being gazed upon from all sides by people with eyes wide with wonder,
he of most auspicious form reached the finest villages on the banks of the Payasvinī river and entered a certain temple of the gods.

Having studied the scripture with its six limbs according to the Dharma, those best of the twice-born— endowed with the determination to discern and describe its meaning— sought that unprecedented Person, renowned throughout the world for its salvation.

People came in great numbers, desiring to see him who had a beautiful smile, lotus-like eyes, a golden complexion, and exceedingly gracious speech— who, though devoid of ornaments, was the ornament of the entire world.
He acts like a sun in eclipsing the stars of the dull-witted through the brilliance of his lightning-like wisdom;
he acts like a lion in shattering the frontal globes of the elephants of evil disputants with their fallacious arguments;
and he acts like a lotus in gladdening the night-lilies of the eyes of the world with his flickering glance.
He shone, his body serving as the ornament for the circle of the assembly, with his own bliss as his sacred bathing place.

Thus ends the fifth canto, titled "The Joy," in the great poem *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, composed by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, the son of the venerable Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
The sixth canto: Then, indicating a certain hymn of Aitareya, that most venerable one in the assembly spoke thus,
as the gathering desired to hear from the blessed ones the nature of that hymn.
His pronunciation— possessing the excellence of perfect phonation, neither too hurried nor lacking in measure, endowed with exceedingly beautiful marks,
and possessing the deep resonance of a cloud-charged heart— conveyed its meaning with full clarity.
By virtue of being endowed with these characteristics, this speaker surpasses even the deities and the teachers;
yet, although they conceived it as "pride" in their minds, they spoke that well-said verse for the sake of another purpose.
It may be so; yet know that even in the Vedas, which possess meanings possible in this manner, there is a threefold purpose, while the *Daśārṇa* possesses ten purposes.
Indeed, the *Bhārata* may even have a hundred purposes, for the *Vaiṣṇava-padasahasra* possesses a thousand purposes. 6.4.
When he of expansive mind had thus spoken, the Brahmins here, desiring to conquer him, said with smiling faces: "Let a hundred meanings of the names of Hari be described. (6.5)
"I shall describe all of that to you; because of its excellence, may you repeat it after me.
As he spoke thus, they replied, "So be it," and attained a resolve of extreme firmness.
Having demonstrated the method of the combination and dissolution of suffixes and roots as prescribed by the science of grammar,
the one of pure intellect immediately set forth the categories of all things as established by the hundreds of Upanishads.
As long as this man, free from hesitation, continued to compose hundreds of verses of praise until he had completed them,
they remained with their hearts agitated, for their minds were weakened by the restraint they had described.
Though they were highly proficient in the Vedas with their auxiliary branches, well-trained in the Itihāsas, and exceedingly bold,
they did not accept these words spoken [by him], just as hosts of demons do not accept the nectar churned from the ocean at the destruction of the world.
"Your eloquence is easily attained among the gods; what talk can there be with fickle mortals?
Forgive us, O gentle one, you who know all things; salutations to you!"—saying this, they indeed bowed down before him.

At another time, the noble-minded one reached another sanctuary built by those born in the excellent region of Kerala—men who were masters of the Vedas and Shastras, seekers of knowledge and wealth, and who had acquired everything in its entirety. (6.11)
Alas, he mocks even those men who are skilled in logic and treatises, for they lack true authority.
How then could he not humble the pride of those assembled here from the lands of Niṣadha? 6.12

Thus those excellent brahmins, having heard from the mouths of men born in other lands, deliberated and questioned him regarding the meaning contained in the hymns that praise the giving of the True Dharma and condemn its withholding.
Making that [meaning] clear and manifest, he spoke of the verbal root *pṛ*, the source of the word;
then the sage, desiring to conquer him, spoke to him as he was uttering the verbal root *prī*.
"O fool, ignorant of the distinctions of vowels and consonants, practice your collection of scripts by scratching them in the dust!
Thus rebuking him, that man of beautiful smiles laughed, stupefying those whose minds were clouded by envy. (6.15)
Through the power of that association, those broad-minded ones awakened to proficiency in all branches of knowledge;
they bowed with great respect to him whom the hosts of gods indeed revere.

While the beauty of the body of Indra, who was honored by the maiden [Śacī], was being described with excellent hymns and words pleasing to the heart by the Dānava, someone in that assembly remarked, "Apālā is exceedingly youthful. (6.17)
"An expert who insists that 'the one denoted by the word "leper" (śvitrin) is she' will come here; ask him about this," he said, and having spoken thus, he departed. (6.18)
"Ah, one of such appearance and perfected intellect has arrived in this land before long!"—
thus he spoke to them regarding the state of that venerable one, just as it was told there by the crest-jewel of sages.
Not only did these broad-minded men believe that all his words were preceded by the full knowledge of the Vedas,
but they also placed their trust in his perception of both the past and the future.
Whatever subject was immediately presented, he understood it all instantly;
thus, in the assembly of all the learned, he became renowned as "the All-Knowing One. (6.21)
Although he had not traveled to every land, he pervaded the entire world with his fame, which was a kinsman to the night-lotuses that are virtuous men;
for, like the full moon with its pervasive moonlight, he was fully endowed with vision through his own widespread renown.
Performing the rite of salutation to the Lord of Indirā amidst the beautiful clusters of celestial abodes, the one of profound discernment finally attained Mukunda, the Lord of Rūpyapīṭha.
Her form was clearly endowed with the abundant wisdom of the most eminent of the twice-born;
her limbs were radiant, and she was beautifully adorned with a necklace of brilliant gems, having become the ornament of the entire world.

Illuminated by the manifestations of beautiful verses and poetic meters, rich with the excellence of clear syllables, providing a fitting covering for those who uphold the best of the *Bhārata*, and possessing a splendor of exceedingly melodious tones. (6.25)

She whose discourse centered on the Rājasūya sacrifice and other noble rites, whose heart was fixed upon the virtues of Vāsudeva, who was skilled in instructing in all duties, and who was honored by the people like a mother; (6.26)

In the assembly, the deceitful and wicked person, pained by the gathering and removal of his followers, utterly abandons the great path of justice even while seeking to establish his own lordship. 27.

Though pulled from the auspicious path by a few very wretched people through the power of the Kali age, she was seen by some with great sorrow, even as they disregarded the pain of being dragged away. (6.28)
She repeatedly cried out in a loud voice, "O Vāsudeva! O Supporter of the Earth! O Lord!
while holding in her heart that unborn one who possesses the six perfections in their fullness, who is free from all defects, and who is entirely distinct from everything else.
"O wise ones, surely let her be restrained! Alas, alas! This is not the Dharma!"—thus she spoke, though she was most cherished by Kṛṣṇa, blameless, having no other refuge, and longing for protection.

Having personally seen that collection of scriptures, which was like a sacrificial altar in ancient times, he—the foremost of the Bharatas, an ocean of compassion whose intellect was mature—composed this work of firm resolve for the subduing of the wicked faction. (6.31)
Desiring to distance himself from wealth— even that most excellent kind— as one would distance oneself from constant consumption,
he composed a commentary on the *Bhagavadgītā* and offered it to his venerable elder.
To the logician Viśaṅkaṭabuddhi, who was seeking permission to go to the Tīrtha,
Puruṣottamatīrtha granted it, while reflecting upon the protection of Puruṣottama.
Free from dust, praised on earth for its course through the Malaya region, and always followed by swans,
that portion of the wind traveled toward the northern direction, dispelling the heat of virtuous travelers.

The one of unflagging intellect thoroughly purified both kinds of sacred sites on earth—those rich in collections of stones that purify the intellect and those born from [divine] waters—simply by immersing himself in them. 6.35.
Constantly devoted to the feet of Vāsudeva, having surpassed even Śiva by his splendor,
and possessing fame that destroys all sins, he then completely overcame the torrent of the Gaṅgā.

Moving here and there, he reached the vicinity of Badarikāśrama, which is within the range of men, bringing to them the manifold wonders of the three worlds that bestow happiness through mere remembrance.
To him who was the supreme Nādirāyaṇa-pada, adorning the entire Bharatakhaṇḍa, the one of abundant intellect offered obeisance and presented this commentary on the *Harigītā* as a gift. 6.38.

To his delight, having cleared away the crowd and reciting an excellent discourse before him, that man of great renown spoke according to his ability: "I shall declare the true nature of the *Urukrama-gītā*. (6.39)
"For this reason as well, you are indeed capable of even the subtle; since you have not stated everything, the phrase 'in brief' (leśataḥ) was uttered here by the Creator of the World. (6.40)

When that teaching had been set forth, even the disciples who were already well-versed heard it sufficiently; "Let it be spoken! they cried repeatedly, while Hari struck the earth with his foot, saying, "Aha! (6.41).

Having discerned that distinction in sound, he whose mind was free from delusion, knowing the inner state of the Supreme One whose body was seated near the image, rose up and delivered a discourse to them.
He performed his ablutions daily at the time of sunrise in the cool waters of the Gaṅgā—waters which men, fearing the cold, do not touch; this is but a portion of the Lord of Drops.
Desiring purity, he observed the silence of wood and performed a fast, though he was already pure at heart;
within his hermitage, he meditated upon the infinite Lord, who is eternally content and whose particular delight is the satisfaction of others.

Mukunda, whose arrival was perceived by others through the sight of his radiance, urged this sun— the orb of days— whose mind is intent on its own course, toward the honey-filled path for the sake of approaching his own hermitage.
When the Blessed One had arrived at nightfall and the thousand-rayed sun had risen,
he who possessed the highest mind, who was compassionate and intent on instructing his disciples, remained silent and did not write.
No place is so capable of destroying impurity as this; nor is there water equal to the waters of this sacred ford.
Indeed, there is no deity like Viṣṇu, and no form of beneficial counsel like that which we have spoken.
"This person here is departing this very moment, desiring to behold the unconquered Vyāsa;
he may or may not return here, for he knows [only this]: 'May it be well with you. Thus spoke Madhva, and then he departed.
"O Lord, O Lord! Alas, do not abandon us here who are left without a protector; for you, O Blessed One, are possessed of great compassion.
Thus was it urged by the disciples, even when it had already been remembered, out of fear of thwarting their Master’s wishes. (6.49)
Unable to endure separation from his true guru, Satyatīrtha followed him;
he who had heard the supreme meaning three times from the other disciples under the tree known as Puruṣa. (6.50)
Even as he pursued him who had gone onto a difficult path, the sun did not grow red;
with ease, he overtook him as he moved swiftly across distant rocks situated between various refuges.
Gently pushed from afar by his heavy hand, which did not withdraw its form,
he— his mind filled with fear— traversed in an instant the entire path that had been covered during that day.

Having seen his own people here in the hermitage and having described to them the greatness of that divine grace as well as the most wonderful account of his immersion, he constantly remembered Him along with them.
Like the king of monkeys, possessing the speed of the wind, and like Bhīmasena, terrifying to the Dānavas,
he whose name is Vṛjinanāśana leaped upon the peak of that preeminent mountain as he proceeded.

With eyes blooming and free from fear, he beheld that mountain, which was like the great Himalayas for the liberation from poison, containing a multitude of many beings and great serpents capable of releasing venom. (6.55)
Enveloped by a lake of blooming lotuses, it served as a bed of infinite enjoyments for the happiness of virtuous people;
it was lofty with the arrival of a multitude of blossomed flowers and possessed the splendor of a preeminent ground made of emeralds.

Beholding that beautiful upholder of the earth, radiant with golden garments, adorned with magnificent clusters of jewels and shining with excellent golden bracelets, and graced by a splendid garland of forest flowers, before whom throngs of great sages bowed at his feet.
Then Svānandatīrtha meditated upon the Enemy of Mura, who embodies his own bliss.

Thus ends the sixth canto, titled "The Chapter on Bliss," in the great poem *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, composed by Nārāyaṇapaṇḍitācārya, the son of the venerable Trivikramapaṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
The Seventh Canto.
Then, on the slope of the Himalayas, adorned with a grove of jujube trees, he, the omniscient one, beheld that famous and supreme hermitage, the very abode of prosperity. (7.1)
There, both kinds of wondrous trees—resembling the splendor of snow-clad peaks, rain-clouds, and the sun;
renowned for their broad canopies; providing refuge for birds; and reaching even toward the station of Viṣṇu—stood in full bloom.
It was filled with flocks of birds whose voices were nectar to hear— chiefly parrots and other auspicious birds—
and even with supreme, peerless swans whose inner hearts were steadfastly devoted to lotuses.

Filled with a multitude of joyful minds, it grants the desires of one's own heart and is not difficult to traverse; with its subjects free from mutual envy, it is indeed like Vaikuṇṭha, the abode of Acyuta.
As he entered this hermitage, possessing thirty-two noble marks, the sages—who knew the essence of virtues—beheld him with curiosity and thought thus: (7.5)

Resembling a golden palm tree of incomparable height, with lotus-like eyes and a face like the stainless moon, possessing the gait of a lordly elephant and mighty arms—who is this unprecedented man returning? (7.6)
The moon itself has a body that is exceedingly tranquil, while the sun is by nature intensely harsh;
thus, no object of comparison for this ocean of virtues can be found within the worlds.
Having indeed cast off all weariness, this man of steady intellect bears the marks of one who has reached the highest stage of life;
yet, though he possesses a body with human form, he spreads great wonder within us.

The four-faced Brahmā himself, or Pavana (the Wind-god) in the form of an ascetic, must have come here; for otherwise, how could one possess all the most excellent marks [of divinity] unless it was out of a desire to behold the Lord of the Vedas? (7.9)
Thinking, "He has been observed by them," they were filled with curiosity;
moving with unhurried gait, he beheld from afar that most excellent of celestial trees.
With smooth skin, elevated and expansive, bearing many hoods like branches adorned with jewels—
the Lord Ananta standing nearby for the service of the Supreme Lord.
With most wonderfully variegated plumage and many colors, a protector of the deer-herd,
he was like the delight of the sages and the supreme favorite of Indra, the lord of birds among those that fly.
It bestows the great fruit whose essence is nectar, difficult to attain for those devoid of devotion to Hari;
it is the Veda itself, embodied as the Purāṇas and the Mahābhārata relied upon by the virtuous, like a vast tree with many branches.
Then, within that vast, stainless, and enchanting enclosure,
the one of infinite wisdom beheld those supreme ascetics, like gods in heaven.
Even those who shine with the seven [limbs], who have transcended all number, who possess virtues yet are free from the attachment to qualities;
even those who are devoid of anger, pride, and the like, who have renounced enjoyments, and who always subsist on air alone.
There, with perfect wisdom, he beheld Hari, the son of Satyavatī, seated in the midst of the circle of sages, serving as the ornament of the entire circle of the three worlds.
Even while constantly and properly observing [the Self] within the exceedingly pure lotus of his own heart, he beheld it again and again as ever-new; thus amazed, he reflected: || 7.17 ||
For he alone is that stainless Nārāyaṇa, an ocean of innumerable virtues,
whom Satyavatī indeed bore here through Parāśara, following the command of Brahmā.
In his pure ocean of mind, stirred by the great mountain of constant compassion,
there appeared the beautiful beloved of the enemy of the Daityas, who is composed of the three Vedas.
From this very [source], while the two ancient and venerable ones— the Mahābhārata and the Pārijātaka—
were already existing, the nectar of the preeminent collection of Sūtras was born of its own accord.
Bestowing unrestrained grace upon the virtuous, such as the sons of Pāṇḍu,
he whose speech was beautiful wandered for a long time upon the earth for the protection of those possessed of wisdom.
Now, like the sun for the sake of the Kali age,
the Blessed One, not abandoning the range of human vision, has entered this hermitage as if to follow the course of the night.
This very body of his is seen here, possessing the beautiful luster of a blossomed blue lotus;
seated upon a deerskin and a yoga-mat, it is a source of delight for my mind and eyes. (7.23)

Filled with countless virtues, complete with immeasurable and excellent personal qualities, this [Self] is indeed solely composed of existence, consciousness, and bliss, with all defects utterly destroyed. (7.24)
The dust of his lotus feet has been borne upon their heads by Kamalā, Brahmā, Vāyu, Garuḍa, the king of serpents, Śiva, Indra, and others; alas, I too carry it constantly! 7.25.
I bow to the two feet of the Lord, which bear the marks of the banner, the vajra, the goad, and the lotus;
they are themselves red, as if turned crimson from the pressure of passion within his own mind.
Indeed, those who have taken refuge in the purely Vaiṣṇava state by means of their own radiance,
and who are destroyers of both kinds of darkness, triumph like a new sun with its rays.
Of his two feet, with their delicate soles and toes and hidden ankles—oh, no comparison for them can be found by the best of poets, except for each other. (7.28)
Bearing a weight that is appropriate, pure, radiant, and most excellent through its well-rounded form,
this pair of shapely calves bestows upon him who worships it here a likeness unto itself.
The immovable seat, the yogic belt, and the excellent girdle—attained once, they grant one's desires;
oh, my mind considers them most blessed as they shine constantly all around Hari. (7.30)
With her beautiful garment of choice antelope skin, which shone with a lovely luster like radiant gold and clung to her most excellent thighs, she shone with supreme wonder.
O lotus-navelled one, upon this slender, smooth, and beautiful belly of yours, adorned with a deep navel and marked by folds, he placed the entire circle of the cosmic egg. 7.32.

In his heart, where the rise of the virtuous has taken place, this crest-jewel of the lineage of sages bears both the three Vedas and the pure, supreme, and excellent thread of Brahman— vast and expansive.

When his father had been perfectly prepared— neither deficient nor excessive— the Creator bestowed upon him this ornament resting on his neck, a banner for the conquest of the three worlds, radiant with the rays of the sun.
We find no comparison whatsoever for these two lotus-hands, which are delicate and reddish, radiant with the marks of a thousand-spoked wheel, and possess broad, thick, and rounded palms.
The fingertips of the Lord, which bestow the seal of supreme reasoning upon those who worship Him, cut through ignorance;
they are placed above the knees, granting the auspiciousness of the repeated breaking of both [the bonds of] the other [world].
The throat of the Guru, marked by three excellent lines, appears like a conch shell that has been perfectly imitated, as it is naturally and constantly adorned by the three Vedas flowing from it.
This face of the crest-jewel of the gods, by its own splendor, surpasses the vast beauty of a multitude of moons shimmering with the blackness of every eighth phase of their waning.
The row of his white teeth, laughing with supreme splendor as the light of his reddened lips shines forth, would put to shame a string of fresh pearls gleaming between the facets of a ruby.
Aho! This Sarasvatī, by means of a thousand excellent streams of inquiry produced out of curiosity (and great reverence) by the assembly of the twice-born, fulfills the Lord of the Vedas all at once.
This glance of him whose eyes are long like lotuses, approaching me and caressing me,
performs an embrace that fills [my heart] and is endowed with a smile that brings joy to the world.
The *tulasī* plant, nurtured and whispered into by his ear, seems as if it were chanting mantras:
"May the lotus and other flowers not seize the station of my lord out of envy"—this is enough.
The rise, subjugation, and destruction of the worlds, as well as that of these two eyebrows of the Lord of the Worlds,
may occur through even a slight movement of them— just as it occurs for those whose nature is born from the lotus-born Brahmā.
In the midst of the Tilakālikā of the three worlds, this tilaka has attained supreme splendor,
resembling a row of bright red rubies upon the summit of the lordly mountain Harinīla.

Beholding the body of the Teacher of the World— adorned with a circle of matted locks and encircled by excellent streaks of lightning that imitated a fresh rain-cloud— I attained a sense of having achieved my life’s purpose.

Even Ramā, though she ceaselessly counts his supreme virtues, could not exhaustively enumerate the infinite excellent qualities of the nails adorning his toes; who, then, could describe his other virtues? (7.46)
There was no curiosity in me regarding this physical body of the True Guru,
for I, who perceive the cosmic egg with its ninefold coverings, have no curiosity toward it through the notion that it is my home.
While the one of great intelligence was thus reflecting, having transcended the path that leads outward,
the King of the Vedas arrived before him, accompanied by those whose eyes were closed in meditation, and even in form he was the sovereign of the Vedas.
With his body bowed down by the weight of devotion to the Guru, he quickly formed the añjali gesture;
for a moment, with eyes half-closed in reverence, he paid homage solely to the Guru.
Adorned with the ornament of discipline, his conduct clearly distinguished by the eightfold path, that fortunate one bowed down at the lotus feet of the most blessed Lord. (7.50)
Beholding his beloved son, who was bowed down by all excellent virtues,
that son of Parāśara quickly raised him up with his pair of beautiful hands that moved swiftly.
Lord Śruti embraced Amitapramati, accepting him as his messenger;
his heart was filled with the nectar of affection, his face was graced with a smile, and his eyes were wide with joy.
If the powerful Yamunā, the bearer of waters, were to flow with the golden water of the Jāmbūnada river,
then she, possessing a dark luster, might be compared to it because of her contact with the honey-like brilliance of gold.
If these two monkeys, born of the lineage of the best of the twice-born, were endowed with royal ornaments,
they would clearly have been equal to my own two selves when we were formerly embraced by one another as kings of the same clan.
Even Śuka did not receive this complete caressing from the grandfather of the worlds;
that he obtained it was considered so fortunate that the ascetics were filled with great curiosity.

The disciples of that [king], who were skilled in discerning the intentions of their preceptor, offered him a seat befitting his status with due humility—those servants of Mukunda acting like the four-faced Brahmā himself. (7.56)
When the truthful son of Satyavatī had spoken "Be seated" and sat down, he [the Bodhisattva],
honoring those lords of sages with gentle smiles and glances, sat down there.
Having understood him to be the most eminent among the hosts of sages, those who knew the ritual rules performed for him the honors according to tradition;
even the conversation of that lord of poets was pleasing to the ear.
Having heard [this] from the two of them, they attained supreme joy.
Having attained the form of consciousness which is bliss through perfect knowledge, those two gods named Vedavyāsa and Ānandatīrtha blazed forth like Viṣṇu and Vāyu in that hermitage upon the earth.

Thus ends the seventh canto, titled "The Joy," in the great poem *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, composed by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, the son of the venerable Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
The Eighth Canto:

Then, at one time, the one of vast intellect, whose own noble qualities such as the power of his genius caused the minds of the self-restrained to be filled with great wonder, slowly approached that Leader of the Vedas in a secluded part of the forest. (8.1)

"Surely, discipleship is appropriate for this one who has awakened to the description of all things, including their most subtle distinctions; and the greatness of mind of such a true lord is itself a teacher. Thus, with these words of praise, the immortals honored him.
Indeed, Kṛṣṇa filled once again that city which had already been filled; for by the calculation of ultimate reality, he is the Supreme.
Just as the Lord formerly took up his own abode within the vast city of the mind, so too did he take up that [city]; it was a marvel.

In no long time, from Ananta, he heard the ultimate truth— which was endowed with its own essential nature as the beloved Pañcarātra, along with the Itihāsas, Purāṇas, Sūtras, and Satyas— from the infinite heart of Ananta, beyond the multitude of countless scriptures.

For that preeminent and upright one who understands everything by himself, even that [knowledge] was sufficient throughout infinite births; yet, through the power of his own grace, the One Who Reclines upon the Serpent King further distinguished his intellect.
Then, accompanied by Bādarāyaṇa and his associates, he who was free from internal duality set out to pay homage;
for even within that hermitage, did he not behold the radiant form of Hari, which is described as being without beginning?
In that excellent hermitage, the one of vast intellect beheld him who was like a blazing fire devoid of smoke,
clad in choice bark garments and a girdle of muñja grass, with a circle of matted locks shining upon him— the Primordial Being.

He dwelt constantly in the forest as if through asceticism consisting of the conquest of the senses, which is exceedingly difficult to achieve; though he was incessantly delighted by the abundant, pure bliss of the Self, which is independent of his own physical form, he remained there.
Beholding with his two eyes— eyes that eclipsed the luster of a lotus and were radiant with the beauty of full-blown blossoms—
that son of Dharma, who was so difficult for unrighteousness to attain, he gazed in wonder and remembered him most intensely in his mind.
He who brought about the dissolution of the fourteen worlds, including those headed by the Four-faced One (Brahmā),
yet remains alone, shining equally with Kamalā— verily, he is that Supreme Ancient Puruṣa.

From Prakṛti, whose form consists of the three guṇas, arose Mahat; from that, the threefold Ahaṅkāra; from that, the immortal ether and the other elements; and from those, the five gross elements. From these, the Lord created here the cosmic egg and the worlds.

He creates, protects, and destroys incessantly the gods such as Brahmā, Vāyu, Indra, Śiva, Kaśyapa, Īśvara, and others, as well as their followers, humans, and asuras; and he leads them all effortlessly to their own respective destinies. 8.12

Having disregarded the multitude of his own excellent qualities, Vidūṣaṇa, though entirely self-controlled, assumes manifold forms for the liberation of his kinsmen through the recollection, chanting, and prostrations [offered to him] without any pretense. 8.13.
This Lord, the master of the immortals, formerly bestowed the four ancient scriptures upon the four-faced Brahmā,
after having slain with his horse-headed form that ancient enemy who was arrogant in body and a thief of the Vedas.

By him, assuming the form of a boar and having obtained the status of a protector through his lordship over the coastal regions of the ocean where the waves surged, the earth was uplifted from the depths as it fell upon the lotus-like surface of the circle of the staff-like arms of the enemy of the Lord of the Gods.

This Narasiṃha, who shatters the fears of his beloved subjects, tore apart his formidable enemy— the great serpent with a quivering body— within a moment from the lake, by means of the splendor of his wheel-like claws at the rise of his fierce wrath.
Or again, this Vāmana, possessing charming childhood and having won the wonder of the Daityas by the power of his genius,
cast the enemy of Balarāma beneath the pretext of a boon, and bestowed the supreme state solely upon his own kin.
They repeatedly describe him as a mortal-god struck down by a bull resembling a battle-axe,
a benefactor of the worlds, like another Hari, born of the lineage of the great ascetic Guruśakti.
In former times, that Blessed One, the mine of compassion who bestows joy upon Vasudeva, was born in the lineage of Himakara;
he became Daśaratha, who conquered the ten directions with formidable wealth, and on this earth Janaka, the slayer of his enemies, was born from him.

Then Bhujageśvara, beloved of the Lord of the World, was born in the birthplace of his enemy’s son; they call that handsome one, who surpassed the moon with his splendor and was the elder brother [of the other], by the name Rāma in this world.
Then, repeatedly gazed upon by Janaka, who could not bear the separation, the Lord was led to the forest;
there, alarmed by wicked people, the ascetic [Rāma] slew an Asura night-stalker woman.

Then the assembly of gods and other noble beings welcomed him as he stood ready with his excellent arms raised in battle, destroying the bond of enmity formed by the seventy-seven sages, and subduing the wicked ones such as Kaṭukeśin, Ariṣṭa, and Padamukhya.

At the sacrifice, while the twice-born ones—whose voices were like blossoming virtues—were resounding, He who is dear to all of Gokula moved about, delighting the beautiful women whose speech was moistened by the nectar of their longing for Him. 8.23.
Accompanied by his innate companions and joined by all his friends, he went to the city of Madhurā, beloved of his father;
as that peerless beauty of the world entered it, he became a festival for the noble eyes of men and women.
Then he, who had effortlessly shattered the bow of the Lord of Khaṇḍika and destroyed the prowess of King Ugrasena’s son,
attended upon his brahmin preceptor— the teacher of the Lotus-born— and gladdened his own people with his immeasurable splendor.
He took as his wife the princess Kamalāmayī, who had eyes like lotus petals and had descended to earth;
having by his own prowess conquered the royal enemies, he attained joy upon reaching the city protected by the ocean.
He went quickly indeed to the forest to please his mother, performing what is desired by the virtuous;
yet he was accompanied by his auspicious wife, but without his dear friend Lakṣmaṇa, who bears the banner of great victory. (8.27)
Having slain many enemies of virtuous men, such as Khara and Dūṣaṇa— who were difficult to overcome due to their mountain strongholds situated beyond the range of sight—
he gradually brought Naraka, the giver of universal fear and the most unbearable, to the great darkness of death.
Together with his beloved, who was honored by the world and possessed of supreme splendor,
he— dear to her— reached his abode, which had been intensely agitated by the pride and negligence of the gods, like the heart of the celestial *pārijāta* tree.
Having repeatedly conquered the terrifying circle of ten kings, the lords of the green lands,
the Blessed One disregarded his own beloved Fortune as she trembled here while an enemy was carrying her away.

Once, having been saluted by the son of the Wind and others, that enhancer of Indra’s son gave his own excellent kingdom— its enemies having been slain— to his beloved son, the son of Hari, along with a cow.
There, having obtained joy through the long-awaited news of his beloved, which had reached him via the mouth of the Wind-god’s son,
the slayer of Madhu, gleaming with the sharp discus of Hari, proceeded toward the city situated in the midst of the ocean and inhabited by the Puṇyajanas.

The Lord, displaying his prowess with sharp arrows and his discus, destroyed the broad-shouldered Kumbhakarṇa— who was as haughty as a lordly elephant— along with his brother, the enemy of the king of the gods,
and the entire burden of the earth, using his wide wheels as eyes.
Then, accompanied by his wife who had entered the fire, and followed by his brothers,
he reached that abode which for a long time has granted the desires of the virtuous, attaining supreme unity with his own primordial form.
Mahidāsa was born from the pure-souled Viṣṇuyaśas, a twice-born man of renowned character;
he who established here in this world, for the pacification of sins, the highly radiant doctrine of the Great Light through many means. (8.35)
Surely he who was born from the son of Manu attained this state because of his delight in hearing the sacred teachings;
for that king of the gods produced well-disposed beings through an agreement with those who were filled with abundant devotion to him. (8.36)
Her form, manifesting the peak of youth through the close contact of her two very full breasts,
that body of a choice courtesan bestowed nectar upon the host of gods, which had been seized by the asuras.
This eternal one, who bestows self-purification upon the virtuous man to whom he grants his foot, and whose nature is as delicate as silver,
has been upheld with supreme reverence by that eminent sage’s wife, who is free from malice and possesses pure intellect.

This bull among the virtuous, the mountain who bears a body marked by the characteristics of a supreme swan (paramahaṃsa), spoke—being honored by Sanaka and others desiring to know the Supreme Reality—with words that were pure and beautiful even without wings. 8.39.
For this son of the Dharma was born, Hari, the brother of Naradeva, of noble prowess;
he who, though called Kṛṣṇa, was himself born as a natural source of joy for the virtuous.

Salutations again and again to the Supreme Self, who is eternally of a single form, yet possesses ten forms, a hundred thousand forms; who is changeless, clearly manifest in infinite forms, whose entire body is bliss and consciousness. 8.41
Thinking thus, with no space between them, he bowed affectionately and respectfully to Hari;
and those two, unconquered and mutually honored, sat down together near the city where they had previously entered.

Listen with fortitude to this which I am proclaiming, which accords with the counsel of the noble ones and concerns the work of the gods;
for your descent as a youth—though it will be more difficult for others to accomplish—will yield great fruit.
Having concealed the heart of the Sūtra, which is dear to the virtuous, and having now composed this commentary according to my own will,
consciousness— struck down— is utterly obscured by others who defile the true meaning of the Śruti and Smṛti.

To remove this unrighteousness wrought by the wicked, and to lead your own people toward an auspicious state, compose the *Sūtrabhāṣya* without delay; O wise poet, bring the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* into harmony.
Having heard these words of the Teacher of the World—words that were both immeasurable and yet measured—the best among speakers, his heart deeply moved, then spoke to him;
for he could not endure the separation of those two lords of the moving and the unmoving.
O Blessed One, may your grace be such that I may bathe here constantly in the presence of you two, without [the need for] ritual service;
for I do not find such supreme bliss, the singular auspiciousness of the world, even throughout the three realms.
On this earth, whose virtues have been darkened by the Kali age, there is surely no noble person today possessed of a fit intellect;
for to one unworthy of describing the supreme reality, such discourse is indeed censured, like the offering of oblations to a dog.
To him who was speaking thus, the Lord replied: "O gentle one, there are men on earth worthy of virtue;
cleanse them with compassion through the pure rays of your speech, like stainless gems that have been brought forth by their qualities. (8.50)
May your fame, like the light of the sun, utterly humble those of afflicted minds who are inauspicious,
and may it constantly awaken the auspicious ones through my supreme command, especially and perpetually, as the sun awakens the beds of lotuses.
Thus that pure Sarasvatī, having issued from the mouth of the Mountain for the welfare of the worlds,
entered the ocean of the vast intellect of Madhva, which was completely filled with the domain of the Moon and the Cow.

Having understood that this was the esteemed opinion of the two great ones, the wise-minded one said "So be it," and bowing, he placed upon his own head—the burden that none other could bear—the command of these two. (8.53)
Like the three Vedas that awaken the truth, like the three fires that destroy the sins of living beings,
or like the three worlds containing all creatures, those three— Ananda, the son of the sage’s daughter, and Dharmasūnu Madhva— shone resplendently there.

Thus ends the eighth canto, titled "Bliss," in the great poem *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, composed by the venerable Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, son of the illustrious Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
The Ninth Canto. Then, having respectfully bowed there to the unborn Son of Dharma who was urging him to depart, he—
preceded by the leader of the Vedas— set out with the Lord of Sukhatirthaka as his guide.

Having reached another hermitage and heard everything from Kṛṣṇa, he, being compliant with the disposition of his mind and having understood that it was right to follow his teacher, became intent on departing. 9.2.
Having paid homage to his venerable lord, whose face was lovely with a gentle smile, that great-minded one—the crest-jewel of the wise—departed with his permission. (9.3)
For that man of vast mind, his dwelling-place was most beloved even more than his own heart;
indeed, he did not leave it for even a moment, and thus he never became separated from his lord.
Displaying the lion-like gait with his heroic gaze, yet bringing forth peaceful joy with his tranquil look,
Sarvadhī descended from the mountain, appearing like wholesome medicine at every step along the way.
Like the lord of monkeys who crossed the ocean, like Vāsudeva who possessed the king of jewels,
and like Bhīmasena who took the heart of his excellent son, he brought joy to his own people.
Five or six brahmins, headed by Agniśarman, brought food; whether it was sufficient or not, he took it all without astonishment, for he was capable of eating everything when his hunger grew.

One should realize Vāsudeva, who is exceedingly dear to the heart of Vyāsadeva, whose excellent qualities are beyond counting, who is free from all defects, and who bestows infinite bliss through knowledge and devotion. 9.8

Repeatedly reciting the supreme Vedic statements that have been stated and are yet to be stated, he clearly elucidated their meaning through the words of the Smṛtis, employing arguments both logical and profound.
He awakened even the assembly of the ignorant, yet his words were exceedingly difficult for the learned to fathom;
his heart was immeasurable and full of grace, his appearance was gentle and lovely, yet he was terrifying to his adversaries. (9.10)
His speech, free from the eight faults, was characterized by all the marks of excellence;
his form, worthy of honor even by the leaders of the gods, appeared as if it were some other, uniquely blessed manifestation of himself.
The one of infinite intellect composed this wonderful collective commentary on the Brahmasūtras, which refutes the twenty-one false commentaries;
it remains unrefuted by those belonging to the past, future, and present, anywhere at all.

Satyatīrtha, who was like a bee dwelling in the beautiful abode of Hari at the edge of the waves of the auspicious Gaṅgā, composed this commentary on the Bhāṣya, having mastered the writing of its very first syllable. 9.13.

There, having paid homage to the deity, he departed swiftly out of respect for his master’s command; accompanied by his followers and possessing a mind free from affliction, he passed over various lands and reached the bank of the Godāvarī.
There, he addressed the eighteen branches of learning that had been presented by the learned investigators who had come seeking the wealth of wisdom,
and he refuted their six philosophical systems.
Having examined him individually according to their own respective branches of learning and philosophical systems, they were defeated;
then they said, "O Sage, you are preeminently all-knowing; there is no one equal to you. (9.16)
In that assembly, he who was the instructor of all the schools of the three Vedas and was esteemed as the most eminent,
the one named Bhaṭṭa Śobhana, repeatedly bowed with joy to the one whose number is complete (the Buddha).

But that wise one, the crest-jewel of logicians, who rejected the doctrines of his own time, having been firmly established in the Vedas, the Mahābhārata, and the Purāṇas, heard this commentary from Madhva. (9.18)
Having heard this wonderful discourse, he found no pleasure anywhere else;
like a pure-feathered bee seeking something other than it, he did not obtain the nectar of the lotus.
In various well-ordered assemblies, radiant with the arguments set forth by the traditions of Nanditīrtha, he shattered those disputants and, having overcome them, uttered appropriate speech. (9.20)
Though he ground various kinds of conch-shell powder and was unable to pulverize it in many ways, alas, his resolve failing,
he did not abandon even the priceless lotus that spiraled to the right.

That wicked person of base intellect who rejects such an immeasurable treatise on wisdom—which has come to him and is so very difficult to find—is equal to him in mind; indeed, there is no one with a mind as low as his.
A certain man, recognizing his particular excellence, sold him and obtained great wealth;
for indeed, a price for priceless qualities is not easily attained here, but depends upon fortune, destiny, and suitability.
It is evident that even though this person has attained eminence, he does not obtain the full fruit thereof; alas, because of his meager-mindedness, he falls into equality with that man. 9.24.

The king, whose conduct was noble, purchased [the horse] with great respect and honor; and by constantly worshipping it, he obtained riches such as cannot even be described in words or conceived by the mind. (9.25)
"Alas! Who could possibly obtain even the entirety of the fruit of this tree that fashions the scriptures?
Only he who would mock him, possessed of such supreme qualities," saying this, he delighted the people. (9.26)
Alas, it was not only by poets such as these that the venerable feet were worshipped;
even by the deities beginning with Śiva, Indra, and Bṛhaspati, they were fully honored during the festival of the emergence of the excellent doctrine.
As he traveled, that virtuous king filled the subjects—who were like low-lying lands—with showers of wealth and food, just as rain fills the valleys;
yet he did not fill the wicked man, who was like a high plateau, with the water of his sight which removes the heat of suffering.
Honored by the people on the road with all manner of curious acts, he who had come there bowed down before Śiva-nāmakīrtana, who was resplendent in the city of Rājatāsana.
The joy that Acyutapramati experienced upon seeing Daśapramati— who was dear to Acyuta— arrived there and paying his respects, has no known limit.
Long ago, the noble ascetic, having been sent forth by him who possesses incomparable speech, attained supreme joy;
and now, upon seeing him of the pure smile—who had been long desired to be seen—he experienced a delight even more intense than that.

This king of ascetics, like a rain-cloud that both withholds and releases, has taken from the ocean of the Pūrṇa’s vision the nectar known as the *Bhāṣya*, which brings happiness; yet, while causing men to grasp it, he did not release us. 9.32

Then this wise man, employing conciliatory persuasion, described the multitude of excellent qualities of eloquent speech to his naturally well-disposed teacher, whose intellect had been obscured by evil thoughts due to the influence of time.
Repeatedly awakening him with well-reasoned arguments on various occasions,
the one of vast intellect considered the root cause of his lack of appetite, which lay deep within his heart, like a physician diagnosing a chronic ailment.
Striking and terrifying with his exceedingly beautiful voice as he soared on his right wing,
the king of swans dispelled the impurity of the Kali age, as if drawing a single gaze from his teacher, the Great Lake Mānasa.
Like the orb of the moon free from stain, like a lotus flower in full bloom, and like the waters of autumn, his mind, possessing great clarity, shone intensely with the intellect of Acyuta. 9.36.

O Ānanda, for he had formerly listened to the teachings of the Madhvas, grasping at false doctrines; like one who, having repeatedly drunk the salt water of delusion, now longs to drink the nectar of immortality. (9.37)
O ascetics, who have attained the state of the vast intermediate space, remain here for the sake of revealing the excellent doctrine;
just as the moon and the sun, oh, dispel the great delusion of men even throughout day and night. 9.38.
With great reverence toward virtuous men, yet naturally disagreeable to sinners,
he caused them to receive even the two Sudarśanas, which shatter the multitude of cruel sins.

Indeed, this one who dwells in Rūpyapīṭhapura once desired to provide a medicine for the defects that present obstacles to the spiritual success of those beings who have no other refuge, through the unfeigned rise of his compassion. (9.40)
Thereupon, the fool, having had a stone image of the Lord of Śrī— the lover of the Gopikās—
cleaned by three or four disciples at the reservoir, immersed it here.
Having reached the state of being in the very presence of Hari through contact with the exceedingly purifying Lord,
he effortlessly brought this monastery— which was difficult even for thirty men standing up to hold— to its place.
He caused that beautiful son of Nanda, whose face was lovely with a gentle smile and whose form transcended the senses,
to be seated here upon a venerable throne of pure splendor.

For even that wicked man, who by his own divine power brought the proud under his control, and who is called "one whose lineage is joined with old age" because he remembered his own quality as a frequent performer of sacrifices—[even he was subdued]. (9.44)
Beholding this person of sin as a destroyer intent upon his most beloved sacrifice,
he cast him out, along with that harmful man and all those who had previously been capable of supporting the earth.
Causing universal amazement by his own splendor, with his feet worshipped again by the people,
and possessing fame for his wonderful world-conquest as well as infamy, he delighted his own subjects day after day.
Then he, whose intellect was most vast and who was beloved by Vāsudeva, properly caused Vāsudeva to perform a sacrifice—
just as in former times this very one, in the form of Bhīma, caused the righteous Dharmasūnu to sacrifice for the Brahmin.

Having attained the office of Hotṛ-priest here, the younger brother of the All-Knower (Viṣṇu) gratified the hosts of deities with *yājyā* and *anuvākyā* verses, along with hymns of praise accompanied by the splendors of the *Pravargya* rite.
Having applied the sharp series of excellent weapons dedicated to the Viśvedevas, he of keen intellect,
like a preeminent hero, caused the gods— who had dispelled the Rākṣasas and Asuras— to receive their sacrificial portions.

Who here can describe that great sacrifice, which was attended even by Vāyu—who drinks first, who has conquered all the gods, and who is swift—and who was sought out even by him in his manifest form? 9.50
For those whose minds are fixed upon the knowledge of Brahman, action becomes a mere instrument therein;
thus, making [the truth] known, he who realizes the Supreme Self performed even ritual duty as an act. 9.51
Whichever deeds were performed and whichever words were uttered, oh, they are truly captivating;
and to one whose mind is expanded, they shine forth as wonders to the entire world. 52.
Having transcended many Sarasvatīs that provide sustenance for embodied beings and having passed beyond [all] lineages,
he of vast awakening once again attained the supreme stage of life, just as Kṛṣṇapriya had formerly dispelled the fatigue of adversity.
For in the past, Viṣṇu bestowed upon him who bore the form of Hanumān a share in his enjoyments that could not be obtained by others;
indeed, disregarding his own supreme interest, Hari strengthened that very being so that he might repay his benefactor.
Then, having bowed with devotion to his guru according to his command and his own fitness,
he— whose heart was most expansive and who was an ocean of great majesty— departed with his followers out of joy for that one who brings about the welfare of the worlds.
Having approached him with his own people, he bowed to Hari, who was seated upon a silver throne.

Thus ends the ninth canto, titled "Bliss," in the great poem *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, composed by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, the son of the venerable Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
Then,

the sun of the month of Madhu, who brings about the excellence of Mādhava’s virtues and causes distress to those traveling on the path of sin, suddenly and intensely adorned the abode of the ornament of Bhṛgu’s lineage. 10.1.
A certain disciple of Daśamati, for the sake of virtuous people and out of curiosity, spoke various well-composed words like a poem, consisting of a cluster of hymns to the Leader. (10.2)

We could not describe even in a divine lifespan his wondrous deeds throughout the world; nevertheless, some small portion of it all is indeed being told for the sake of those virtuous people who desire to hear it. 10.3.
In one place, seeing King Īśvaradeva having the ground dug by travelers and even urging his own men on, he said: "By such action, you awaken those who are unskilled. (10.4)
Having begun to reveal his nature, the villain did not stop;
out of the greatness of his intellect, he was compelled by necessity to continue digging into the earth.
Not by this, not by that, not by this—surely they were not driven away by one who was not deficient;
for us, surely not by various means, was he, the one whose nature is never deficient, driven away.
That the ocean of the happiness of remembering [the Lord] departs from one whose existence has its origin in Yama—that is not surprising;
for when the wind blows thus, those whose existence has its origin in Yama are seen to be delighted by praising him. 10.7.
Wandering about, the all-pervading Lord Viṣṇu, the foremost of Vaiṣṇavas, once reached the bank of the Viṣṇupadī,
surrounded by his own trusted disciples who had abandoned the flood of worldly existence due to their fear of the enemy.

Then that compassionate one, whose self is the fundamental substratum, effortlessly caused those who had disregarded his words regarding their own former abodes—those who were otherwise impossible to transgress—to cross that river, or rather, the cycle of rebirth (saṃsṛti). 10.9.

"Hold them back! Hold them back! Kill these enemies and friends before they reach the other shore! Seize those who are attacking! Thus he spoke loudly to the king's attendants in words unbecoming of a servant. (10.10)
Alas, you fools! Why do you fall into the water so recklessly? You have no fear because there are many people here.
Desiring to see your lord, the King of the Earth, why do you wish to provoke a quarrel with us? 10.11
With his speech alone, he restrained his enemies as a king restrains serpents by the power of mantras;
and he rescued his attendants simultaneously from the river of death and from the river of the gods.
Though his conduct was free from change, the Lord of the World was surrounded by a thousand cruel servants; yet as he walked, he surged forth like a lion-king amidst a pack of jackals.

Standing on the roof-peak of his palace, the king beheld him—of unshakable form, with the powerful build of a lion, lofty, and having arrived near his own city—and spoke: 10.14. Standing on the roof-peak of his palace, the king beheld him—of unshakable form, with the powerful build of a lion, lofty, and having arrived near his own city—and spoke:

O Sumukha, how is it that you have not been harmed by those harsh men—who, fearing the designs of the enemy king, were consecrated for the task of cutting up travelers—any more than if they were the messengers of Yama? (10.15)
"How indeed do you intend to cross the river Aplava-devanā? What is it that you wish to do?
To him who was speaking thus, Mahāpuruṣottama-dāsa replied here with these words. 10.16.
"That god who is the lamp of the universe, blazing brightly—all this we do through his supreme grace.
Let us now go quickly toward the northern direction," such were the first of those wonderful words spoken by him. (10.17)
Having clearly perceived his profundity, steadfastness, vast heroism, noble character, supreme brilliance, and speech endowed with both propriety and timing,
the king was struck with wonder and immediately bestowed half of his kingdom upon him.
Thus, he who was once the object of the kings' intent to punish became the object of their intent to bestow sovereignty;
for it was precisely to demonstrate that policy which must be applied even in times of calamity that the Lord acted in such a manner, even by force.
Once, seeing a band of thieves rushing toward him,
he halted them and, for the sake of his own handkerchief and bundle,
moved among them and then had them strike one another down— oh, what a feat!
The All-pervading Lord, having first deluded them, [slew] the hosts of Saṃśaptakas, just as Vijaya [did]. || 10.20 ||
Elsewhere, when a hundred brave thieves, led by Dhanyapravara,
arrived seeking to kill him with axes drawn by their disciples, he instantly drove away that entire band by striking them with a single disciple.
In one place, mistaking him and his retinue for a cluster of rocks, bandits abandoned them; yet, seeing them again, they bowed down out of curiosity.

When truth was being destroyed, the wise man, with a mere play of his vital breaths, swallowed that tiger-like Daitya who had come at will and assumed the form of a tiger on the slopes of the Snowy Mountain.
From Nārāyaṇa, he obtained images made of pure stone, in which the Lord,
accompanied by Padmā, was present and intent on the welfare of the world.

The son of Parāśara, considering this fortunate man to be preeminent in the world, directly appointed him to clearly proclaim the supreme intended meaning of the Mahābhārata for the sake of establishing the ultimate reality. 10.25.

Having paid homage to Govinda at every sacred ford— being himself a ford of happiness— and having honored him in every holy field as the foremost among those who know the fields, he, accompanied by his followers, went once more to the Gaṅgā with its lofty garlands of waves.
Seeing that the river was free of rafts and that the sun, the friend of the lotus, had reached the ocean,
and observing his disciples seated on the bank in extreme despondency, he crossed over it.
Neither by the lord of monkeys who leaped across the ocean, nor by this lord of men who sports here, have these [lotuses] been plucked;
otherwise, how could they not have suspected calamity for him, given his power? (10.28)
When the sun, rich in its rays that act as lamps for the world, and the sun-like Madhva appeared in their unmanifest form, his lotus-eyes immediately abandoned their splendor along with the lotuses.
Having crossed the river, the son of Vinatā, undaunted in spirit, reached the ground of the beasts;
there, without his garments being wet, he was saluted by the faces of gods among men and gods among brahmins, which were moist with curiosity.

There, he ferried his disciples across that river by means of a boat, while the enemy's terrified soldiers— neither those on shore nor even those in the boats— were utterly amazed by his own splendor and driven away by the kings.

With their hearts longing for the sight of the Lord, they beheld your broad riverbank, illuminated by lamps, filled with people, and graced by circles of eminent scholars who were urging them forward. (10.32)

There they beheld Sukhatīrtha in person, an expert in the sacred tradition who knew the scriptures, capable of discerning the nuances of assemblies, and speaking here as the lotus-born Brahmā might in the divine assembly.
Then he reached the capital city of Hastinapura; there he dwelt for a month in a monastery suitable for residence, situated in a secluded spot near a river, possessing infinite virtues within.
The celestial river, having split the earth, went forth through a special branch to serve him;
and that Speech, having attained her purpose by becoming his servant—she who is to be honored by Śiva and others—is not surprising in this regard. (10.35)
She, personified, bowed from afar at the lotus-feet of the preeminent Guru;
and beholding her body, which was the very embodiment of magnanimity and beauty, those disciples were filled with great wonder. (10.36)

Then, having arrived at Vārāṇasī, which wards off all evil, the powerful one spoke these words to his disciples, who were arrogant on account of their ease, as he observed them during a moment of leisure. (10.37)
"O you who consider yourselves heroes, attack me at once for the sake of proving your skill in wrestling!
He who does not exert his full power here violates my command. (10.38)
Uttering these words, he simultaneously struck down fifteen youths who had arrived and were ready for combat;
saying, "Let him rise whose capability there may be," he laughed softly. (39)
"Your limbs and our very fingers bring us a weight as heavy as Mount Sumeru;
O compassionate Lord, we shall perish here before long—release us! they said at that time. (10.40)

Then, released by him, those beings were filled with extreme wonder; for, without even considering his true nature—that by the mere movement of whose eyebrows the entire world, including Śiva and Indra, is completely and utterly restrained—[they were amazed]. (10.41)
A certain ascetic, whose every partisan had been refuted by his constant discernment and who held the station of Amarāvatī, declared:
"Let the Lord be propitiated as the means for the task of acquiring knowledge through the desire for victory. (10.42)
When the Blessed One had established the matter, he of fierce intellect asked about the nature of knowledge in an illogical manner.
[The Buddha replied: "If that were known by you, you would be a knower; if it is not, then this question would not be appropriate. Thus was he refuted. (10.43)
In every assembly, the disciple of Vyāsa shone brightly with his exposition,
which completely dispelled the thickest darkness and was honored by the lotus-like hands of all those present.
Just as in every autumn the moon [shines] for the sake of the perfection of its moonlight. 10.44.
The birth of the world occurs at every moment within the celebrated, immeasurable, and ever-present time;
it abides in that state which is free from expectation, devoid of conflict, and characterized by its own luminous manifestation, through an intellect that is not bound by temporal limits.
"Rule over all this; let Viṣṇu, who is independent and eternal, play here.
Subdue the wicked and protect the virtuous—he who, though full of all qualities, is himself devoid of [worldly] attributes. (10.46)
He, the Lord of Śrī, who is considered peerless and whose nature is distinct from all else, fully revealed the supreme objects of desire, beginning with *setu*. (10.47)
By means of that extended illusion which was uniform, he who was seated upon his seat did not go to the state of being tormented by the play of suffering.
The wise Kaurava, having attained the celestial realm of kings,
