then remembered the festivals of elephant duels that had occurred during his own pastimes;
he was surrounded here by those whose souls were truth and who perceived him as the future Mārīca.
They were filled with wonder and exceedingly delighted by the sight of their own king’s body and its weapons.

The Lord of the Self, whose splendor is infinite, having been clearly seen for a moment by the Brahmin Hṛṣīkeśa as he bowed down in that place, yet remaining unseen, instantly caused wonder among embodied beings;
[he did so] by means of various foods and delicacies brought by people from other lands, whom he had impelled in a dream.
He fed his own guru with abundant offerings, making known that he was the teacher of all, the kinsman of the Vedas.
Having obtained [the kingdom], he again remembered the Lord of Ramā with reverence— the Paraśurāma—
and then received from him a thousand excellent royal plantain trees, which had been offered for his consumption.
Having received from Śaṅkara four hundred cows, each resembling a massive plantain tree, which had been offered at his feet, he grazed them; yet,
though his path was unseen by the circles of kings who rose up [to block him], he proceeded with five jars of milk, three, two, and one [respectively] filled [for the brahmins].

In some assembly, even before the cowherds, he was implored by the people; with the excellence of his singing, which surpassed the gift of sleep-inducing mantras, he instantly produced flowers or fruit—oh, what a marvel! (10.53)
Blessed was Bāṇa, who delighted the gods and whose heart was hostile to the enemies of the gods;
he who was equal to Aja, who destroyed false doctrines through the teachings of Madhu, who possessed the splendor of the foremost moon, and who removed the illusion of desire.
For he joyfully bowed to Viṣṇu, the bestower of universal victory, the one worthy of service, and the source of true happiness.
Through skillfulness, the yogi is always a friend who is free from the absence of Śrīdhara and the like. 10.54.

"Alas! The many deeds of this ornament of the world, performed without regard for the end, grant one's desired goals through hearing, reflection, and recitation; thus do the immortals proclaim. (10.55)
Thus, the cloud of the learned one, skilled in various lowing sounds like those of a cow,
devoted to the feet of Hari, and illuminating the quarters of the sky with the lightning of sacred knowledge,
[shelters] the circle of his own feet which has been scorched by the great heat of the fear of worldly existence.
It produced dense bliss for those with fruitful minds, being free from any blemish.

Thus ends the tenth canto, titled "The Chapter on Bliss," in the great poem *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, composed by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, the son of the venerable Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
The eleventh canto: Having heard the extensive inner discourse from the King of Serpents, the sage Sanaka and his companions,
their forms barely visible in the sky, quickly vanished from sight and reached their destination.

Having saluted this Infinite One, who delights in his own abode of most wondrous splendor and possesses a thousand heads, the sages— adorned with humility— asked him for a boon concerning that very purpose.
O Lord of the World, will the fruit not arise for those who repeatedly recite this most enchanting rule of the Blessed One of vast wisdom—a rule honored even by you—in this world? (11.3)
For those qualified [to practice], the fruit for the wise becomes such that their activity is exceedingly vigorous;
may the Blessed One, whose speech is fruitful and who possesses abundant compassion, elaborate upon that fruit. 11.4.
Having heard these noble words uttered by them, he of exalted mind spoke these words:
"Listen with attention to the most venerable fruit of the time when the feet of the Venerable One were honored. (11.5)
Even the fruit attainable in the triple heaven and other realms is not said to be his reward, just as the heap of straw is not the reward for farming;
rather, his own fruit is the state of liberation, which is the supreme goal for those who know the ultimate truth, such as Śuka and Śāradvata.

For those who devote themselves to this supreme treatise on the meaning of the highest tradition, composed with superhuman artistry, the Unconquered One bestows his own realm for their delight as they proceed toward supreme Vaiṣṇava-hood. 11.7
Indeed, there shines the city of the Perfect Person, the sole abode of the manifestation of the universe;
for therein is perceived the very image that serves as its point of comparison, appearing within the jeweled walls. 8.
Here, the radiance of the rows of red stone mansions, shimmering on all sides with the glow of the succession of white palaces,
follows the form of the enemy of the Asuras as it shines upon the circle of my body.
With its folds made of emerald, which possess the brilliance of crystal set within variegated rows of eyes,
the city shines at every house as if joined by the Yamunā with the waters of the white Sindhu.
If there were not here this fixed rule of delusion for people regarding rows of dwellings,
then how could one ever have perceived that the row of artificial leaves made upon the eaves was merely a fabrication?
With clusters of jewel garlands hanging from various well-woven, variegated tapestries,
they shone within the recesses of the pavilions as if falling in a profusion of graceful movement due to being filled to excess.
The stainless form is indeed the very nature of the great jewel, consisting of gold and all things;
here it may arise as the essence of all splendor, and for this reason it has been described by poets with hyperbolic expressions.

Having disregarded from beginningless time his own longing for liberation because of the countless multitude of faces on Śambhu’s head, this city of the Lord rivals the great city of the Asaṃhati-malla; oh, how great is this majesty! 11.14.
The palace of the sole Lord of the world shines forth, surpassing the marvelous qualities of the three worlds;
situated amidst a series of excellent mansions, it resembles the orb of the moon resting in the midst of a circle of stars.

In that house where Indirā herself, acting as the master’s honor-guard, performs the household duties most excellently—who could describe the prosperity there, even if it were attended by a thousand handmaidens? 11.16

The Supreme Lord, the husband of Kamalā, reclining upon the soft coils of the king of nāgas as if they were ambrosia, delights there exceedingly with his consort Kamalā— who is stainless, beautiful, and lotus-eyed— even more so than in the celestial realm itself.
Meditate upon him who possesses the radiance of a thousand rising suns, who is clothed in golden garments and adorned with jewel-encrusted ornaments;
whose moon-like face is graced by a smile, whose eyes are like lotuses, and who bears the enemy of the gods (the discus). 11.18.

Even the four-faced Brahmā, though possessed of clever speech, could not enumerate all of his virtues; nor could we, even with a thousand mouths, speak again of those qualities beyond what has already been said.
Countless birds, lords of the sky, and the foremost of serpent-kings together with their mates,
having beheld him who partakes in the abundant bliss of supreme yoga, bear a surge of joy within them.

There, men with four arms, eyes like lotus petals, wearing excellent garments and saffron-colored robes, possessing a ruddy luster and the brilliance of fresh clouds, wander about with the appearance of lords. (11.21)
For those who approached the presence of the Blessed One, joy was not only beyond compare;
for those who partook of that world-transcending state, which is exceedingly difficult to attain even through abundant merits, it became truly unsurpassed.
Where death, birth, and old age do not exist, how much less can there be the threefold fear or the multitude of sufferings?
Furthermore, nothing else whatsoever that is impure exists there, nor even the root from which such qualities arise.

Infinite happiness is experienced by all those who possess wisdom, constantly and fully, even though they are accompanied by degrees of excellence, are devoted to their own gurus, and share great mutual affection with one another. (11.24)

Exceedingly beautiful and fragrant, those men here move about, anointed with yellow sandalwood as radiant as the new moon, attended by followers bearing moving and lovely whisks, and remaining eternally youthful.
With eyes delighted by graceful dancing and ears gladdened by soft singing and instrumental music,
these lovers delight their own young wives, who possess the eyes of fresh lotuses.
Indeed, doe-eyed women are emerging from the palace gardens toward the prince,
like radiant beams slowly issuing from the stainless orb of the moon within its circular halo.
Here, other slender forms appear with bodies the color of red gems, possessing a luster like that of beautiful necklaces;
others, too, shine with the dark brilliance of sapphire, adorned with various ornaments.
These other rows of clouds, possessing long-lasting luster and themselves bearing exceedingly fine garments, surely possess excellent breasts, for they are indeed exuding parrots. 11.29.

The crystal floor, by means of its own excellence, reveals the red luster of the excellent nails upon the sprout-like feet of the fair-eyed women whose coral-colored soles have long since passed away— a luster that was not previously visible.

We conclude that the garments of the fawn-eyed women, variegated in their luster by the radiance of their broad, beautiful hips and lovely thighs, serve as the victory banners of Love for his conquest of the world.

With lovely hands like sprouts repeatedly waving and making the golden bracelets jingle, with slender waists where the soft line of new hair quivered gently, and with eyes exceedingly tremulous; (11.32)

Upon their chests, they were adorned with excellent rows of necklaces that seemed to be churned by the radiance of the drops of nectar-essence remaining from the overflowing splendor of their jar-like breasts, as these drops spread forth. || 11.33 ||
Moreover, with other hands playfully adorned with blooming blue lotuses placed by their companions,
they appeared with faces radiant with pure smiles and the play of sidelong glances, their pairs of cheeks shining with dangling earrings.

When those [women] had previously moved forward as if with the tinkling of lightning-stone anklets, the young men then turned their faces away, having been told [by them]: "Behold this graceful play of the body. (11.35)
Having somehow approached their beloved husbands— who had been cherished by them— the women, bent under the weight of their breasts,
slowly enter that supreme grove again, supported by the strength of those very arms.

Embracing all the trees laden with clusters of blossoms that bow under the weight of their abundant fruit—trees made of gold and jewels—the breeze, the friend of the ocean of nectar, increases the happiness of whom not? (11.37)
This celestial grove, which delights through mere proximity, does not bring such joy to people as it does by its very rule;
for the supreme Nandana, the grove of Upendra, always brings delight to all.

Ah, how the seasons adorn him—who is like a grove of *pāribhadraka*, *kalpataru*, and *pārijāta* trees, as well as *haricandana*—together with the mountains that serve as the feet of his meditative composure! 11.39.

Madhu and Mādhava— delightful with the *mādhavī* flowers of their smiles, radiant with fresh *campaka* and other blossoms, and sweetened by the humming of bees— bring joy to the beloveds of the Conqueror of Madhu.
Placing a garland of fresh jasmine flowers— most beloved and born of purity— upon the head of his beloved,
he himself presses her broad breasts against his chest, as if saying, "I am not skilled in this."
With their sweet voices and the brilliance of their eyes revealed by the rows of their fanning tails,
the peacocks follow the thousand-eyed Indra to his own great dance festival, which bears the joyful sign of the clouds.

People delight with their beloveds, who have eyes like blooming blue lotuses in autumn, faces as beautiful as full-blown lotuses, voices as melodious as the call of the parrot, and who are accompanied by cackling swans. 11.43.
Welcoming the winter season as a dear friend, the cool season— acting through the snow upon the crystal mountain—
seems to laugh with the splendor of blossoming new *kunda* flowers while causing the clusters of *phalinī* plants to flower.

In this world, the quality of dancing—the very root of the defects caused by the afflictions of cold, heat, and rain—always accomplishes what is dear [to the dancer]; oh, how marvelous that he is "possessed of liberation" (vimuktimān) among those who possess liberation! 11.45.
There, the multitude offers to the Immortal that which yields the fruit of the most excellent garlands of nectar;
yet everyone, though desiring to enjoy it, always reverts to their original nature due to the power of the bonds of destiny.
As the throng of women, overcome by excessive passion, wandered through the grove,
they constantly sang sweetly of the deeds of the Conqueror of Madhu, accompanied by their circles of beloveds.

One woman, most excellent and graceful, sportively plucks the finest flowers; others cut blossoms; still others weave garlands; some delight their husbands, while indeed there are none who do not [do so]. 11.48.

Delighted by various forest sports, the youths embrace the young women whose firm breasts press against them; drinking the honey from their lotus-like faces, they find pleasure within the bowers of beautiful creepers.
Then, in the lakes filled with nectar-like water, the connoisseurs of pleasure— whose anklets mimic the cries of cranes—
plunge in together with their husbands and sport, their faces laughing like festive clay drums.
Having performed various diversions in the water, the women went to the rugged shores of coral; there they took fragrant, golden cosmetic pigments held in the hands of their female companions.

By means of the garments from their hips, the ornaments of their limbs, the saffron on their breasts, the excellent garlands in their hair, and even the collyrium of their eyes— all these things mutually exchanged by the lotus-eyed women— suffice to create their full adornment.

The slender-waisted women went together with their own attendants to their respective houses; there they drank the nectar, difficult for worldly beings to obtain, from goblets made of great silver and jewels.
On the occasion [of lovemaking], women with lovely eyes, though urged by their husbands, slowly ascend the jeweled couches covered with soft, fragrant beds; for modesty indeed adorns every pleasure.

With her lovely breasts raised in delight as she binds her flower-adorned braid, the fair-faced woman—whose folds at the base of her arms are clearly visible—is embraced with intense passion by her lover. (11.55)
Who here, being himself happy, would not delight the beloved by embracing her with his pair of arms—arms whose broad, rounded, lofty, and firm pair of breasts prevents any space between them? (11.56)

Having gazed for a long time with restraint upon the face of the fair-limbed woman— whose jeweled earrings gleamed with the radiance of her smiling, blossoming, and shimmering eyes, and which was skillful in its gentle side-long glances— the beloved kisses it.
Lifting up her moon-like face,
the youth did not cease for long from drinking the sweet nectar of the fair-eyed woman’s lips, filled with joy born of their embrace.

Urging her with the eager desire for the festival of love, he hastened his sprout-like hand toward grasping the hem of her garment; yet, when she suddenly held back his hand, that most beloved lover made her haste redouble.
Or rather, a multitude of young women delights them, embracing their broad chests with impetuous force and, in that very instant, becoming more expansive;
they are skilled in the full array of amorous arts such as cooing and the like.
While he delights those lovers who are themselves exceedingly worldly, his women delight him with their supermundane qualities;
thus that supermundane amorous dalliance shines forth, possessing a form suited to it and a bliss exceeding that of the world. 11.61

In that state free from all defects, there was no pleasure marred by fatigue and the like, nor for the bride and groom any pain of separation from their religious observances, nor any quarrel arising from the advances of rival lovers. (11.62)
Because their bodies consist of the experience of bliss, they possess fragrance both externally and internally;
therefore, even the gods in the abode of Indra honor the sexual union of the couples there as something worthy of praise by the sages.
Listen also to this subject beyond the world, which is the object of the eyes of the entire multitude of liberated souls:
the Lord of Lakṣmī truly and incessantly manifests his beautiful form, which possesses the essence of Mount Mandara.

His great crown was adorned with rows of the finest jewels; his dark and beautiful hair flowed in a thousand locks; his forehead was graced by a tilaka shimmering like a half-moon; and his ears were adorned with swinging makara-shaped earrings.
With a face that rivaled the full moon, eyes like lotus petals, and lips as red as the dawn,
he greeted his prostrate son with incomparable grace through the playfulness of his smile and gaze.
He possessed the splendor of the moon upon his neck adorned with nine conch shells, and he wore a magnificent necklace of choice emeralds;
he was like one adorned with beautiful clusters of gems, shimmering bracelets, rings, and excellent armlets. (11.67)

His hand, with its broad and rounded palm of an exceedingly coppery hue, wields a wheel that causes pain to the solar disc, a conch as sweet as the moon’s orb, a lotus, a blazing mace, and a magnificent bow.
With excellent, well-developed shoulders, a crown of hair shining like a supreme pavilion of jewels,
and a lotus-like navel that is the slender center of the seven worlds, he is praised by the Kali age as the lotus-born source of the auspicious universe.

With the beauty of her girdle-ends exceedingly lovely, with a garment tawny like the luster of molten gold, and with a pair of thighs resembling the trunks of excellent elephants, she possessed shanks that were beautiful, rounded, and tapering. 11.70.
With excellent anklets and feet possessing great luster at the toes, with fingers and nails having the brilliance of fresh coral,
and purifying the world with the dust of her feet which shone like the stain upon the lotus-emblem on the enemy's banner— she was a boat for crossing over the ocean of existence.

He is eternally one with all His limbs, from the soles of the feet to the crown of the head, which possess infinite qualities such as blissful consciousness— qualities of immeasurable extent understood through the entirety of the scriptures— and He is entirely free even from a trace of defect.
By virtue of the specific qualities of those qualified [to worship], [the Lord] appears with two feet up to an infinite number of feet;
He is brilliantly illuminated by various other primary and secondary attributes appropriate to each case, which are themselves exceedingly radiant.

Possessing the luster of nine suns, the supreme beauty of gold, and the captivating green of a fine emerald; endowed with a variegated radiance like various flashes of light, and the qualities of bliss, awakening, fragrance, and beautiful form. (11.74)
Among all wondrous jewels, it is the greatest wonder for the crossing of the world—a wonder indeed, a wonder again and again!
O Lord of Ramā, Your form, whose sole essence is the quintessence of beauty, eternally gladdens (here, brings supreme joy to) those seeking liberation.
That sacrifice is performed by those devoted to ritual; it is proclaimed among the wise as the supreme, while others describe it as such.
Its fame is sung in beautiful songs, bound by the rules of Vedic injunction, and ever dense with bliss.
In Vaikuṇṭha, those particular glories of Śrī are a source of great wonder for people, beyond the reach of mind and speech;
in Vaikuṇṭha, which is praised as being free from [worldly] birth, such a nature is indeed fitting.
Whatever object of pleasure one desires here, all that shall come to pass by mere volition;
even the Vedas themselves proclaim this liberation—what, then, could be a greater abundance of power? (11.78)

Those beginning with the gods and ending with humans who, by their own power, repeatedly turn the nature of the commentary on the Mahānanda-tīrtha over in thought and speech, eternally attain this liberation through the grace of Mukunda. || 11.79 ||

Thus ends the eleventh canto, titled "Bliss," in the great poem *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, composed by the venerable Nārāyaṇapaṇḍitācārya, son of the illustrious Trivikramapaṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
The Twelfth Chapter:

There, while the lion-like Vedāntin Anantasvāmin was letting forth the roar of his primary exposition—a roar terrifying to the intoxicated elephants that were the disputants—the herds of jackals, the proponents of illusion (*māyin*), fell into a state of agitation. (12.1)
Having assembled together near the cities of Amīcola and Jaḍvīpa,
the fierce and wicked ones held a consultation out of envy toward Vāyudeva, the ornament of the earth, just as the foolish sons of Dhṛtarāṣṭra had previously done.
Out of envy, someone among them spoke with restless and wicked words against the keeper of the cow;
likewise, another who was equally talkative addressed the Gāndhāraka with base conduct in their midst. (12.3)
This illusory power desires one single reality, yet through ancient words it ordains that which is inexpressible;
alas, how wonderful is the policy of the Teacher of Vision—strange and ever-new, adorned with the beauty of its own incongruity! 12.4

Who, without attaining Her, could perfectly realize the entire visible universe—beginning with mortals and immortals, and extending to those who hate the Immortal, from Brahmins down to Caṇḍālas—as being devoid of difference, equalized by all measures of distinction? 12.5
Truth indeed ordains all that is subject to worldly convention; yet that [convention] carries everything along within delusion.
When knowledge arises, it is perceived as being like a burnt cloth; when that [knowledge] is matured, it is like water poured upon heated iron.

O you who stand in the state beyond the qualities (nirguṇa), among the assembly of the best of the best of the wise and knowers—O my lords, now hear my cry! Alas, alas, this doctrine of Māyā is going to its destruction. 12.7
Wherein the followers of Bhaṭṭa have fallen from their path, and the Prābhākaras and Māhāyānikas and others are terrified;
desiring to burn that difficult-to-traverse sacrificial session of Māyāvāda, our tongue of fire—the doctrine of Reality—must not be neglected by us.

Whatever region the one of vast mind reached, from each of those places an obstacle to his arrival was clearly perceived by the Noble One; yet he reached the vicinity—alas, we are devoid of fortune! (12.9)

The question asked by the inquirer is surely shattered by him, for he speaks with reasoning that cannot be refuted; it is heard that he puts the assembly of disputants to shame, especially those who raise objections—what indeed can we do? 12.10

"Harṣatīrtha has condensed the entire Eastern Śāstra, numbering one hundred and twenty-five thousand verses, into a single sentence"—hearing this description from travelers, my mind was first filled with distress. (12.11)

He is surely Vedavyāsa, or perhaps the Veda itself incarnate; for that divine form of his, accompanied by a gentle smile, is such that the very words of those who behold it become a sword that cuts through the very root of the side of Māyā. 12.12.
If that Sūtra-bhāṣya, being uncorrupted and endowed with logic, is more powerful, what harm is there to us?
Having spoken thus, certain of our own [followers], devoid of shame, have submerged us in an unbearable ocean of shame. (12.13)

Lest other systems of reality be grasped within the ocean of this assembly by his extensive network of secondary disciples who bear the conch, discus, and other [emblems], provide us with the means there for the attainment of our well-being. 12.14.
By means of secondary arguments protected by secondary statements, they increase the secondary understanding of men;
they are experts at obstructing the speech of the swans, just as clouds fill the ocean again with showers of water.
For having spoken this indeed with great abundance, they suddenly pervade the universe to their heart's content;
just as at the time of the destruction of our world-view, there is a dissolution into water at the time of the world's destruction.

Having thus heard his speech, another among those proud men—one who knew the hearts of the proud, who delighted the minds of his own kin, yet was himself dull-witted and miserable—spoke these bold words aloud: *ākarṇyetthaṃ tasya vāṇīmathānyo mānī teṣāṃ mānināṃ cittavettā | svānāṃ ceto nandayan mandacetā dhṛṣṭāmuccairvācamācaṣṭa kaṣṭaḥ || 12.17||*
Fie upon the mind of the timid, devoid of honor, which melts away from the mere suspicion of fire!
For it is only when melted by actual contact with fire that ghee shines, remaining steadfast [in its essence]. 12.18.

For those whose knowledge is both purifying and auspicious, which accomplishes the subduing of gods and others, and which would put even the son of Śukrī—who is honored by the gods—to shame—what cause for despondency is there in their presence? (12.19)
If non-duality is obstructed by harsh, secondary arguments and thus cannot even appear as something to be established, let it be so for now;
yet, there is certainly no one who can conquer us, who are protected by these [disciples] skilled in the six rites and enriched with divine mantras and medicinal herbs.

Even if this were so, the adversary must certainly not be disregarded; yet, now is not the time for lamentation, for even the teachers such as Śaṅkara and others—who have realized the non-dual nature of their own Self—entertain this very doubt. (12.21)

Having declared, "Alas, this treatise on reality, which has come down through tradition, is being destroyed by a new one," the faults of those [opponents] should be described by the wise among the neutral public, whether they be virtuous or not. 22.
One’s own intention should be as ineffable as Brahman; through the power of *māyā*, the accomplishment of all things is possible.
According to this principle, and by the very logic of the scriptures, everyone who is other than one's own self must be restrained.
In every village, let this honor [of others] be checked by means beginning with conciliation (*sāma*), each preceding method being applied first.
Our own people, exerting themselves in drawing out books and other such means, must act to break the pride of those who have arrived. 12.24.
Thus, having considered their duty, these crooked ones acted at that time against the devotees of the Wielder of the Discus;
for otherwise, how could they have been fit to plunge into the ocean of blinding darkness, whose waters are fierce with suffering? (12.25)

Desiring to cast out that man named Puṇḍarīka— who, though considering himself wise, was an enemy of Vāsudeva and a hypocrite in his vows— these wicked counselors made an effort at the Rūpyapīṭha temple under the pretext of debate.

Just as a village dog longs for the filth of a lion, or as a crow [longs for] a swan, or as one with a single vision [longs for] a master of illusion, even so did a fool challenge that preeminent scholar, who was like a hyena of vast longevity.

Though it was but slight, he did not disregard it, just as a moth with a restless soul does not ignore a flame; for alas, by its very nature, it was like a mass of splendor, radiant with honey that is difficult to cross, as if with fire.
Shining with honors from those worthy of honor, yet setting aside his own view by means of incomparable arguments,
he— Vedavedī, whose sacred bathing-place was the highest love for Viṣṇu— composed an exposition of the Vedas.
Those brahmins who had previously studied the sacred tradition arrived there out of curiosity;
seated there in great numbers, they gazed upon the excellent teacher as he was being beheld.

Seeing him manifesting the letters beginning with *ka* from the aforementioned limbs, skilled in the initial manifestation of their respective vowels and consonants, and imbuing the three states with those qualities, the gods forgot the God of gods. (They indeed forgot. 12.31.

At first, appearing to move through the feet of the *mātrās* by following the calves with shortness, the devotee of Govinda performs other supreme circular movements during the *rāsa* dance of Govinda. (12.32)

With her auspicious limbs manifesting her true nature, she who causes the three worlds to ascend the stage of wonder—like another Kṛṣṇā with her feet placed upon the venerable [altar]—the sweet-voiced Vedic speech shone like a honeyed maiden. 12.33.

That utterance, endowed with profundity and other qualities, performed with nobility and various praiseworthy sounds, is the objective of both those who have mastered the phonetics and those who have not; I consider it venerable and peerless for one of blessed intellect. (12.34)

Manifesting the *kālpī* and *kl^iptī* arrangements as well as those belonging to the *Chāndasa*, and further elucidating the clearly expressed verbal science (*śābda-śāstra*), he—who followed the path of grammar and etymology (*nairukta*)—thus explained the Veda for the sake of the knowers of light (*jyotirvid*). (12.35)
Who indeed could describe your two beautiful feet, which are worthy of being explained and uttered in the Vedic tradition, by one such as I?
Having bowed down to those feet which have been described by the masters of speech, the lords of birds, and the living beings of this world through many wonders.

Having heard this caravan of the Veda explained here in such a manner by the Brahmin as if by Brahmā himself, all those gentle ones, desiring to know the Victor, approached and spoke to the one named Citrakāya. (12.37)
"O man of abundant wisdom, by means of your abundant wisdom, please speak that which is designated by the words of the Vedic hymns.
We, who desire to hear it, and you, who are wise, are both petitioning you to explain this matter. (12.38)
Thus addressed by them, this evil-minded man set out to attain equality with Vistāribuddhi;
he became an object of ridicule there, just as Pauṇḍraka Vāsudeva once was when he sought the splendor of Vāsudeva.

Having heard the word "rā" following the substitute "āṅ," they censured that person who had uttered the word "nāra," blaming him as one unworthy of praise for his greed for commentary on the *Aitareya* and other hymns. (12.40)
Having previously gained renown in the world as a "tiger," this rogue and deceitful jackal, upon encountering Madhva—
the lion who destroys the leopards that are mere disputants— has thus become nothing but a name.

The son of Pṛthā, known as Agrayānanda-tīrtha, heard that his own Śrī—who was beloved by Kṛṣṇa, whose name was made clear by the scriptures, and who had been protected by the virtuous twice-born Saindhava named Padma—had been abducted. 12.42.
Then Sārya, having crossed swiftly through the cloudless sky and having terrified him with herds of cattle, reached him;
desiring to restrain him within, she who had attained glory laughed at him who had been conquered.
This evil-minded one became the cause for casting off the auspicious [Buddha], who was alone and known as the giver of happiness;
this portion of Hari could not endure it further, like a lion toward a pig when its young are in danger.

Out of fear of him, even those people who had previously been victorious now stood behind him, seeking safety; yet today, that conqueror, amidst the herds of cattle urged on by others, has won five or six choice cows.
The son of Madhu, having split that army— which was beautifying the very horizon of Viṣṇu and which was being driven forward in succession yet remained irresistible—
captured the one named Kañja, the lord of Sindhu.
"Let it be, let it be! This entire world belongs to you; O you thieves who preach illusion, flee!
A witness, a witness, and a punisher has surely arrived for you; the time has come to quickly enter the depths of a cave. (12.47)

The splendor of the disputants, who were like stars, has been eclipsed and utterly destroyed by the moon of your wheel of fiery wisdom; that which pervades the universe is the root of its radiance—your most beloved [teaching], and thus darkness has been dispelled.

Filling the eastern quarter, illuminating the universe with his rays, and possessing the seven sciences as his steeds—is this God, the omniscient lamp of all, not seen by you shining so brilliantly? 12.49.

Whoever supports that which is the support of all, known as Brahman, whose form is delightful like the sky, shining like an autumnal blue lotus, determined by its manifold qualities through various words, and who has taken refuge in the sun of honey—[he alone sustains it]. (12.50)
Flee, flee with all haste, O Asuras who speak like Atrins!
For the Man-Lion (Narahari) blazes forth with his vast intellect;
he [will destroy] the sprouts of suffering of the noisy fools with his sharp, reasoned claws.
The roar of his harsh speech rends those who are unpleasant to him.
May he who assumes infinite forms even while remaining with but one wing in his heart toward the Lord of the World;
who, though capable, gave the nectar of immortality here to all virtuous beings but not to his own mother;
who, being the best of birds, humbles the pride of others—may that other [Garuḍa] lead you to prosperity.
O deceitful serpents, do not indulge in pride; quickly resort to those various caves of the double-tongued ones.
Vedavrātasudarśana, resounding with the conch-sound of brilliant logic (Tarka), wielding the mace of the radiant Purāṇas, equipped with the Śārṅga bow of the multitude of verses,
and skilled with the Nandaka sword of the Itihāsas among the true Sūtras— He is the Nārāyaṇa known as Madhva.
He has arrived with the desire to seize you; flee, O enemies of the gods who are skilled in illusion!
"Expel him!
thus cries the multitude of virtuous people, who are dressed in the guise of hatred toward the proponents of illusion; having heard this, he has departed from this place of his own free will.
The heavy-minded one dwelt in the abode of the gods called Prāgryavāṭa, rejoicing in the god who is the very embodiment of bliss.

Thus ends the twelfth canto, titled "The Joy," in the great poem *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, composed by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, the son of the venerable Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
The Thirteenth Canto:

Once, a certain man approached the Mountain King, who had risen with far-reaching vision, who had achieved his purpose, who had accepted the prostration [of others], and who had joyfully received his own disciple. 13.1.
"May the Blessed One come here without delay for the sake of showing favor to us, his own servants who have approached him.
Desiring to accomplish this task, he addressed the King, saying, "He entreats you," and having bowed to him, he spoke thus. (13.2)
Then, having left the quarter of Indra and proceeding toward the western direction with increased splendor,
that sun among wise men shone as he purified the earth by the contact of his own feet.
Having abandoned the impurities frequented by Māra, as one leaves behind base mountains with the torrents of a mountain stream,
he was swiftly approached by virtuous men who, through their supreme affection, had gradually become serene.
In this world, a man of irresistible valor—who, like a tree adorned with jasmine fruit, bends down the lofty trees with his rays;
who brings about the breaking of those who do not bow; and who, through his firm nature, does not spare even others—[is truly great]. (13.5)

Constantly attended by various people from the countryside who were amazed by the festival of his departure, and being traveled to from distant lands by men seeking liberation from suffering—his fame spreading rapidly in all directions. (6)

Served by the immortals, their followers, the lords of sages, and others who are beyond direct perception, he is the very essence of contact with the lotus feet of Hari; in this world, he is exceedingly the purifier of the purifiers. 13.7
This king, the supreme teacher of the excellent ford of supreme bliss, was irresistible in his departure;
he shone with an exceedingly intense splendor, like the continuous flow of the celestial river.

In due course, he went to that most extensive realm known as Stambhapadopasarjana; there he entered the abode of the Lord of Love, a repository of nectar, which is worthy of veneration by all the worlds.

The hosts of disciples quickly recognized that he, who had spent the night here and had performed his morning devotions, was now intent on departing, by the signs of his preparations for the journey. 13.10.
In front of him, ascetics clad in saffron robes stood ready for the purification of their meditative absorption;
with the effort of assuming their appropriate insignia, such as the staff and other marks, they suddenly drew aside their cloths.
Having discerned with a wise mind that those who bear the marks of the manifest conch possess a softened disposition,
she placed upon his neck the radiant garland of *tulasī*, fit to be the remains of Hari’s own offering.
Having purified his hands with water that was full of the forms of the Guru, the lineage, and the deities, and which was as pure as the breath of those disciplined in yoga,
he bore a chariot adorned with earrings of virtue, bound by excellence, and covered in armor.
The group of young disciples bore, with no effort at all, the heavy burden of water-pots, ritual vessels, and large books themselves; for there is indeed no other quality equal to skill.
There, some laughed at the new disciple, who for a long time had been wandering about in great agitation, looking toward Bharadvāja, repeatedly intent on questioning yet distracted.
Then, at that moment, urged by another under the pretext of the deep sound of a large bell struck against his thigh,
Amitapramati went out as his own people were departing.
Holding his excellent sunshade, that noble king of ascetics, as he rose higher and higher, attained the splendor of the full moon rising above the clouds. 17.
Bearing within himself Mukunda, the sustainer (or bearer) of the three worlds, that Guru himself bore him;
yet it is no wonder that he was carried by someone else as well—for indeed, he is the Lord of Life who bore him.

Ascetics, householders, and the foremost of the twice-born, who had abandoned prohibited and desire-driven states as prescribed by the Vedas, followed him in numbers of hundreds—like their own inherent duties embodied here in this world. (13.19)

The members of his retinue did not feel the hardship of the road while gazing upon that jewel among men; for it is no wonder that living beings attain liberation from existence merely by remembering him. (13.20)

Then, in the region beloved by Madaneśvara, as the Lord was approaching, the noble Nṛsiṃha—of auspicious intellect and named Siṃha distinguished by his pillar (stambha)—suddenly encountered him. 13.21.
Having already dismounted from his vehicle and having cleared the soldiers from even his own path,
he approached the presence of the one whose feet are worshipped by the three worlds together with several brahmins and bowed down.
Followed by the lord of the earth, whose mind was moist with the sentiment of devotion due to his disciplined humility,
he soon reached the vicinity of that most excellent sanctuary of Viṣṇumaṅgala.
The people from both villages, as well as others, gathered together with a desire to see the god among men;
they gazed repeatedly at him of infinite mind as he approached, submerged in an ocean of curiosity.
He was being attended by those in front of him who, with sweet voices, sang songs of Mukunda composed by themselves that were pleasing to the ear,
and who, skillful in dance, performed dances while bearing the marks of lotus seeds and wheels.
Followed clearly by the lord of the earth, who joined his palms in salutation, endured the crowding of the people, and—
desiring to make himself an object of compassion— went along with sincere servitude.
His form, the greatest light, was such that it could not be defined by men through observations such as "this is thus";
he clearly appeared like another Lord of the Day rising to further adorn the earth. (13.27)
Advancing slowly, as it were, in a carriage as bold as that of the foremost of young lions,
he was leading the earth to a state of purity with his two feet, which were like exceedingly crimson sprouts.
His feet possess the luster of rubies surpassed by his toenails; his heels are like those of a noble tortoise, and his ankles are well-concealed.
His shanks are to be served by the fingertips of the best of gods, and his pair of thighs are like the magnificent trunks of elephants.
His lower garment was a special, fresh silk cloth shining upon his beautiful and pure rounded hips;
he was graced by three distinct lines clearly visible upon his slender waist, neck, and forehead.

He shone with a soft, fine, thick, reddish, and translucent outer garment (a manifest and excellent cloak), like Mount Meru with its golden peaks bathed in a mass of rays from the exceedingly fresh and sharp-rayed sun. 13.31.
He possessed a broad chest and high walls of shoulders, with long, heavy, rounded, and beautiful staff-like arms;
he was endowed with the marks of the upward-pointing banner and other signs, shimmering within his most crimson, sprout-like palms.

At first, by his sudden appearance, his face—possessing a stainless purity that made it an object of doubt as to whether it were the orb of the full moon, and bearing a supreme, distinct splendor like an ocean of the play of clear light—was beheld. (13.33)

With a most beautiful gentle smile that bestowed the luster of fresh jasmine buds upon his auspicious, reddish lips, he gladdened all the worlds even with the glances of his lotus-like long eyes. (13.34)
His ears were adorned with clusters of sacred *tulasī* that shone with intense brilliance; his cheeks possessed a mass of immense luster;
his excellent eyebrows were skillful in bestowing both worldly prosperity and spiritual liberation upon the three worlds; and he wore a beautiful crown.
Measuring clearly every single limb in order to observe the characteristics of a divine image, the experts fashioned her body; she is now called by us "Sulakṣmī" (She of Excellent Marks). 13.36.

Though situated in the midst of a vast multitude of people, he— whose chest was raised high— out of compassion revealed himself to those with excessively longing eyes who stood afar for fear of the crush of the crowd.
Surrounded by a circle of people who resembled his own joy, with palms joined and bowed in supreme reverence, Prabarhabodha entered the temple of Murāri, the beloved of the world.
Seated in the midst of the various lords together with the king of men, that hidden deity shone like the full-orbed moon in the center of the stars along with the son of the Earth.

While his preeminent disciple, who possessed a voice with qualities such as resonance and pitch suited to the subject, was reciting the *Bhāgavata*, the Blessed One spoke this story of the Wielder of the Discus, which destroys worldly existence. (13.40)

That discourse—possessing the essence of noble fortitude, sweet, abundant in feeling, and serene—was sufficient to plunge both the learned and the unlearned who heard it into an ocean of the aesthetic flavor of bliss. (13.41)

How could even the gods possibly describe the playful movements of Madhva—his walking, sitting, and conversing—which grant liberation upon mere remembrance? Indeed, those like me, of limited intellect, certainly cannot.

Born into the lineage of the Aṅgirasas, a family of *likuca* trees endowed with excellent qualities such as penance and poetic talent, there was a wise man named Guha, a preeminent poet honored by all disputants. (13.43)
His beloved wife, virtuous and worthy of his qualities, though by the power of fate her children repeatedly died, yet—
desiring sons and devoted to the two sons of Vasudeva, the lords of the world— sought their favor.
Through the grace of the two supreme lords, the wife of the sage gave birth to that jewel of a son;
in the cities of those who hold the rank of scholar, no one was found by the foremost examiners to be his equal.
Beholding the moon-like face of Nandana, who possesses the marks of being capable of uplifting his own lineage,
the poet, performing his duties with a sense of fulfillment, gave him the appropriate name Trivikrama.
Even as a child, the young sage was a poet who spoke flawless verses; for indeed, even as a mere infant, the Lord Sun shines forth with the power of radiance despite being shrouded in darkness.
When the proper time arrived, that *likuca* tree— its branches shining with all its parts complete, and worthy of being served by noble birds—
produced the fruit of poetry, delightful in its flavor, for the benefit of the good travelers.
He himself demonstrated how the vast undertaking of the illusory [destruction] was difficult to accomplish;
though his own teacher was unable to prevent it, he heard enough about it from his friend. (13.49)
When the Blessed One rose with his playful grace, and the noble Trivikrama abandoned his state as a student,
even all those led by the Sun quickly attained the brilliance of fireflies.

When one hundred and fifty thousand years had passed, his father spoke in private to his son Nandana—who was exceedingly clever-minded, a hero in logic for the world of illusion, and highly honored on the face of the earth because of his greatness: *atidakṣamatiṃ sapādalakṣe samaye māyijanasya yuktiśūram‌ | mahitaṃ hi mahītale mahimnā janako nandanamabravīdupāṃśu || 13.51||*
Listen to these words whose meaning has been deliberated: in the Kali age, meditation on the attributeless is not for the sake of happiness.
Therefore, my son, for the sake of secondary liberation, remember (worship) the God Vāsudeva alone, who is rich in attributes.
Having heard these words of his father, and having reflected upon the essence of the scriptures, he— though somewhat agitated in spirit—
desiring to ascend to the supreme state, listened from others to the practice of yoga which transcends the [three] qualities.

Devoted to his own duty, the foremost of householders, though his heart was agitated by the Kali age—alas!—once reflected clearly and intensely with a sharpened mind by his very nature as follows: (13.54)
Surely the Sūtra composed here by the son of Satyavatī himself is the authority for the wise;
otherwise, all the commentaries, even when mutually consistent, would not attain the status of authority. (13.55)
If we were entirely free from attachment to those [works], we would indeed find nothing at all easy to compose;
nevertheless, out of affection, we do not fail to study that which has come down through tradition, even if it contains elements of mixture.
Considering that this practice is not easily accomplished by one of small intellect within the secret teachings (Upanishads) of the Ghaṭa, we reflect thus:
no one attains liberation here except through this very worship prescribed by the tradition. (13.57)
The pervasive Self, which is bliss, existence, consciousness, and non-dual, is indeed ordained as the object of worship by those who know the truth;
yet it is not defined as a composite whole, nor is it merely a mass of light—this is the secret. (13.58)
If such a form of his is worshipped, it appears as darkness by way of elimination;
and if the fruit were likewise liberation of this kind, then this worship would not at all satisfy us. (13.59)
Now, having personally examined the Vedas, Purāṇas, Mahābhārata, and other scriptures,
we worship the virtuous Mukunda here according to our understanding, while strictly practicing the duties prescribed by tradition with great clarity.
Having determined that this was what must be done, the Noble One proceeded to act out of discernment;
then he heard of the pure and complete fame of the Perfectly Wise One throughout the worlds.
For some person, though highly eloquent, destroys our traditional agreement that has been handed down through generations;
cast him out, you who are a hero in the art of irrefutable reasoning, so that others may not attain competence in that regard. (13.62)

For you, who had plunged further into the rivers of the Vedas and were dwelling within the oceans of the Samaveda, there arose no obstacle to warding off the lordly elephants among disputants, even though you delighted in the flavor of new poetry.
Come forth, O one as white as the moon; dispel the fear of your own herd. Now, having warded off that opponent of opposing disputants brought forth by fate, [protect us]. 13.64
Thus, being entreated here and there by the people of Mithilā as if they were his own kinsmen,
he— whose speech was agreeable and who considered himself the greatest of men— fell into doubt in his mind, even though he was one who cuts through all doubt.
This poet, disheartening those men who wielded the goad of sweet and honeyed speech,
further blinded them with indignation by showering upon them various kinds of dust in the form of rebuttals.

During those nights, that discerning man, having perceived the essence of the scriptures—which are rich in wisdom and pleasing to the mind—produced a great internal wonder, full of serenity, unknown to others. (13.67)

Having understood [the situation] through his conduct and having observed Sudarśana’s extensive awakening, he did not hastily adopt his opinion out of mere certainty; for indeed, a wise man performs everything only after due reflection.
Then the noble one, whose prowess is unequaled, approached Viṣṇu—who had gone to the auspicious place of Maṅgala and possessed abundant awakening—and paid him homage;
he, who bestows bliss, did so with the splendor of a smile from his four faces, just as Indra approaches the lotus-born Brahmā to learn the ultimate truth.

Thus ends the thirteenth canto, titled "Bliss," in the great poem *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, composed by the venerable Nārāyaṇapaṇḍitācārya, son of Trivikramapaṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of illustrious poets.
The fourteenth canto: Amidst the dense assembly of sovereign clouds, the lion-like king, through his power of vigor,
completely abandons his state of dejection due to his lack of moisture.
When the radiant sun of spring clearly rose with its brilliant splendor,
the entire world became enchanting for the sake of the beauty of the lotus-like virtuous people.
"Whatever has been done or whatever harm has been caused by us, O noble ones adorned with forbearance, may it be forgiven"—
with such humble words and earnest entreaties from their masters,
the collection of texts belonging to others was taken away through the power of incantations.
Śaṅkarārya received [it] through the application of the ten hearts. || 14.2 ||
The lion among men, whose vast mind was bowed down at the side of the tree, was surrounded by village leaders and commoners who had previously been his subordinates;
gracious due to his innate victory and noble prowess, he was free from all strife.
This crest-jewel of the family of poets gratified him with a blessing. || 14.3 ||

Alas, the dust of the feet of that supreme pilgrimage site of bliss— the dust which the daughter of Puraṃdara (Śacī) attends most intensely in the assembly of the gods, yet which is difficult for those of meager fortune to attain— may that dust grant you, O Upholder of the Earth, perpetual happiness within your heart. 14.4.
It is no marvel that this lord of poets perceived the exceedingly profound essence of the virtues of this work, even though it was not yet fully familiar to him;
for the king of bees, emerging from his hive, seeks to obtain the honey of the flowers.
Surely one who lacks familiarity might become a master even in the forest. || 14.5 ||
Increasing the fault of hatred among the entire multitude of the wicked, yet creating curiosity among mediocre men,
he bestows prosperity upon those auspicious ones who are worthy of his own path.
In this manner, he spent several nights with a heavy heart.
At that praiseworthy hour, he who is the foremost among those who know what must be done, having performed all his duties, rises in the son of Vinatā;
[he reveals] the Brahman known as Nārāyaṇa from behind the curtain of Aruṇa.
Seated in the yogic posture appropriate for him, he meditated upon the qualities of the Guru.
There, many lords of ascetics bathed simultaneously with excellent tooth-sticks that made their teeth exceedingly white;
they clearly demonstrated their mastery over the various rules of conduct as taught by their gurus, through the excellence of their ritual actions.
Having previously risen before their final hour of sleep, the disciples performed service for their teachers, even that which is difficult to do;
and from that time forward, they remained devoted until midnight with great reverence.
How could a desirable happy rebirth ever be theirs? 14.9
Due to the causes of hearing and reflection, having long been sleepless, his mind is suddenly seized by a paralyzing sleep;
even while he himself swiftly offers his limbs, garments, and so forth to the venerable one, [he remains unaware].
Suddenly awakened from sleep, a certain disciple followed after him. || 14.10 ||
"Why was what was prescribed done previously as if it were not prescribed?"—
with such apprehension of censuring their teacher, the disciples, their bodies bowed low, remained for a long time unable to descend [from the path], having abandoned the way.
While the gurus were present near the water, he remained silent.
Having offered water for honor and other gifts with waters filled to the brim in vessels that blaze with the light of lamps at the sides of his vast heart,
the ascetic of most restrained mind [proceeds] from the assembly of the images of the Discus-bearer.
He respectfully offered the foremost of fuel-sticks made of flowers.
Even upon seeing that the nectar was leaking from the stalks of the discarded flower-offerings,
the disciples, though immediately possessed by delusion, believed it was indeed clarified butter because of his authoritative words; yet later, their confusion vanished.
Day by day, he should serve that person worthy of service with ambrosial food according to his ability.

There, the sovereign Sun, possessing the three powers, arrived with his rays— his subjects— in accordance with the counsel of those three who had risen, whose souls were approved by the wise, and who were learned in the five branches of knowledge.
Possessing exceedingly large tusks, he bore within himself a sixfold splendor of his own essence.
The sun, resembling a mass of collyrium, has filled the abodes of the world with an exceedingly intense and most persistent mass of darkness that has blocked the paths of all living beings.
Like Hari with his claws, he scattered [them] with the foremost clusters of rays.
The rivers have sweet waters, their vapors are stilled by the night,
and they are suddenly clear from their own flow;
the quarters of the sky, like women, possess vast ruddiness and are bright with the very red sun in the utterly clear heavens.
With their own hands, they embraced those whose faces were like smiling lotuses.

The friends, having attained their place amidst the multitude of the virtuous, acquired a special beauty from the dust raised by the impetuosity of prostration; they brought benefit to others, making known the arrival of the appointed time.
They were like the banners of the one with a thousand banners (Kāma) for the sake of the disciples. || 14.17 ||

In the assembly of the speaker, these beings endowed with courage, having swiftly completed their duties, quickly gathered around the high and appropriate seat of yoga occupied by the blessed group of renunciants.
They gathered together and stood waiting for that supreme task of hearing [the Dharma].

Ah! The inner meanings of the Vedāntic doctrines— those which possess stainless qualities, beautiful coverings, and reside in the enemy of Mura (Viṣṇu)— shone forth suddenly when their contents were fully revealed by the intellect, just as the interiors of houses shine when their beautiful covers are suddenly removed.
Heaps of various folded papers. || 14.19 ||
Though not too sparse, they do not touch one another; they possess a beauty attained through rows of various bodies that are more upright than straight;
resembling elephants and horses from afar, their extremities are avoided [from being seen].
The colors shone upon them, depicted in the form of auspicious figures.
Some immediately perceived the portion to be recited and so forth through their familiarity and skill, while others did so only after a long time; meanwhile,
these [others] quickly performed the salutation to the Guru Hari with effort.
They proceeded toward peerless perfection, for effort must lead to success.
As this person remained silent and bowed,
he cast aside that curtain of his garment, which was as red as an evening cloud; then,
like the sun, he whose feet are worshipped by the sun stood within the assembly-hall.
Shining with a thousandfold radiance, he was exceedingly resplendent.
Those excellent letters, which are the supreme splendor of the three worlds and are described as possessing the essence of the three white [syllables] whose Vedic meanings are manifest—
Pṛthumati, having properly brought about their unification,
The learned one offered praise for the sake of purifying the teaching. || 14.23 ||

At the time of their final breath, as the reciters clearly uttered the very last syllable of the Upanishads, there occurred a most wondrous phenomenon for the living beings whose ears heard it: [The translation of the verse: "At the time of their final breath, as the reciters clearly uttered the very last syllable of the Upanishads, there occurred a most wondrous phenomenon for the living beings whose ears heard it. (Note: The provided source text appears to be a fragment of a longer verse. The translation above reflects the literal meaning of the Sanskrit fragments given.)
He made this the cause for the state of immortality for [the attainment of] the immortal.
Like the son of the Sun (Yama) bestowing clouds upon those who are clouded,
or like the fierce Pārtha (Arjuna) granting hundreds of arrows to those seeking battle, he,
free from weariness, ceaselessly bestowed [his gifts] upon us.
He gives a reply that is never dejected to all those who challenge him. || 14.25 ||
Then, having set aside the teaching of the West, he who possesses a thousandfold splendor came to the lake to bathe; meanwhile,
Pṛthumati remained here, longing for the company of the most excellent.
He immediately arrived together with the celestial river and other excellent holy places.
This mass of intense aesthetic flavor, which is exceedingly pure within and possesses affection like a multitude of sages,
first assumes the likeness of the Omniscient One through direct perception.
He clearly attained a form beloved by the virtuous upon his immersion.
May those noble forms of the one of immeasurable intellect— who possesses arms as radiant as conch shells and who performs the consecration here with stones shaped like chariot wheels—
be fully present within them.
They shone like the slender limbs of the beloved of Pāñcajanya.
The Lords of Sages declare that the service of this [water], performed with devotion, is fully equal to the fruit of twelve years of fasting;
it is even more meritorious than bathing in the celestial river (Gaṅgā) and other such venerable waters—
he who possesses but a fragment of awakening has drunk that water from the feet of Viṣṇu.
With twelve upward-pointing white sectarian marks (*ūrdhvapuṇḍra*) like sunbeams,
possessing the exalted splendor of the supreme *Sadarapa* mantra, and beloved by Hari,
he was unbearable for embodied beings who had turned their backs on the Enemy of Mura.
Another, wise in mind, appeared like one in a state of dissolution.
As the multitude of people gazed upon the naturally sweet face of that one of superior intellect— which was like the disc of the full moon under the guise of a mask—
they first cried out, "Move aside! at the words of the disciples.
He quickly moved forward from nearby along that path with palms joined in reverence.
The water used for washing the pair of lotus-feet of the Guru,
when held by the multitude of people, contains everything found upon the earth;
even though the earth itself does not welcome this, it nevertheless endures it.
How indeed could her reputation for forbearance possibly remain otherwise? 14.32.
Holding at his side the finest [lotus], which has not yet experienced the distinction of being tasted, which is cool, light, fragrant, pure,
and untouched by impure hands, and which he carries on its side out of fear of the breath from his mouth; the one with stainless hands.
The self-restrained Kamatha brought it, filled with water from his hands.
With its excellence of beauty, like a smile that breaks the stalks of lotus fibers, the moon— white with brilliance— filled the lovely water-born flower with floods of nectar;
it is to be cherished by those who perceive the specific qualities of the season.
With fragrant jasmine flowers, he clearly appeared as one with white wings.
He worshipped the Lord with drops of pure sandalwood water,
and honored Him with a royal array of flowers from fresh and charming *tulasī*,
including all varieties of terrestrial and aquatic creepers, trees, and shrubs.
Like the goddess Indirā herself, she was the personified glory of the successful completion of childbirth for the Lord of Indira.
Bestowing sixteen services here with superior understanding, he abandoned the thirty-two faults that precede them; thus,
with immeasurable virtues, he highly gratified the wielder of the Śārṅga bow.
With supreme devotion, he also assigned six attendants to perform services.
Indeed, he constantly worships Him who has the color of a red coral gem, who is bathed within the temple known as the divine body by the waters of the mind’s river of immense faith,
and who resides upon the seat of the heart-lotus.
But it is not "at once," meaning with eight flowers consisting of the flowers of the [eight] mental states. || 14.37 ||
Having performed the highest rites of hospitality, the wise man—his arms, chest, and shoulders anointed with the fragrance of thick, pure sandalwood water;
his moon-like face radiant with a gentle smile; and clad in smooth, silken garments—[stood there].
It was a festival for the eyes of the father-in-law, the sages, and the men.

Furthermore, that lord, who was proficient in the doctrines of the Vedas and constantly regarded himself as one whose supreme devotion remained unconquered, here partook of the finest rice without any effort, having obtained it as if it were already his.
May Śauri, the sovereign lord of the entire world, be pleased by this.
Seated upon a couch covered with fine cloth, adorned with companions and excellent sandalwood paste in the form of young sprouts,
he delighted [the assembly] here with various charming displays of learning.
Adorning the preeminent pavilion, which was surrounded by a circle of poets.
Having found the opportunity, his beloved— whose sprout-like hands had become the very seat of the beauty of her face through the play of her eyebrows—
and having understood his intention through the blossoming of his smile and eyes, [acted].
He quickly deliberated upon some matter in private.
Having passed by those throngs of people gathered not far away— who were united and whose sole purpose was the act of prostration before him of noble mind— [he entered].
Many householders here, desiring to perform preliminary service, quickly reached his side and prostrated themselves with a spirit of eager rivalry. (14.42)
Inhabitants from various lands, previously amazed by his qualities as heard of them, now beheld him with a hundredfold greater wonder;
with their lotus-like hands folded, they were granted the command, "Be seated."
Others honored him with hearts of even greater abundance.
"Enough, enough with this recitation! It shall be recited later;
for now, the teachers have indeed risen to speak. Cease your reflection and come quickly!"—thus he called out to them.
The foremost of disciples [instructs] the disciples who are devoted to the mastery of what they have heard. || 14.44 ||
Beholding this preeminent intellect, who shines with his commentary like Hari— the son of Satyavatī and best of poets—
they remain with hearts full of joy, gazing upon him constantly and without blinking.
Even when the appointed time had arrived, the people did not perceive it. || 14.45 ||
Like the sun at its rising, he shone clearly with a stainless form— lovely to behold and full of affection;
he attained the pure state of Hari for those who take refuge in him amidst the abundance of his prosperity.
For there is indeed no distinction among those who are elevated by their own self-luminosity.
Upon the earth, who possesses the hue of an excellent emerald, the lady of the ocean shines for half a moment as if partially concealed; then,
under the guise of the intensely red orb of the rising sun, she appears as a ruby.
It was a sight to behold, appearing like a mass of honey-colored rays. || 14.47 ||
In the earth, water, fire, wind,
ether, ego, and intellect— endowed with the qualities of primordial nature and the unmanifested space— he, being without body or mind, contemplated that one Reality through meditative absorption.
He is the Lord who possesses excellent qualities, superior to the Vasus, the Suras, and human beings.
The gods of the earth, who had clearly perceived the light, properly performed their twilight rites even while the light was still visible,
following the established rule as those well-versed in the Dharmaśāstras.
Meditating upon Savitṛ as the progenitor of the three worlds.
Those sixteen deities mentioned as being far more distant than this—
beginning with Hara, Hari, and Hayagrīva, and ending with the final digit (kalā) of Him—
are the Agnihotras of those who maintain the sacred fires, as they offer excellent oblations while emitting [the breath] through the mind.
They performed a fitting and unprecedented feat, by which the world of singers was moved.
"If he were not separated from her, he would surely be free of blemish, for she is like the beautiful moon to his own innate face"—
thus was he cherished by the celestial women, the *khecarīs*.
Then the full moon arose with an exceeding sweetness.
Having attained a separation that was unbearable even for the lotuses with their discs,
which had long been scorched by the former heat yet were now deeply satisfied;
[the moon] was attended at its feet by the soft lilies and the cakora birds through contact with the King’s rays.
One should never imagine destiny to be anything other than entirely agreeable to the heart.
With her smile, which possesses the luster of a dark sapphire and rows of teeth as white as fresh jasmine buds, she graced the head of that best of mountains.
He was endowed with a heart made fragrant by a forest garland.
He delighted the beautiful cowherd girls with his gentle gait and magnificent celestial palaces;
he was radiant, free from all distress, well-born, and clad in excellent, most subtle garments.
Dispelling the darkness with its rays, that Blessed One revealed a distinct reality that grants liberation to all beings;

yet this is the only difference: [the former] possesses a multitude of qualities consisting of blissful consciousness, while the moon possesses the quality of sound as its substance, despite both being full of perfect awareness.

Thus ends the fourteenth canto, titled "Bliss," in the *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, a great poem composed by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, the son of the venerable Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
Fifteenth canto. Then, having attained further awakening, he again expounded his wonderful commentary while dwelling there in that celestial abode, like an ordinary villager in a village. (15.1)
He saw Trivikramārya before him, mounted upon the chariot of the opposing faction and armed with the great weapons of harsh logic, like a rival hero.
Then, from the lotus-face of that lady, the speech consisting of well-composed arguments issued forth like a divine army emerging from its camp.
Neither too hurried nor too slow, without stumbling and continuous, it was proclaimed by those far away as having no diverse parts. (15.4)

Rich with a multitude of flowing streams of sūtras, it is an elephant-goad for the scriptures that are otherwise difficult to restrain; it is a great vehicle of sound reasoning and possesses the sevenfold team of diverse traditional memories (smṛti).

With her beloved like the ocean’s swelling waves, possessing beautiful breasts and a lovely voice, and having the splendor of a canopy for her purpose, she was like another Śrī, the goddess of the ocean. 15.6.
Having performed service at the lotus-feet of the Lord of Padmā,
her body was caressed by the Lord upon her head, like the Gaṅgā, purifying all.
Nārāyaṇa, who possesses infinite qualities, is named Brahmā and is known through the Vedas; as the creator of the universe and the knower of all, he was established by both scripture and reasoning.
If it is argued that the primary cause (*pradhāna*) is an independent, transforming cause,
like milk, then there would be a deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) regarding the illustrative example (*nidarśana*).
"The creation under dispute follows the will of an intelligent being, because it is a creation, like the creation of a cloth"—this inference establishes the subject [of the thesis]. (15.10)

That which they consider to be the relationship of principal and subordinate between the conscious and the unconscious would not be tenable if there were no dependence upon Īśa (the Lord) during creation. || 15.11 ||
Everything created by an omniscient being is occasional because it has an occasional cause;
that which is not so is not thus, like the self—such is the inference regarding God. (15.12)
For the sake of strength, the Vedas should be protected by all inferences;
otherwise, they proceed from mere desire, like lustful women with their husbands. (15.13)
Brahman cannot be a transforming cause because it is not sentient;
for that which is not thus is not thus, just like milk and the like. (15.14)

Paśupati is not the creator of the universe because his qualities are [only] heard [in scripture], just like Caitra; how much more so, then, for Vighna, Bradhna, and others who are suspected by the ignorant? (15.15)
Is it not the case that the Lord possesses happiness and so forth, because He is devoid of suffering and the like?
For whoever does not possess such [qualities] would not be thus, just as one who is subject to transmigratory existence is not [the Lord]. (15.16)
Thus, the wise man is not agitated because he is free from delusion; it is inferred that "he who is such is not so," and "he who is not so is not thus. (15.17)
If the Veda, which is to be trusted, contradicts the ignorance of the Omniscient One, then how could that [Veda] be worth hearing when it speaks of bliss as being non-bliss? 15.18
He who desires to avoid suffering and does not wish to accept happiness—that dull-witted man strikes down the suffering that has already fallen upon him, having forgotten the Lord. (15.19)
This inherence which is in Caitra is indeed non-different from that [inherence] which is in Īśvara;
otherwise, there would be a plurality of inherences. (15.20)
If its differentiation is said to be due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi), tell me: is it real or unreal?
For both of those options are subject to the aforementioned defects; therefore, do not speak of the Supreme as being like an illusionist (māyin).
If they should say that the distinctions of knowledge and so forth belong to the self only adventitiously (aupādhika),
then by this reasoning, through the refutation of that [adventitiousness], its possession of infinite attributes would be established.
Since there would be no end to the regress even if one were to depend on a relation when there is a distinction of qualities and so forth,
it is only by means of the particularity alone that the infinity of the qualities of the All-pervasive Lord is rendered beautiful.
Others, enemies of the scriptures, consider emptiness alone to be reality;
those Madhyamikas are also held to be twofold: the manifest and the concealed. (15.24)
The Vedāntins have declared that even Brahman is void;
meanwhile, the wicked in the end claim the Veda to be non-revealing of reality.
Because everything else is an evolution (vivarta) of the supreme reality, and because this [reality] is without distinction, there is no difference whatsoever between these two. 15.26
Shattering even the *Khaṇḍana-khaṇḍakhādya* through his logic of unimpeachable refutation,
he who knows the indivisible shattered the enemies of Indra, who themselves were not divided [in their devotion] to the Two.
If it were not of such a nature, a dissimilar cause could not exist because of its non-existence; therefore, it is inferred here that it is of such a nature, just like a potter. (15.28)
Aha! O ascetic, our cause is not empty, like that of a potter;
that from which the universe arises through conventional reality is designated as the "cause. (15.29)
If this is so, do not speak of emptiness as being causeless in any way;
O long-lived one, seek its foundation by studying under a teacher in his home.
That which lacks existence cannot be the locus or basis for dispute;
this is stated as a counter-example, like mother-of-pearl and the like. (15.31)
Since the claim that "valid cognition reveals what is not real" is self-contradictory,
he who asserts it thereby intends for the Veda to be non-authoritative.
How can that which the subverter of the Vedas calls the Veda and the Vedānta—revealing reality—be a revealer of reality, given that reality is inexpressible? (15.33)
If sentences function by means of the three characteristics, then it follows that those very characteristics would themselves become objects [of another sentence], which is undesirable. (15.34)
Moreover, in this indivisible [reality], sentences do not indeed enjoin anything at all;
if they were to declare a state of non-existence due to insentience and so forth, that would not be fitting. (15.35)

Because there is no existence of non-existence, and because that [reality] consists of existence, there is no distinction between existence and non-existence for that which is devoid of distinctions. (15.36)
Therefore, let it be determined by the wise that he who constantly proclaims the abandonment of the meanings known through the Vedas is outside the Vedic fold. 15.37.
By the very refutation of the elder [position], even the one considered clever is refuted;
for there is no distinction between these two sides, both of which possess opposing counterparts. (15.38)

This reason, "because of non-existence," is unestablished for the proponent of Brahman (Brahmavādin), because there is no distinction in the statement "not this" regarding both that [Brahman] and emptiness. (15.39)
If he accepts that the being of Brahman is qualified, then it would be a [limited] being;
if not, then by the principle of elimination, its non-being is established—so do not reject that. (15.40)
That which is censured by the wise is not to be investigated; it is not to be meditated upon, nor does it bestow fruit.
It is the void Brahman, the primordial non-duality, which is not within the scope of ritual injunctions or intellectual cognition.
Because it is indivisible like a sky-flower, there is no distinct example;
thus, one should infer [the lack of an example] as desired, just as in the case of the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and so forth. 15.42.
If the scriptures (āmnāya) lack authority, then dharma and so forth would lack a means of valid cognition;
and in the absence of dharma and so forth, there would be no means of cognition for one who holds perception alone to be the sole pramāṇa. //43//
A human statement is not determined to be authoritative, because it is a human composition, just like the speech uttered by a madman. (15.44)
"The person under discussion must be ignorant, or he must be a deceiver, because he possesses masculinity, like Caitra; thus are refuted all mere inferences against his omniscience. (15.45)
For that fierce attachment to evil scriptures which makes one's fate miserable causes suffering;
therefore, for those who possess such [attachment], the world will certainly become terrible.
If Adhokṣaja would grant liberation according to our desired view, then in that state virtuous beings, rejoicing in their own bliss, would enjoy manifold sense objects. (15.47)
Liberation, which is a state devoid of distinctions, must be disregarded because it contradicts [one's own experience] and other such criteria;
for in response to inquiries such as "When will this occur?", no specific qualification can be provided in the answer.
Even if devoid of intellect and the like, the person cannot be entirely without purpose for himself, because of the absence of all experience, like a wooden puppet or a corpse. (15.49)
One who possesses knowledge, effort, and desire is not powerless; indeed, he would not proceed toward what is unwholesome.
By his own power, he would therefore make himself such as that.
Seeing that happiness for one who is bound is permeated by suffering, [the seeker] abandons it through liberation;
yet if he were to abandon his own true nature as well, he would then become a proponent of emptiness (śūnyavādin).

"Surely one who possesses a body would be subject to error and possessed of waves, just like Caitra; therefore, 'being an impure embodied being' would be the limiting adjunct (upādhi) in that case. (15.52)
The reason [adduced] is inconclusive because of the body-possessing nature of the Lord;
if he were bodiless, then, like a rabbit's horn, he would be devoid of desire and the like.
If it is argued that its form as the knower and so forth exists for the sake of its distinction [from the body],
then that very [form] is what is denoted by the word "body," for this [Self] does not possess a material (prākṛta) configuration.
Thus, even for the liberated one, the possession of a body consisting of its own essential nature (svarūpa-deha) is accepted;
therefore, there can be no experience of what is undesirable arising from a material field (prākṛta-kṣetra).
That which is subject to dispute does not possess parts, because it would follow that it is perishable;
if it were like a cloth, then what kind of parts could be excluded here? (15.56)
If those [elements] are distinct from the Self and consist of non-consciousness, then your reason is one of proving what is already established;
