for proponents [of the Self] must necessarily accept that the Self is devoid of differentiation. (15.57)
Just as the self has spatial divisions extending from the location of an atom up to the extent of a fathom and beyond, so too do those [substances] have parts. (15.58)

The liberated one is a knower of form and so forth because he is sentient and distinct from insentient matter, like Īśvara; [this argument is invalid] because the example is deficient in the property to be proved, since Īśvara is held to be omniscient. || 15.59 ||
"Do not say that the Lord is not happy even while experiencing form and so forth, because of the consequence of suffering; for that [consequence] is refuted by the lack of pervasion. (15.60)
For one who does not accept this example, there would be a lack of negative concomitance (vyatireka);
therefore, [the self] is like a stone, [and thus] pure consciousness, the body, the senses, and the objects of enjoyment [would be non-existent]. 15.61

Why do these disputants harbor hatred toward liberation—which is described in the Vedas, established by reasoning, and consists of one's own bliss—or why do they maintain such dogmatic adherence to what is contrary to it? (15.62)
Therefore, because the Lord Viṣṇu is known through the Veda— which is a means of valid knowledge in itself— as the bestower of liberation and other goals, the entire universe becomes auspicious.
Then he heard Trivikramārya expounding meanings such as these, combined with detailed explanations, for one who was omniscient regarding the universe.
Then, impelled by the virtues of his awakening-bow, he discharged with vigor various sharp arrows of subtle reasoning, joined with opposing arguments. (15.65)
Then, with arrows of logic that were exceedingly powerful, he of unfathomable intellect cut them down with ease as they were being hurled, even while smiling.
Weapons that could not be borne by other men and were irresistible to ordinary persons, the best of the twice-born, desiring victory, employed against the missiles. (15.67)
By means of exceedingly powerful Vedic statements, like counter-missiles,
he turned them back by revealing a different meaning.
Having thus engaged in debate with him for seven or eight days, he who is dear to the wielder of the discus rendered him speechless and beyond reproach.
Having prostrated, that disciplined disciple said: "O Lord, may this rashness of mine be forgiven;
let the service of the dust of your lotus feet be granted to me forever. (15.70)
Then, with increased wisdom, the son of the sage began the commentary on the Bhāṣya; the virtuous commenced it with joy, while the wicked did so with the opposite feeling. (15.71)
Out of reverence for the command of his guru, this noble Śrīvikrama, while composing a commentary on the Bhāṣya which is difficult to master,
spoke thus to the Great Teacher (Mahācārya).
Since the jewels of logic within this ocean of commentary cannot be exhausted even by the lords of poets who collect them incessantly, its profundity is truly marvelous. (15.73)
The ten goddesses of the Upaniṣads, like gods longed for, fully propitiate their intended meanings within these abodes of commentaries. 15.74.
By these two— the Gītā and the Tātparya-bhāṣya—
the universe is illuminated even more intensely than by the sun and moon with their unimpeded rays of light.
Who that is wise would not partake of the nectar of the *Bhārata*'s purport, born from the ocean of *Itihāsas* and *Purāṇas* churned by the mountain of your mind? (15.76)
You have composed the *Śrībhāgavata-nirṇaya*, a true friend to those who travel the ancient path and who understand the three non-literal languages (Abhāṣās). 15.77.
Having attained the essence of the Kāṣṭha-tantra, who would not have his desires fully satisfied, like one who has reached the supreme Kalpa-tree whose shade is sought by the immortals? (15.78)
For the sake of beholding the worlds, you have established this path,
which is characterized by the honor of debate and possesses the appearance of the eyes of the Compassionate One.
Who indeed would not honor him who, all alone, set his foot upon the crowns of his enemies? (15.80)
Though small, the sparks from the fire of your treatises—debates and the like—are sufficient to consume the forest of opposing views when fanned by you, like a wind. (15.81)

An infinite meaning has been revealed by you within the *Bhāṣyasaṅgraha* concerning the atom; oh, how it serves for the full realization of the Self, like Kṛṣṇa [revealing Himself] within the mouth! 15.82
O Blessed One, while displaying worldly skill in painting and poetry, you indeed composed the *Bhārata-saṃkṣepa*, which was a secret [work] that caused wonder to the entire world. (15.83)

Who would count the excellent compositions— such as various well-spoken discourses, hymns, and verses— created by you, who are like a mine of jewels, any more than they would count the rows of gems within it?

In these assemblies, the council of the virtuous laughs loudly at those who are small-minded, even as it contemplates wish-fulfilling gems that grant immeasurable wealth despite being limited in number. (15.85)
Even though these scriptures exist and even though Indra and the other gods exist, another [teacher] is desired by us, just as the gods formerly desired the slayer of Tāraka.
From these unfathomable treatises, our arguments are difficult to extract due to the dullness of our minds; therefore, compose a work consisting of a clear series of reasonings. (15.87)
Thus requested, Madhva composed this Anuvyākhyāna, which is nectar for the virtuous, a thunderbolt for the pride of evil disputants, and a flash of lightning for the darkness of the Māyins. 15.88.
Sometimes he would compose this work continuously all at once;
indeed, he effortlessly caused four clever disciples to write it down.
Regarding that *Yuktimālā* which was composed by myself and is endowed with reason, this [work] provides a clear commentary; it is difficult even for the lords of poets to accomplish. 15.90.
Because of his eternal connection with the moon of honey (Madhu), which dispels the darkness and heat from their minds,
his younger brother lived in the house of his parents, who had gone to Vaikuṇṭha.

By him— who was weary of the world, a knower of the Vedas, and the sovereign of those who discourse on the Vedas— the abundance of wealth, cattle, and grain fell away as his eyebrows flickered at the ritual injunctions.
Looking at him who repeatedly bowed at his feet and entreated him for the life of a wandering mendicant, he, with a glance that awaited the proper time, sent him back to his own abode.
That man of steady intellect neither ate, nor slept, nor laughed;
seeking the right moment, he remembered his elder brother Rāma, just as Lakṣmaṇa, the younger brother of Rāma, would do.
Having somehow entrusted the kingdom to the king who was tormented by separation,
the Blessed One departed for his place of incarnation at the end of autumn.

Having enjoyed sense objects, Madhva made his younger brother—a man of pure lineage on both sides, learned in the Vedas, pure, one who had performed the rites for the ancestors, and dispassionate—a renunciant (yati). 15.96.
Brahmā, who is equal to Brahmā himself, imparted that most secret of secrets to him who was performing the five-fire penance— a secret which other ascetics do not know.
With a face bright with the nectar of love, preceded by a smile and a sidelong glance,
he who was named Śrī Viṣṇutīrtha bestowed upon him the Prītitīrtha.
By hearing, reciting,
and reflecting upon the Vedānta scriptures, he who was like a brother to his teacher of Vedānta spent his time not in vain.
Through the abundance of his self-restraint, devotion, sweetness, service, and other virtues,
he made the great tree of his guru’s well-established root of compassion flourish.
The majesty of that one who possesses an infinite mind and a wish-fulfilling tree of compassion cannot be described by people; yet, out of longing, it is being described here slightly.
He, whose mind had attained perfection through the human state within the sacred teaching, made me the fourteenth by adding "Madhva-dāsa" so that my number might be complete.
As he traveled toward the region of the moon, moving upon the earth, he purified the Tīrthaka and Viṣṇutīrtha, and Viṣṇutīrtha and Tīrthaka. (15.103)
While many ascetics were striving against their will for the stage of spiritual perfection, he,
with his true self concealed, reached the mountain of Hariścandra.
In the fire of the suffering of duality, the hero, free from envy through his lack of envy,
abandoned it, realizing that it served as fuel for the fire of hunger and other afflictions.
Requested by his devotees, the crest-jewel of ascetics was led to the foot of a mountain,
where he drank a small amount of the five products of the cow on every fifth day.
Abandoning that [practice], the reckless man performed most severe penance;
he was satisfied with bilva-colored leaves fallen upon the ground and even with water.
Yamī sat upon that stone as he desired, for he was well-disciplined;
it is a stone which ascetics, broken by fate, cannot occupy even for a single day.
Having conquered the wind through breath-control techniques such as *recaka*,
the younger brother of Pavana (Hanuman) restrained the horses of the senses from their objects by means of the chariot of the mind.
Recalling the form of Murāri, the knower of the supreme self meditated;
he attained that samādhi which pacifies mental afflictions and is obtainable through yoga.
Immersed in his own wondrous jewel— a beautiful form adorned with armlets and an ocean of qualities such as self-bliss— he perceived nothing else at all.
For him who was free from the fear of desire and possessed the eye of excellent wisdom, there was no value for the jewel of yoga except for the sovereignty of absolute liberation. || 15.112 ||
The favor that Madhvanātha then bestowed upon Madhvānuja cannot be described, either because it transcends the scope of the mind or because it must be kept secret. (15.113)
Oh, how great is the majesty of service to Mahābodhi in this age, since that blessed man attained this perfection and was thus praised by the immortals! 15.114
One who was firm in his vows, a knower of that which transcends the senses, an ocean of learning, and a scholar in logic;
a beloved disciple who took refuge at the feet of Aniruddha approached him.
This silver throne, which had been sought after and obtained by him, was regarded by the subjects as the Omniscient One himself who had returned among them out of compassion. (15.116)
The crest-jewel of poets, the crown of the learned, and the foremost among those who have conquered suffering—
Madhvakelīśuka was his disciple, taking refuge at the feet of Vyāsa.
He, performing a favor for that great being who was surely destined for servitude even among the great, created wonder in men by means of his powers. (15.118)
He, who brings joy to Hari, ascended that mountain difficult for others to climb—
a great peak of immense majesty, beloved by Guha.
Another disciple of that wise one was he who, drawn by his all-pervading virtues, came from the Godāvarī; he was known as Padmanābhatīrtha. (15.120)
Pleased with his constant study, devotion, detachment, and perpetual service,
the omniscient Lord immediately granted him auspicious knowledge.
He who was a timiṅgila fish among scholars never abandoned the ocean of Vedānta; through the forceful current of his reasoning, he traversed the rivers of other philosophical systems.

He, the lion among debaters, refuted those who considered themselves heroes within their own circles merely by the sound of their explanations— those who were like village lions in appearance but possessed only illusory power.
He who, though possessing only four faces, became manifest as a five-faced lion in tearing asunder the heads of the intoxicated elephants of the Dūrvādins and others. 15.124.
From Bodhasāgara also arose the auspicious Saṅnyāyaratnāvalī, an invaluable commentary on the Parānuvyākhyā. 15.125.
He was honored as the disciple of a teacher of Vedic exegesis;
he was a member of the assembly who, knowing the essence of the Vedas, expounded the Veda in the hall.
Of these two, there were many disciples in the former and many great ascetics from various lands in the latter; such was the case for Anantabodha. (15.127)
Having brought their senses under control and having destroyed the cycle of birth and so forth,
they take refuge at the feet of Narasiṃha and have practiced the name of Upendra.
Those who take refuge at the feet of the illustrious Rāma are not long in their speech;
though their virtues are beyond perception, they are overflowing with oceans of devotion and detachment. || 15.129 ||
Purifying the earth with their feet and revealing the footstep of Hari, they—
having shaken off the darkness of the evil age— went to the earth like suns.
Constantly satisfied by serving the nectar-ocean of the scriptures of liberation,
these worshippers of the feet of the Lord of the Discus (Cakrin) engage in the most excellent worship of His forms as the Wheel-turner (Cakrin).
Madhvāpra had many disciples, whose own disciples in turn repeatedly adorned the earth to their full extent, all of them being decorated with excellent virtues.
They always dwell in the ocean of the nectar of bliss from expounding all the true scriptures;
they are the ornaments who shatter the harsh arguments of all wicked disputants.
Some possess a great weight of devotion yet have little wealth of learning;
others have little understanding yet possess the great virtue of extensive learning. (15.134)
Many householders also received complete favor from him, in whom the three fires were like blazing flames, yet he wore a crown of *likuca* fruit. (15.135)

Those best among the learned, who for the most part did not abandon their Madhva-lineage injunctions, were consecrated solely to sowing the seeds of true knowledge within the fields of their disciples. (15.136)

The village leaders and the foremost of Brahmins attained the status of disciples with their eyes full [of faith], for by the mere presence of his protection, they say, the supreme state is surely attained. (15.137)
To some, out of service, partiality, and other such qualities, he granted his own state—
which is difficult even for yogis to attain— just as Rāma, the beloved of Rāma, did.

Such is the excellence of his disciples and grand-disciples through the arising of his compassion; who would not desire that tree of the gods at his feet, which is so easily attained through devotion? 15.139
Thus, worthy of honor by the virtuous among the virtuous, he made his dwelling upon the earth while reclining on the bed of Śeṣa,
in a village purified by the winds from the Kāṇva holy sites.
Out of devotion to his disciple, he of undiminished wisdom remained in the excellent monastery. || 15.140 ||
The lunar orb of the face of the Lord Ānandatīrtha—
its luster expanded by the nectar of knowledge and most beautiful in its exquisite beauty—
was beheld here by those devotees for the sake of quelling the heat of worldly existence.
Does it not even grant a man the status of a servant to its servants and maidservants? || 15.141 ||

Thus ends the fifteenth canto, titled "Bliss," in the great poem *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, composed by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, the son of the venerable Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
The sixteenth canto:
The greatness of the one of vast intellect toward the virtuous who partake of the food from the feet of the Slayer of Madhu, and toward those learned in the Vedas.
Then, a certain wise scholar here clearly expounded the Vedānta, which is itself the root of bondage and liberation. 16.1
On the banks of the Gomatī, a king born of the lowest caste (antyavarṇa) hated the moon of pure fame, the knower of all things,
who was a practitioner of the virtues of the Vedas and the Vedas themselves.
The talkative one spoke these words to the best of eloquent speakers.
For that statement which deviates from its result in this world is not valid knowledge, like the ravings of a madman;
such serves as an example for its lack of authority.
And "in every way" refers to all the words of the Vedas. || 16.3 ||
"It is said that the fruit declared in the Vedas is fully obtained through qualification; to this, the rogue, with his mind not yet composed, replied:
'Indeed, a qualified person is not observed to exist;
therefore, he must be as non-existent as the horn of a donkey. (16.4)
Unable to endure that reproach and being thus addressed,
he immediately took up with both his sprout-like hands the seeds of medicinal herbs and scattered them.
By means of the hymn, he performed the creation of sprouts, leaves, flowers, and seeds.
Once, when the lamp had been extinguished during the night,
that ocean of great compassion again caused his own disciples to recite by means of the very light from the nails of the toe-nail of his own foot.

The great-eyed Lord [Śiva], for the sake of visiting sacred fords, accepted with great effort the waters brought by a thousand men from the Ganges, whose currents were capable of enduring the force of the vast waves cascading down the mountain slopes.
He beheld a massive rock somewhere that appeared like a pearl.
The people there said, "Whence has this stone been brought for the benefit of the world?
For men do not lead such a preeminent ascetic as this.
If Bhima exerts himself here, he might lead [them] away or not. || 16.8 ||
Having transformed himself into a monkey, he carried her like a mountain with his pure, playful lotus-hand;
there too, she was sufficiently indicated by him.
Indeed, even now, one's karma remains at the very threshold of that lofty state.
The path, adorned with clusters of flowers and abundant discourse,
belongs to disciples of restrained mind as well as others;
there, the moon dwells in this very lunar day.
Thereupon, that Sakalamati set out for the ocean. || 16.10 ||
With their limbs drenched from having just bathed in the lake belonging to Kaṇva, that bull among the twice-born,
the villagers there [proceeded] for the purpose of the eclipse of the sun’s rays.
Even all [of them], including children and the elderly. || 16.11 ||

Beholding the Omniscient One together with his retinue, those auspicious ones, their eyes blossoming and their faces smiling, rejoiced; while others, assuming a sullen expression, reviled him; yet it was no wonder, for both states depend upon one's own nature.
"Do not revile this teacher of the world!"— having thus rebuked them, he,
agitating all and possessing a terrifying appearance with a deep, thunderous roar, rushed forward like one with tossing waves for hands.
The King of Sindhu was indeed impetuous for the sake of subduing the wicked. || 16.13 ||
More restless than joy, rushing forward with speed,
possessing a deep resonance and praise, with foam for its laughter,
it [the ocean] here at the shore possesses exceedingly great waves as its limbs.
The ocean offered what seemed like a prostration with its honey.
The two oceans of Madhu and [Kṛṣṇa], which possess jewels that manifest various qualities and whose profound natures are unsurpassed by Goloka and Lāvaṇya, are dear to those of supreme intellect;
yet this is not the distinction of the ocean of salt water. || 16.15 ||
Seated upon a formidable rocky throne on the shore of the ocean, which was being caressed by the hands of its exceedingly swift waves,
the Lord expounded for a very long time the hymns of the Aitareya branch in an exceedingly beautiful manner.
In its profundity, this sound eclipses that of the ocean; yet, how wonderful, it possesses such a quality of audibility!
Who is this blessed one, whose face possesses the radiance of the full moon?
Having thought thus, that ocean of people quickly surrounded him.
In that place,
the people cried out intensely, "Shame, shame on those great envious ones who, out of malice, called this man— who is expert in proclaiming the true nature of the Vedas— a hater of the Vedas!"
Out of their own wonder, they indeed bow with palms joined in reverence.
Having bestowed great honor upon him with devotion, they bore upon their expansive hearts his foot-dust, which is worthy of being served by the gods;
and in that king of rivers, purified by more than his own bathing—
The groups of twice-born men performed the consecration at the auspicious hour. || 16.19 ||
Overwhelmed by powerful waves that are like irresistible herds of elephants,
tossing down multitudes of people as they surge upward,
and being violently churned about;
Many here, like the waters of the ocean, have become objects of ridicule.
The virtuous man laughed at him who was submerged, his form hidden by the broad waves, though he possessed complete wisdom—
he who was renowned as the teacher victorious over the three worlds.
"Alas! This very one falls down with a light, playful motion. || 16.21 ||
He, whose number was vast, did not heed the low and contemptuous words of the insignificant,
nor their tumultuous cries;
he disregarded the barking and yelping of the jackals.
For the five-faced one of noble prowess would not even count them.
The one of vast intellect brought about a glance that bestows birth, maintenance, and destruction for the worlds within the ocean;
he was indeed overwhelmed by that very glance, which was exceedingly heavy.
Releasing its movement, it became like a small pond.
Despite such deeds as these, which could not have been accomplished by anyone else, the wicked man did not gain great respect for him;
rather, he harbored hatred toward one whose fortune had been cast away.
When the mind is troubled, even that very thing may become auspicious.

Having reached the pleasure garden along with his companions, he fearlessly commanded the manifestation of his own splendor, saying to the onlookers: "It is appropriate for me to perform a small service for the people. (16.25)
In the temple of Śrīkaṇṭheśvara, there was indeed one man who, having struck with his heavy mace alone, brought down the banner-staff of thirty excellent kings,
as well as coconuts and other offerings.
He obtained at will fruits from the most trembling [trees]. || 16.26 ||
Possessing such power and majesty, even those two eldest sons of his seized his throat from both sides simultaneously and exerted the utmost effort to crush it.
Through friction, there arises sharpness that increases progressively. || 16.27 ||
At the command of their father, those two— strengthened by the Ashvins and aided by fire, the sun, and the wind—
cast off their heads, whose skins were exceedingly hard like iron, and fell to the earth with voices clearly articulated in turn.

Once comforted, these two, pure-hearted and free from pride, approached with great effort to lift her finger which rested upon the ground; yet, despite their forceful exertion, they were unable to move it.
Having effortlessly ascended the banyan tree, that gentle-smiling one proceeded here all around the house of Nṛsiṃha;
thus endowed with sovereign powers such as levity and the rest.
The king of wondrous jewels in the three worlds became honey-sweet. || 16.30 ||
He who brought up a wooden staircase for his residence, having had it carried by fifty men and porters— he,
Vyākhyāsvara, was the son of Damana of the eastern quarter.
From the instruction of his guru, he suffered the crushing of his throat.
Even while this [tradition] was perspiring as he strove with fierce persistence, the sound of his teaching surpassed that of the East;
yet, though his heart was vast, he was not able to raise up even a single finger.
Thus, curiosity arose among the people that he had been born. || 16.32 ||
The Lord scrutinized him with others headed by Śiva and Agni,
yet he was not overlooked despite their most powerful efforts;
nor was any deficiency in his power perceived anywhere in him, for he was necessarily perceived as Bhīma himself.

Though he was repeatedly pulled by being tied with a pen, not even a single hair on his body was torn out; nor did the blows of his fists, though delivered upon the soft tip of the nose, cause any injury.
The clarity of this moon was not attained by those of exceedingly great strength.
Like a five-headed serpent with snakes devoid of venom, or like the ocean with the meager waters of rivers and streams,
or like the sun with fireflies, he treated his adversaries— who were but men— like common animals. (16.35)
Having reached the celestial abode of Pāraṇtī, he who possesses vast consciousness remained there for a very long time, free from the need for offerings;
yet within merely half a day, he was [honored] by the foremost kings of the villages.
His manifestation produced many offerings of living beings.
Since the fivefold Lord of the Muras, established from of old with his innate companions in the state of Bhīma,
was honored here by the Princess of Pañcāla as she offered him the water for the Bali sacrifice;
Then he, who was worthy of worship, having honored him, remembered this very [teaching]. || 16.37 ||
It is said that he was about to travel to a region called Antarā,
where in summer there is no water; having heard of a lake there,
he caused a mass of clouds to pour down rain at that very time.
To fulfill that [desire], he aroused the curiosity of men.
Urged on by wicked ministers and groups of villains,
the village headman, a lord of low-born men, arrived there intending to strike him; then, seeing him departing, he pursued him.
Filled with wonder, he bowed down before him as if before the rising sun. || 16.39 ||

Having set out from that foremost field, the Lord of the Lord of Physicians of the three worlds, he who possesses vast inner power and majesty [reached] that which is named the Supreme Ocean of the Nectar of Śrī Kṛṣṇa.
He composed a series of true words for the welfare of his devoted followers.
"O learned ones, go even further to the highest state of exalted prosperity; where else are those like frogs in a dark well?
Thus spoke the one who considers himself wise through intoxication to the All-Knowing One.
He thought only of how to destroy that person. || 16.41 ||

Though he was omniscient, that ascetic remained firmly convinced that the other did not understand the underlying purpose of the sacrifice; thus, out of envy, he questioned him in the assembly regarding the nature of the fragments of the Vedic texts concerning the meaning of ritual action, which appeared so profound.
On the sixth day, he spoke to him— having been appointed by the lord of subjects as one skilled in collecting the distilled essence from the Vedic hymns—
concerning the various beautiful *narāśaṃsa* mantras that follow the final [verse], while dispelling his doubts.
Having observed his supreme scholarship,
the assembly of opponents, their minds agitated by such rivalry,
then described you, saying, "This man shall not be our goal."
"Tell him that," urged by Urumati, he ran off immediately.
He then asked about those great calamities described there as having the nature of being instigated by the followers of Manu;
and he spoke to him the meaning of that collection of words.
For the sake of stability, he immediately had it inscribed.
Like a lean dog agitated upon seeing the full moon risen, a multitude of inauspicious omens rushed from afar,
as if the enemy himself were charging forward.
What harm was done to that mine of nectar by this? || 16.46 ||
The compassionate one provided a few mouthfuls of food for the destitute and fourfold portions for his devotees;
he himself partook of the food fit for consumption by gods and men.
He, possessed of vast awakening, was for the delight of the wealthy. || 16.47 ||
Is this wheel of the regulation of rain and so forth a marvel in the wind that governs the world?
Even so, we describe him here as the foremost in his deeds, for he is the teacher of the world whose actions are merely a restatement of what has already been done.
Thus spoke the earth-dwelling deity: "O Mādhavī, this manifold narrative is not merely esteemed among stories;
it is proclaimed even by the foremost of the immortals in person."
For his delight, he was sung of by the Gandharvas in the celestial realm.
Having caused that [song], which was uttered in verse,
to reach a state of climax through the appropriate application of the *tāna*s, they produced the brilliant *gāndhāra* scale, whose domain is heaven, while employing the *pañcama* and other notes.
Those with crooked necks sang to the village, making it devoid of crows.

The lords of the gods, with their heads bowed low and crowned with beautiful diadems, and with their lotus-like faces touched by fingertips that were slightly reddened and adorned with smiles, listened with most steadfast devotion.
Thus ends the song concerning the conduct of the most noble among the ten sages. 16.51.
At that time, the gods, performing the worship for the great festival of victory, were filled with incessant conversation,
while the hosts of sages and subordinate deities looked on in amazement.
Then, with gentle smiles, she went to look at him.
Describing this well-composed true scripture as a mirror for beholding the multitude of Murāri’s virtues,
we illuminate the path of the moon for Pradyota.
These beheld the abundant play of the mind.
The lords of the Nagas did not bow to him as he dwelt in that region of the earth,
adorning the worlds with his glorious hymns and possessing the sweet Upanishad of the Aitareya.
He was expounding [the teaching] in the midst of various distinguished disciples. || 16.54 ||
Beholding their own guru— glorious, moon-faced, lotus-eyed, possessing a deep voice, and enriched with most divine marks— they worshipped him and felt they had achieved their life's purpose.
With their speech, these [goddesses] addressed him, whose desires were fully satisfied by Hari.
O Guru, you dispelled the darkness of ignorance through the rays of your own virtues, enabling me to behold the multitude of Mukunda’s qualities;
you conquered the fourteen worlds with your excellent attributes—may you likewise be our refuge through your compassion. (16.56)
Salutations to you, O Lord of life, whose power is manifested by those who bow before you;
salutations, O Master, dearest to Rāma, Hanumān, possessor of weighty virtues!
Salutations to you, O Bhīma, most powerful, beloved of Kṛṣṇa, O Blessed One!
Salutations to the illustrious Madhva; grant us clear vision; victory, victory! 16.57
Having spoken thus, the lords of the gods there,
cherishing that great and victorious Guru,
showered a fragrant rain of flowers over all that was visible.
In Śrīmad Ānandatīrtha, the most excellent beloved of Hari.

Thus ends the sixteenth canto, titled "The Chapter on Bliss," in the great poem *Śrīmat-Sumadhvavijaya*, composed by Nārāyaṇapaṇḍitācārya, the son of the venerable Trivikramapaṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
May this be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa within the Supreme Breath, the Lord of the Hearts of the World.
Eject.
(Anu-madhva-vijayaḥ) For the pleasure of the Lord of Śrī, the illustrious Hanumān was born, possessing most exalted majesty;
at the command of Rāma, he leaped across the ocean with the monkey-host, and having built a bridge, he crushed the wicked one.

Having worshipped the enemy of Rāvaṇa—who bears the earth upon his head—and having beheld him along with Sītā at Puragapura, that foremost of those possessed of great vital power descended from the Kimpuruṣa mountain to protect me. (Or: that great leader of the Prāṇas descended for my sake. || 1 ||

He who was Bhīma, who was impenetrable, who effortlessly drove away the calamities created by startled enemies, the slayer of Rākṣasas, who attained Kṛṣṇā, the performer of sacrifices, the destroyer of the wicked in the forest,
and the slayer of Kīcaka; he who, having slain Duryodhana and others, reached his own station, while the enemies of that [station] were enslaved by anger.
Having become a blade of kusha grass upon the earth, he who was preceded by Maṇimān performed a sacrifice; may he protect us. || 2 ||
For the purpose of uprooting ignorance, he was indicated by the words of the best of gods (Śiva) through his lord Rūpya;
born from the noble lineage of Madhyālaya, he was named Vāsudeva due to his profound intellect and asceticism.
He is the giver of liberation to the donor of the earth (the King), and a servant of the feet of the Lord of Silver (Rūpyapati). By the Lord of Beings (Brahmā)...
May Prāṇa, who is worthy of honor and who was satisfied even with kuluttha beans by his own brother, be pleased with me. || 3 ||

May the Blessed Lord Vāsudeva, the God who is no source of suffering, dispel my calamities such as ignorance— just as he himself did for the bull-king by holding its tail and driving away the danger— bestowing bliss upon all creatures through the nectar-drops of his gentle smile, through the beauty of his moon-like face, through his sweet words, through his playful childhood sports, and by such acts as supporting the bull with his tail.
He who, at the age of three, traveled alone two *yojanas* away from his father’s palace;

he whom the world’s mother used to fondle during his first lessons in writing, causing his father to marvel; he who defeated the self-important one named Śiva in debate before an assembly and expounded the meaning of the Vedic branches—[he is this man].
May he who was brought by his parents to the fortress and honored by the best of gods be magnified for me with these words. || 5 ||

May he who served his preceptor protect me— he who swiftly subdued the serpent and his adversary, who excelled all in the arts of leaping over great distances, swimming, wrestling, and other forms of prowess;
by whose pure words, as taught by the Guru, the head-ache of deluded doubt was utterly destroyed.
Then Surārtha, who was a knower of Nārāyaṇa, explained the Upaniṣad to his friend.
With his mind fixed on renunciation and his heart devoted to Hari, he first approached the wise ascetic— who was worthy of Arjuna’s worship,
fully authorized by his guru’s command, a knower of Hari endowed with excellent qualities, and one who had satisfied the gods through his austere penance—
from whom he received the boon known as the "Disciple of the Omniscient. Then, having gone twice to his own father to dissuade him [from worldly life], he departed.
He who, possessing innate wisdom, attained the unsurpassed state and delivered his mother and me. || 7 ||

There was one known as Pūrṇaprajña, an ornament to his lineage, of auspicious conduct, granted by the Lord, who performed ablutions in the celestial river [of wisdom] received through the command of the Lord; he who held the banner of victory over difficult verses and the cutting of doubts in the world, skilled in exposition, displaying intelligence in the narration of the true Purāṇas and Itihāsas—may that leader of the upright grant me auspicious vision. (8)
Ānandatīrtha himself, known by the name Anumātīrtha through his inferences,

swiftly conquered the ocean of intellect— that lion among disputants— thereby dispelling the wicked commentaries; with his unassailable speech, he brought joy even to his father when he spoke words of jest imbued with profound meaning.
May he who spoke the essence of the Sūtra to his dear friend for the purpose of composing a commentary protect me. 9.

Having departed for the southern direction, the Lord beheld the Kṣīriṇī tree, which yields abundant fruit; then, having reached Syānandūra, he swiftly conquered the Daitya there and arrived at the Phālguna Tīrtha.
Furthermore, at Setu, he made the wicked one laugh, and finally, he reached Raṅganātha, the Conqueror of All.
Having bowed to those whom the Lord of the Universe, who is worthy of universal veneration, taught to Upanadi—that fortunate one has indeed instructed me. || 10 ||
Skilled in expounding the meaning of the *Viśva* and other [Vedic] texts up to the *Śata-patha*, a proponent of the meaning of the hymns on giving (*dānasūkta*),
illuminator of divine knowledge, named Akhilajña, conqueror of all, one who has attained true form;
whether he be Bhīma or Bhīmasandhi, he is the author of the commentary on the *Gītikā* for the subduing of the host of the wicked.
May that Madhva—who seeks his guru, who bows to his guru, who shines in my mind, and who purifies the sacred fords—be present. 11.

Gaṅgātārin, who reached Badarikā through his virtuous deeds, having bowed there to Nārāyaṇa in a secluded spot, then rose up as a teacher of the doctrine; he, a man of great austerity, urged by Kṛṣṇa,
recorded from the authoritative sources the work that follows his own inner impulse, based on the mere palm of his hand.
May he who resembles the wind-god, beholding even Hari along with the heavy mountain for the sake of prosperity, be mine. 12.
He who beheld his own preeminent hermitage, the wonderful divine *sāla* tree honored by sages,
and there, in the assembly of seers, even Hari born of Satyavatī through a sage—
the author of the *Bhārata* and other works, the teacher of the Bharatas, and the author of the *Brahmasūtra*— alas! [he beheld all this].
May that Lord, who is faultless and possesses eternally full, innumerable qualities, be pleased with me. || 13 ||

I bow to the Lord, who shines with all his limbs worthy of universal veneration, dark as a stainless blue water-lily, composed of the most excellent qualities of the splendor of perfect bliss of knowledge (*jñānānanda*), and endowed with a form of complete beauty;
he whose lips are like the *bimba* fruit, whose feet are like lotuses, whose matted hair is auspiciously tawny, and who wears a deerskin.
Having seen him, having bowed, and having embraced him, may that Guru, who is beloved by the sages and now well-seated, protect us. 14.
Then [he saw] Nārāyaṇa, the disciple of Vyāsa; and Sumātsya, who has gone to the cause of all;
the reassuring Kūrma and Kola; then Nṛhari, Manu, Vāmana, Buddha, and Rāma;
Vyāsa, Kākutstha, and Kṛṣṇa; and for a very long time, Kalki and Yajña, the delight of others.
I bow to that Siddheśa, known as Dhanvantari and Varavanitā, who remembers him.
Bearing in his heart Dattātreya, Kumāra, Ṛṣabha, Haṃsa, Kṛṣṇa, Hari,
that righteous one known as Nārāyaṇa, and his infinite incarnations numbering ten,
a hundred, a thousand, and more— he, impelled by Him, has attained the state of being served by the most excellent and worthy men for the sake of proclaiming His true nature.
Even that Hari, known as Vyāsa-Nārāyaṇa, who is my refuge, has set out on a difficult journey. || 16 ||

Having obtained permission from Mukunda, he returned to his own people; enjoying many alms and delivering incomparable discourses, he departed again, possessing a multitude of qualities equal to his own.

Victorious over all branches of the six systems of philosophy, having obtained an excellent disciple, a preeminent teacher of surpassing triumph, and having attained various forms of wealth, such is my destiny. 17.

Having explained the Bhāṣya to his friend and removed the impurities of the Kali age, and having brought from the silver mountain the immovable image of Kṛṣṇa’s sister— which even the young gods could not move— by means of his power;
and having established it and cast out those intent on obstructing sacrifices, he caused his own sacrifice to be performed.
Having bowed to Vyāsa and having again returned from Rajata, that Madhva became fully serene. 18.

I desire to behold that Great-eyed Lord (Mahesha), who—being Sagarasva by nature—struck down the god Ishana as one powerless; who, without a boat, crossed the Ganges by his own method (or by his own way); who, as the ruler of the Yavanas, subdued thieves on some path while they were going to kill others, and caused them to slay one another; who, in another instance, quickly terrified his own disciple; and who, in yet another case, became like a stone through Yoga along with his attendants.

The destroyer of the tiger-like Daityas, who obtained the stone for the Gaurī-temple from the hand of Narasakha; who, at the command of Vyāsa, brought about the solidification of the waters of the celestial river by means of his mantra;
and who was saluted by the personified River of Heaven as she emerged through the earth and approached his monastery.
I praise him who effortlessly defeated many youths who had approached him simultaneously. || 20 ||

I take refuge in him whose deeds were proclaimed as auspicious: he who shattered the claims of heaven by his commentary, who formerly shone in battle as the conqueror of all disputants; who, honored by the Wielder of the Trident (Śiva), manifested weapons before his disciples; who was sometimes perceived directly as the teacher of a thousand [disciples] while subsisting on water; and who, through his virtuous singing, instantly caused flowers and other offerings to appear. || 21 ||

May he—who, having heard the commentary from the sages, declared according to the agreement that the Lord of Serpents (Śeṣa) shall attain Vaikuṇṭha, the palace of the Lord of Lakṣmī made of golden jewels and free from all defects;
and who is incomparably resplendent with Brahmā and others, who possess the vision of the Master and enjoy union with Him, partaking in the delights of beautiful women—grace us abundantly. 22.

May we be the servants of the servants of that lion among Vedāntins, who—having conquered Kurava and Puṇḍarīka, who were filled with great pride by the lords of the Māyins and Asuras through various fallacious arguments—delivered a discourse of universal wonder, which others, attempting to rival it in their own compositions, became objects of ridicule among the assembly of the best of the twice-born. (23)

May that Hari, known as Viśvajña, who triumphs in the world, grant us victory— He who, having encountered the king of Sindhu named Padma, who had committed the greatest offense against His beloved people and was instantly driving others before Him from his own home with herds of cattle for no reason, caused the deceitful Daityas to flee with their hearts shattered by the arrows of His words.

Through association with the feet of Śrīkānta, he became exceedingly pure and auspicious, just as the Ganges' current becomes so through contact with the feet of the King; his feet and other limbs were lovely, endowed with a multitude of all virtues;
he was pleasing to behold for all, born of the Likuca lineage, and a knower of the Vedas, scriptures, and so forth.
I praise that noble one, the teacher of all, named Ānanda-tīrtha, who attained [the state of] the stride of Yuga through his power; (I bow to Ānanda-tīrtha). || 25 ||
Having mastered the scriptures and being highly praised here by Likucakavi,
he spent his days performing only various auspicious deeds for the increase of the Lord’s affection;
free from worldly taints and having burnt away his karma through his intellectual and artistic endeavors, he acted thus to provide instruction to the world.
May he who has rays of nectar showered by the gods, who is skilled in the teaching (or devoted to the teaching), grant me the gift of being a speaker. || 26 ||

Having bathed, the preceptor— holding a conch and a drum and having properly worshipped Viṣṇu with excellent *tulasī* according to the injunctions of the Tantras— should then be worthy of being beheld; and after eating,
he who delights various worlds should perform the evening rites with a radiant exposition.
Having performed [this], let him who narrates the pastimes of Govinda indeed cause us to hear the Vaiṣṇava story. || 27 ||

Hari, whose infinite virtues are worthy of praise, who is the sole object of knowledge for the Vedas, and who is the creator of the universe— He who bestows upon His devotees liberation characterized by auspicious bliss—
having thus established this through sound reasoning supported by hundreds of scriptural citations and having defeated the son of the Sage (Śuka), [Vedavyāsa]...
May Pūrṇaprajña, its commentator, nourish me daily with his exposition. 28.
The author of a hundred works composed a commentary on the *Sāmatantra* based on the *Traivikramāryā*,
made his own detached elder brother Viṣṇutīrtha a monk endowed with great virtues,
and [established] Padmanābha, a lord of disputants, as well as other dear disciples of excellent qualities who were worthy of praise.
He who, while residing near Kaṇvatīrtha, conquers even many virtuous householders. || 29 ||
He who, at the end of an instant, dispelled the pride of Veda-māna while supporting the medicinal herbs;
he whose finger was radiant as he split the mountain with his ear-cavity; he who is praised for having solidified the ocean;
and he who, with a single finger, was unable to move the two temples of Gaṇḍavāṭa, which were marked by incomparable strength.
Or perhaps Prāgvāṭa Vaṭūḍha, with not even a single hair on his body that could be grasped, shall shine forth in my mind.
Rejoicing in the Lord of Pāraṇtī, he immediately caused rain within the rivers;

during the summer, he made even his enemies his friends; having gone to Vaidyanātha for his own prosperity, he was a proponent of the meaning of the *Chandaḥkhaṇḍa* and a subduer of the host of evil-minded ones, remaining indifferent to the envy of the wicked.
Even a small amount of food will nourish the wealthy man, though he may eat much; yet he shall be satisfied with even a very little. (31)

Proclaimed as the controller of rain and other phenomena, praised by all the jewels of the gods and the Gandharvas in the celestial assembly, and approached with curiosity by all those dwelling in heaven;
being seen and extolled, and showered with flowers from the celestial trees, this noble Madhva blazes forth and triumphs in the world for the auspiciousness of the assemblies of the virtuous. (32)
He, whose valor is tenfold, composed the work titled *Sumadhvavijaya*— which is like gold in its manifold nature— and the one called *Bhāvadīpa*; furthermore,
he produced this *Prameyanavamālikā*, which is skillful and honored.
This Nārāyaṇa has fashioned an ear-ornament for the virtuous. || 33 ||
(Thus ends the *Aṇumādhavavijaya*, composed by Nārāyaṇa Paṇḍitācārya, son of the venerable Trivikrama Paṇḍitācārya, the ornament of the assembly of poets.
May it be offered unto Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who resides within the Supreme Breath, the delighter of Sarasvatī.)
I [shall recite] the sixteen cantos of the *Śrīmadhvavijaya* in their proper sequence, [which is titled] *Sumadhvavijayaprameyaphalamālikā*.
I shall explain their objects of knowledge as well as their results in brief. || 1 ||
The three supreme forms of Vāyu described in the hymn beginning with "balitthā" are as follows:
the first is declared in the first [verse], and the second is [declared] after that. || 2 ||

When the true scriptures were corrupted by the wicked, [the Lord] descended at the request of the gods and by the command of Hari; herein are the excellent stories of His childhood in His second [incarnation]. (3)
Well-guided by his father through proper methods, he studied many Vedas from a twice-born man in a mere moment; this is what was told in the third [chapter]. (4)
Having entered the fourth stage of life, he became devoted to the Vedānta;
he taught his disciples, ensuring that the tradition was not lost.
By making known that the commentary composed by Māyī was flawed, and indicating the defects of that [work], he defeated his opponent with the subsequent commentary. || 6 ||
Displaying various miraculous deeds here and there,
he traveled through all the sacred fields and beheld the Himavat mountain.
Honoring the chief preceptor Vyāsa within the sky of his heart with his mind,
he beheld him there with his physical eyes as well, surrounded by hosts of sages.
Having paid homage to Nārāyaṇa who resides there along with his preceptor,
and having been permitted by them both, he departed to compose this commentary for the delight of the virtuous.
Having heard the scripture from the mouth of Vyāsa at another location, he then departed and composed a commentary that refutes twenty-one erroneous commentaries.
Just as the narration of Hari’s deeds brings joy to the wise, so too did he perform his own most wonderful exploits. (11)
When the time for exposition arrived, he of perfected intellect showed the king of serpents to his disciples and then spoke of its significance.
Having shattered the illusory circle, which brings many calamities, within his own circle, he of unbroken power shone like an undivided sovereign. || 13 ||
Having thus conquered the host of magicians, renowned throughout the circle of the earth,
the lion among poets bowed down to that Jayasiṃha who had summoned him.
With his mind always filled with devotion for the lotus feet of Śrī Hari, he—possessed of wisdom and ever happy—performs his bathing, teaching, eating, and other daily duties every day. (15)
Having been defeated in debate by Pūrṇaprajña, the commentator on the Brahma-sūtras, he became his disciple and composed the *Tattva-dīpikā* (commentary) upon that [work]. || 16 ||
When he had accomplished his task, all the deities, remaining in the sky, joyfully showered a rain of flowers upon the Omniscient One while intent on offering praise. (17)
Proximity, the manifestation of qualities, the awakening of one's true nature, fame through excellent means, and the consecration to the kingdom of the scriptures. || 18 ||
The ejection of discursive thought is the awakening to the nature of the object of knowledge;
it is the excellence of worship and the firmness of devotion toward Hari and the Guru. (19)

The attainment of all that is desired, the ease with which the scriptures on liberation are mastered, the destruction of obstacles to spiritual practices, and the realization of one’s own greatness. || 20 ||
The destruction of obstacles for one who perceives directly, the granting of that [perception], and the bestowing of liberation—this is declared to be the sixteenfold supreme fruit. (21)
Thus, in the *Sumadhvavijaya*, this "Garland of the Fruits of the Objects of Cognition" has been composed by the mendicant; may it rest upon the chest of Viṣṇu. 22.
Thus ends the *Prameyaphalamālikā*, a commentary on the *Sumadhvavijaya* composed by the venerable Anūru Viṣṇutīrtha.
May this work be offered to Śrī Kṛṣṇa, who dwells within the Supreme Breath (Mukhyaprāṇa) and is the Beloved of Sarasvatī.
